text:
At the outset of my contribution to debate on the Greyhound Racing Prohibition Bill 2016, I acknowledge the good people in the gallery who have been here since before question time. They have been very patiently listening to this debate. I congratulate them and welcome them to the Parliament of New South Wales. Labor will always stick with you. I do not support the Greyhound Racing Prohibition Bill 2016 and I will be voting against it. It is surprising that an ideological party of the centre 
right would produce such legislation. It is surprising that any Liberal or member of The Nationals would support and vote for it. The Deputy Premier is present at the table. I recently visited Orange and Mudgee and I 
know that the local community is opposed to the bill. 
This bill intends to give effect to the shutdown of the greyhound racing industry in New South Wales from 1 July 2017. It uses the coercive powers of the State to ban an entire industry with the stroke of a fountain pen. Philosophically it violates freedom of association, freedom of action and the principle of property ownership. These are all philosophical principles one would expect those opposite to defend. By supporting and voting for this bill, Coalition members are happily abandoning the very philosophical ideology they claim to hold dear. This bill is a social media creation. There is no doubt that this bill is clickbait for Facebook likes and Twitter retweets. 
It is a diversion from the range of problems besetting the Government, such as rising household electricity prices and the hospital crisis where $3 
billion in budget cuts is now impacting through the sad death of infants and diluted chemotherapy treatment. It is a diversion from the cost blowouts in the Government's infrastructure projects such as WestConnex, from community fury over forced council amalgamations, and from the failed sell‑off of the second tranche of poles and wires. Both the Coalition and the Opposition know it; even the member for Kiama knows it. 
It is an attempt by Coalition political strategists to attract so-called progressive voters, the very voters who in ordinary circumstances are opposed to each of the Government decisions I just referred to. I have read the commission of inquiry report published by former Justice Michael McHugh. The world-famous Dapto Dogs is based at the Dapto Showground in my electorate. Every Thursday greyhound race meetings are held there. It is one of 34 greyhound racing facilities across the State. There are 44 small businesses associated with the Dapto 
Dogs that will be directly affected by this bill. I note the Parliamentary Secretary for the Illawarra and the South Coast is present in the Chamber and listening to this debate. There are 15 charity and community groups that will be directly affected by this bill. 
Full-time, part-time and regular casual employees will lose their jobs at the Dapto Dogs because of this bill. The Government's legislative response to the McHugh report is premature. As I have previously stated, there was no consultation by the Government before the Premier and Deputy Premier convened a press conference in Sydney to announce the shutdown of the industry. Prior to making that announcement, it would not have been difficult for the Premier and the Deputy Premier to contact the members in this place who have greyhound racing facilities in our electorates to seek our recommendations. I am sure that those of us with facilities in our communities would have given the Government the same message  No, you are not to shut down greyhound racing in our communities based on present information. 
We would have said, "Reform the industry and give it time to implement the changes recommended in the McHugh report." But no, the Government's kneejerk reaction was to dictate otherwise. None of us would have recommended taking the extreme arbitrary decision that has been made and that is reflected in this bill. The McHugh report concludes that the greyhound racing industry has made significant changes to its governance culture and animal welfare practices since the revelations aired in the ABC'sFour Corners program. These reforms have been completely ignored by the Government and by animal welfare advocates. As a member in this place I am disappointed and offended that the Government has usurped the very first recommendation of the McHugh report that stated that the Parliament's role to determine the future of the greyhound racing industry is not primarily the role of the Executive—that is, the Premier and the Deputy Premier. 
We should have a frank and full debate about the future of this industry, and the report should have been tabled on the floor of this House. The Government should have set aside time for this frank debate and given every member the opportunity to contribute to that debate. It is not beyond our collective wit as elected representatives to have a full debate and to make a contribution on how the future of the greyhound racing industry is to proceed. Indeed, the McHugh report outlined a further 79 recommendations on how this could and should be achieved if the Parliament and not the Executive concluded that the greyhound racing industry should continue to operate. 
The Greens representatives in this place go on and on about the primacy of the Parliament when it suits them, have given the Executive the right to trample all over members of this place. The Government has conveniently ignored the first key recommendations of the McHugh report. I consider that the 79 
recommendations foreshadowed in the report for the reform of the greyhound racing industry provide more than a reasonable foundation for the continuation and the reform of the practices for the governance of the industry. Indeed, the Opposition has adopted these recommendations in its Greyhound Racing Amendment (Greyhound Racing Integrity Commission) Bill 2016, which was recently introduced into this House by the shadow Minister for Racing. 
The McHugh report has also highlighted a number of unacceptable practices in the greyhound racing industry. No-one can condone instances of animal cruelty, but the report since its release has been subject to sustained criticism in the evidence presented to it, including the statistics used for many of its assumptions and the reliability of some witnesses. These are very serious matters when it comes to the foundation of the commission's inquiry report and the subsequent decisions made by the Government as reflected in this bill. 
Commissions of inquiry are meant to get to the bottom of matters of controversy. Inquiry reports are meant to get to the truth; they are meant to be factually based. The findings are meant to be beyond contention. This is not the case with this commission of inquiry—in fact, far from it being factual it has become engulfed in controversy and disagreement. Many of its findings have been subject to substantial contention and criticism. Respected sports commentator Rebecca Wilson published comments in theDaily Telegraph on 16 July. [Extension of time] 
Rebecca Wilson said in theDaily Telegraph  
I HAPPILY jumped on board the anti-greyhound bandwagon last week. I wrote a couple of paragraphs supporting NSW Premier, Mike Baird, claiming extreme cruelty to animals was unacceptable and, given this whole industry is apparently beyond reform, I 
was happy to wipe it. 
Now I'm not so sure and nor should anyone else be … 
Now I know better. There are grey areas and I know there is a lot, lot more to this story than what a few animal activists have insisted we believe. 
Ms Wilson went on to say  
The Baird Government cannot ignore what they've ignored to this point  that some of the evidence was biased; some came from overseas and not this state; the witnesses included people from animal welfare lobbies … and that innocent, decent hard workers are about to lose absolutely everything. 
The commission of inquiry indicated that the greyhound racing industry cannot change. However, its report finds otherwise. It clearly finds that the greyhound racing industry has changed over the past 12 to 15 months. It says explicitly  
The Commission accepts that GRNSW today is not the organisation that it was as at February 2015. Under the leadership of Mr 
Paul Newson, the interim Chief Executive— 
who is here tonight— 
GRNSW has undergone significant change, most of it for the better. 
The former Board and some management employees are no longer with GRNSW. The management structure itself has been radically changed. GRNSW now has a Leadership Group that appears to be capable of governing and managing the industry as well as it can be governed and managed. 
On animal welfare the report says  
Achieving appropriate animal welfare outcomes is no longer a mere aspiration of GRNSW, which it was to an extent as at February 2015. 
Animal welfare outcomes are now the driving force behind GRNSW's activities. No longer can it be argued that, under its present management, the commercial interests of GRNSW trump animal welfare interests. Furthermore, GRNSW now recognises that its stakeholders go beyond industry participants and includes the wider community including animal welfare groups. 
I note that, overall, the report of the inquiry makes a contrary observation to these findings but the conclusion still stands  That the commission has observed that the greyhound racing industry has changed and continues to change its overall governance and animal welfare practices. I note that the greyhound racing industry has directly contradicted many assertions made in the report of the commission of inquiry. It disputes the assertions in the report on the key issue of wastage, noting that the statistics used in the report are, to be kind, "guesstimates". The 
commission of inquiry notes this too. It says  
The data was not sufficiently robust to allow the Commission to determine the precise number of greyhounds that are destroyed each year in this State. 
The number of greyhounds born in New South Wales has fallen by 46 per cent. Breeding reforms have been implemented nationally since 1 July 2015. I am very concerned that the industry shutdown that will be brought about by this bill will overwhelm existing animal welfare organisations. We are aware from press reports and direct representations to the Government that the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals [RSPCA] and the Australian Veterinary Association [AVA] concede that thousands of greyhounds will need to be—in the Premier's words—"slaughtered" as a result of this industry shutdown. The AVA indicated in a report in theSydney Morning Herald on 12 July that it planned to write to the Deputy Premier pleading for a review of the shutdown decision. The article said  
… what the AVA is concerned about is the welfare of the dogs on the ground right now. What's their future? 
I fear that this industry shutdown will lead to, in the Premier's words, the "slaughter" of thousands of greyhounds. 
It is simply inexplicable that animal welfare supporters are cheering the Government's plan to shut down the industry while knowing that thousands of greyhounds will be slaughtered because of it. They happily applaud the Government's decision, not knowing what the unspecified transition plan will mean. It is a typical social media reaction  Click "like" on Facebook, or retweet on Twitter, and feel the warm inner glow of banning this industry because of cruelty. That is what people will feel, but it is not true. The real impact will be the slaughter of greyhounds—the very greyhounds they assert they seek to protect. It is an appalling, counterintuitive rationale that I find difficult to understand. An editorial in theSydney Morning Herald on 9 July this year lays this bare, stating  
We need to know what happens to the estimated 10,000 unraced, racing and breeding greyhounds whose financialraison d'etre has vanished. Mass euthanasia of those poor dogs would be anathema to Australians … 
But is that right? The RSPCA statistics across the country appear to indicate that Australians do not consider mass euthanasia of animals anathema at all. Over the last five years Australians appeared to be quite content to euthanise all kinds of animals. We have collectively killed or slaughtered 239,451 animals of all species in the last five years. We have killed dogs, cats, cattle, chickens, ducks, geese, goats, pigs, sheep, donkeys, possums, turtles, kangaroos, wallabies, koalas, magpies, doves, ferrets, guinea pigs, mice, pigeons, rabbits and budgerigars. RSPCA figures indicate that in the last financial year alone we killed 40,296 animals in Australia. Does our hypocrisy know no bounds? It seems we will get angry and distressed when we see television reports or social media coverage of animal cruelty, but what is unseen is the killing of nearly 240,000 animals over the last five years. Clearly we can live with that, because what is out of sight is out of mind. 
The Deputy Premier said in his second reading speech that prohibiting greyhound racing in this State does not represent a slippery slope for the banning of other gaming sports involving animals. We should be asking why it does not. There are other examples of underwhelming animal welfare practices in a range of other gaming industries. I am sure that if there were ever a commission of inquiry into thoroughbred racing, it would inevitably uncover practices as disturbing as those in the greyhound racing industry. Why are we targeting only one gaming sport and one species of animal? Why are we banning greyhound racing but not harness or thoroughbred racing? We are not banning the beef, pork, chicken or lamb industries. Each of those industries have faced challenges of appalling animal welfare practices, but we would not dare to touch any of them. This so-called courageous Government would not lay a finger on any of these industries. It certainly would not touch the thoroughbred racing industry in this State. Too many of those wealthy, perfumed donors to the Coalition might get a little upset at election time if the Premier announced a shutdown of the horseracing industry. 
The Government also intends to ban greyhound racing in New South Wales but not interstate gaming on greyhounds. Why not? This Government wants to have a buck each way. I find it incredible that the Government found the time to push out a Facebook post but has not nailed down the details of its transition package for the greyhound industry. Instead it is leaving those details to a task force which is busy scurrying around this State trying to work out what this mess is actually going to cost. That is what they are trying to do. But there are still no details on what or who will be eligible for transition and assistance. It is simply a disgrace that the Government's numbers with the support of the unctuous The Greens will knock off this industry and leave thousands of people and businesses, especially in regional New South Wales, with uncertain futures. This bill has the stench of hypocrisy that hangs on its every word, clause and page. I cannot and will not support its passage.

I refer to the Greyhound Racing Prohibition Bill 2016, a bill which will have a profound impact on the people in the greyhound industry in my electorate and the communities that support greyhound racing. I have thought about these people, the good people in the industry, every day since the ban was announced. I am compelled to be their voice in this place. I cannot support a bill which strips them of their livelihood, of their love for their dogs, and of a sport and entertainment which has been a part of them for decades. I cannot support a bill that shreds the very fabric that makes up the regional community that I am a part of. The dishlickers are as much a part of Grafton as the Bendy Bridge and the Jacaranda Festival. Similarly, in Casino they are as integral as the Beef Week festival or Londy's Cafe. To be true to all these good people and to myself, I have to oppose the bill. As difficult as that is, I will vote against a good Government and sit with the Opposition, who are political opportunists. 
The Australian Labor Party banned the live cattle export and caused damage to the industry. It has harped in this place to pretend to support the greyhound racing industry. Unfortunately, there is no halfway for me in this debate and I choose to be with my constituents 100 
per cent. This is exactly the reason I joined The Nationals. This decision does not reflect the respect that I have for the Premier, the Deputy Premier or the leadership. This has been a very good Government for my electorate. Some $4.34 
billion has been spent on the Pacific Highway in my electorate, $200 
million has been allocated for a Grafton bridge and a 1,700 
inmate jail will create 500 
jobs in my electorate. This is a good Government, but this is a bad decision for my electorate. 
That is not to say that I do not recognise that there has been animal cruelty within the industry and it may still exist in some quarters to this very day. Animal cruelty is as abhorrent to me as it is to every decent person in this State. It should not be tolerated in any form in our society whether it be sport, the pet industry, our natural environment or in animal husbandry. But the fact remains that there is cruelty to animals in our society and it is across the board. Bad people live amongst us, but surely to goodness the good outweigh the bad. If that were not the case, most of us would be, or should be, locked up in jail. The fact is that most people are good people and do the right thing. 
So I ask  Why has this premise not applied to the greyhound racing industry? Why have they all been tarred with the same brush and thrown on the scrapheap? I have read enough of the McHugh report, the rebuttal by the greyhound industry, the rebuttal of the rebuttal, emails supporting and emails opposing the ban, to come to the conclusion that no-one knows the exact number of people who are carrying out live baiting. There is no exact proportion of the wastage in the industry and there is no conclusive evidence that the industry is unsustainable. Quite frankly it is a case of this expert says this, another says something completely contradictory and the people getting screwed are the people in my electorate who love their dogs, love their sport, pay their bills and are an integral part of my community. If the McHugh report is correct in its numbers relating to wastage—that is, 48,000 
to 68,000 dogs euthanised over the past 12 
years, which is totally unacceptable—what does that mean for the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals [RSPCA], which euthanised 58,227 dogs across Australia in five years up to and including the 2014-15 
year? 
Those figures are directly fromRSPCA Australian National Statistics 2014-15. In 2014-15, 3,435 
dogs were euthanised in New South Wales alone. That is aside from the 9,148 cats euthanised in the same period in this State. Why is the pet industry not being subjected to the same scrutiny as the greyhound racing industry? The 
RSPCA statistics for 2014-15 indicate that there were 15,012 animal cruelty complaints and only 62 
prosecutions in New South Wales. I cannot help but believe a similar ratio of successful prosecutions to complaints would exist in the greyhound racing industry. However, the industry is seen as the villain and everyone involved in it is paying the penalty for the actions of the few who have done the wrong thing. If the same social licence standard were applied to other sports and industries that involve animals, they, too, would fail to meet current community expectations, but they are not being singled out for extinction. 
I have two TAB tracks in my electorate, and there are tracks nearby at Lismore, Tweed Heads and, of course, across the border in Queensland. As a consequence, Casino and the surrounding area has become a greyhound racing hub, as has Grafton to a sightly lesser extent. The Richmond Valley Council has completed an economic and social assessment of the impact of the ban. The Casino Greyhound Racing Club has 62 
members and there are more than 120 trainers running more than 1,000 greyhounds in the local postcode area. The council estimates that the ban will result in a total loss of $10.5 million annually to the local government area, the loss of 49 
jobs, and a $2.4 million reduction in wages and salaries. There would be similar losses on a slightly smaller scale in Grafton. 
Like Richmond Valley Council, I am concerned about the devastation that will result from the ban for trainers, owners and breeders who live among us, and the financial loss to the economy that will follow. The electorate of Clarence has a high level of social disadvantage, and we all know that regional jobs are hard to come by. How will people in my community be compensated for the personal tragedy of losing their livelihood, and possibly their house and dogs? The destruction of the industry will have an impact on veterinary services, pet food and rural suppliers, catering and fast food services, fuel stations and other retail outlets. The ban is being imposed without any mention of financial support for individuals or for the local communities that will suffer. 
In this place the legislation is about banning an industry; it is a line item on a Cabinet agenda. In my electorate it is about real people whom I know, and that includes the 16 people who live in caravans at the Grafton greyhound track, who are up to 85 years of age. What will become of them? started out as an animal welfare issue is fast becoming a human welfare issue. There is widespread support for the greyhound racing industry across my electorate, not because everyone is into greyhound racing but because those involved in the industry have not been given a fair go. A 
Salvation Army minister approached me in Grafton at the commemoration of the fiftieth anniversary of the Battle of Long Tan and congratulated me on my support for the greyhound racing industry because he knows about all the good work that those involved in the industry do in the community.

Yes, participants were caught out by theFour Corners report and, yes, they have been warned repeatedly in the past, and those in charge chose to cover up rather than clean up the industry. Yes, they realise that self-regulation has failed. However, the good people in the industry made a determined effort to clean up their act after theFour Corners report. Over the past 18 months they have spent tens of thousands of dollars, if not hundreds of thousands of dollars, on improving their kennels, their tracks, and their testing and compliance regimes. But before the outcome of these reforms could be tested, animal welfare outcomes could be assessed and the community could measure the success or otherwise of the reforms, it was banned. All they want is the same opportunity that has been given to other industries involving animals, such as the thoroughbred racing industry, puppy farms or the chicken industry. They just want to be given a chance like they were in Victoria. 
The Victorian greyhound racing industry was also reviewed but instead of banning racing a decision was made to reform the industry. It undertook serious reform whereby Greyhound Racing Victoria committed $3.5 
million to expand its greyhound adoption program, which is one of the largest in the world and has rehomed around 7,000 
greyhounds to date. It is also working with other greyhound rehoming agencies. It also created new senior integrity animal welfare and legal roles and is putting in place major initiatives to reduce breeding, injury and euthanasia rates and to strengthen greyhound racing clubs as community centres. All the New South Wales industry is asking for is to be given the same consideration as its counterpart in Victoria and to be treated like the other racing codes. It just wants a fair go.

year?

started out as an animal welfare issue is fast becoming a human welfare issue. There is widespread support for the greyhound racing industry across my electorate, not because everyone is into greyhound racing but because those involved in the industry have not been given a fair go. A

Why can it not be given three years to demonstrate that the reforms are working, wastage has been reduced, a whole-of-life program for greyhounds has been developed, injuries during racing have been minimised and cruelty will mean banning for life and/or jail? All they want is the same opportunity that has been given to other industries involving animals, such as the thoroughbred racing industry, puppy farms or the chicken industry. They just want to be given a chance like they were in Victoria. 
The Victorian greyhound racing industry was also reviewed but instead of banning racing a decision was made to reform the industry. It undertook serious reform whereby Greyhound Racing Victoria committed $3.5 
million to expand its greyhound adoption program, which is one of the largest in the world and has rehomed around 7,000 
greyhounds to date. It is also working with other greyhound rehoming agencies. It also created new senior integrity animal welfare and legal roles and is putting in place major initiatives to reduce breeding, injury and euthanasia rates and to strengthen greyhound racing clubs as community centres. All the New South Wales industry is asking for is to be given the same consideration as its counterpart in Victoria and to be treated like the other racing codes. It just wants a fair go.

I begin my contribution by saying how bitterly disappointed I am that the greyhound racing industry has been brought to its knees and finds itself in this position as a result of the practices that have been exposed and that have apparently been occurring for many years. I 
feel particularly aggrieved that the industry has enjoyed my support for many years while I have been a member. I 
have supported funding applications for Community Building Partnership grants, written letters in support of applications to upgrade racing tracks and other facilities, and done whatever I could to support those involved in the industry. 
However, like many Australians, I was shocked when I saw the footage of the abhorrent practice of live baiting. I was sickened by seeing our native fauna tied to a lure and screaming in fear and pain as their guts were ripped out. I said at the time that no reasonable, thinking Australian would say that that practice was acceptable. Of course, that footage shone the spotlight on the industry. A parliamentary inquiry has been undertaken and a special commission of inquiry has produced a report. Like many members, representations have been made to me. I have received 130 pieces of correspondence, mostly from local people, supporting the Government's decision, and 121 opposing it. I have responded in person to most of the callers who have rung my office to express their opposition to this legislation. The first question I ask them is, "Have you read the report?" In most cases the answer is no. I then say that they should read it and that we will discuss it when they have. 
My initial response to this proposal was, "Gee, what on earth are we doing?" However, I did not respond to media questions about the issue until I had read the special commission's report. As I worked my way through it—line by line by line—I found that nine of the 10 witnesses who appeared before the special commission admitted to live baiting. The tenth said, "Your Honour, I've never done that", to which the judge effectively replied, "You're a liar." The others said that it was absolutely necessary. Having examined the testimony, it is very difficult to support the greyhound racing industry. Originally I thought I should support it, but having investigated further and having talked to the people who have come to my office—    One person responded and said, "I disagree with 10 per cent of the report." I 
said, "So you agree with 90 per cent?" He said, "Oh yes, it is definitely occurring, there is no doubt about it, but I disagree with 10 per cent." I am going to vote for this legislation. Importantly, I have said to people who are affected by it that the Government has committed to put forward a package in consultation. I will ensure the affected people get the same access they have had during the discussion since the Government announced this proposal so that their views on the packages can be adequately addressed. Indeed, a lot of effort is going into engaging with the industry to deal with the issues that have been raised about hardship, animal welfare and so on. Those things are important. 
This has not been easy for anyone. No-one has come into this place with the intention of banning greyhound racing. In government, as difficult as it is, we have to deal with things that arise in the course of running the State. Indeed, when the former Government was in power it had to deal with those things too. I understand that sometimes members have to take a position that they may not agree with. In the confines of the party room we have had robust discussions. But we are the Government. People expect us to make decisions and we have made one. It was not easy—they are never easy—and this will not be the last difficult decision that the Parliament has to deal with. We have to consider the ramifications of the decisions made and do our best. 
We must ensure that, like the discussion that happened in the lead-up to this, constituents can write to members and seek appointments to discuss their industry when the package is considered. Of course, it will then be brought to our members so that we can give our input as well. This is a very difficult thing for the Minister, the Cabinet and all of my colleagues to do. We all have to consider the ramifications of these things in our electorates but we have to do what is right. There has been a suggestion that this will lead to other issues with animal husbandry in other industries. May I say that footage of animals with their guts being ripped out is not being broadcast around Australia and/or the world in those industries referred to by members.    That is the  issue and it is what has brought the spotlight onto the greyhound racing industry. As late as last week people told me where you could buy live rabbits. They gave me the address. They also told me where the dogs with their ears cut off were and much more. There has not been a one-way discussion opposing what we are doing. I would have to say there has been a very balanced approach to this from people with information who have been in the industry and who are appalled. I know that a lot of good people will be affected by this. I acknowledge that. But the fact of the matter is this has to end. The cruelty and the cover‑ups have to end. That is what this is all about.

text:
Each and every one of us elected to this place has a solemn duty to represent the views of our community. On an issue such as this our duty is made much more difficult because there are compelling arguments on both sides. I have listened to the good people across the Parliament who have struggled with the implications of supporting or not supporting the Greyhound Racing Prohibition Bill 2016. I believe a debate such as this should be respectful and should consider all the different views because those views depend on experience, location and electorate. I listened respectfully to a number of speakers before reaching my position. I have to fall back on the fact that one of the most important tenets of our Australian society is a fair go. 
Politicians of all persuasions like to evoke those words on a regular basis when talking about the positive character of our community. It is something we cherish and celebrate. Unfortunately, this legislation seeks to end a whole industry. Every trainer, breeder, person who works at the track and supplier who supports the industry will be affected. The industry had only just started a series of reforms to address serious concerns. This legislation takes the almost unprecedented step of not waiting for analysis of those reform attempts but instead ending a whole industry. This legislation brands every person involved in the New South Wales greyhound industry as guilty. It will destroy livelihoods and most probably lives. This legislation marks the death of not just an industry but also the idea of a fair go in New South Wales. 
Let me state unequivocally and unambiguously that I abhor and reject cruelty to animals. That is why it has been so difficult to decide my position on this bill. I will never condone cruelty towards animals. The abhorrent practices of a few in the greyhound racing industry make me sick. Anyone caught breaking the law should be prosecuted to the full extent possible and banned from the industry for life. As members from both sides have said, there is no doubt that the industry needs reforming and it needs effective regulation. Not a single person would argue against that. 
Labor took a strong policy to protect animal welfare in this State to the 2015 State election. It was a policy that covered animal welfare across the board. Labor's approach would allow the New South Wales greyhound industry to reform and continue to exist—it would allow the industry a second chance, but it would also be a last chance. As mentioned by the shadow Minister, the member for Maroubra and Deputy Leader of the Opposition, and by the Leader of the Opposition, Luke Foley, Labor stands for two things on this issue. One is cleaning up the industry and the other is keeping it alive for the vast majority of participants who have only ever done the right thing. 
Labor chooses to work with the industry to protect animals and protect incomes, but at the same time, as has been recognised, to improve standards. Essentially, Labor believes in supporting regional New South Wales while unfortunately the majority of those in the Coalition Government are fixated on inflicting its Sydney-centric view of the world onto the whole State. I am surprised that the Liberal Party in general is standing behind this decision. I have heard several members speak out in the media to raise this exact issue. One of their heroes, Menzies, said  
We took the name 'Liberal' because we were determined to be a progressive party, willing to make experiments, in no sense reactionary but believing in the individual, his rights, and his enterprise, and rejecting the socialist panacea. 
This legislation hits every participant in the industry, whether guilty or not, and flies in the face of Menzies' words about what the Liberal Party stands for. As has been said by many of my colleagues and as outlined in great detail by Labor leader Luke Foley, the Government did not proceed past recommendation 1 of the McHugh report. There were 80 recommendations in that report and there were two options available to the Baird Government. One was to produce legislation which would seek to better regulate the greyhound industry, as the Labor Opposition has done through a private member's bill brought by our shadow Minister, the member for Maroubra and Deputy Leader of the Opposition, and the other, as the Premier has done in this case, without any consultation with his own party room or his Coalition partners, was to outlaw a whole industry. 
Many people who live in my electorate will be adversely affected by this decision. They are devastated by this ban and the way it has been done. The lives of these people and of people from across the State will be irrevocably changed. Make no mistake  Premier Baird is criminalising the livelihood and hobby of thousands of New South Wales residents. As has been stated in this place, they are not glamorous jobs but an honest living for trainers, suppliers, part-time bar workers and showground employees. The Central Coast has a track at Gosford which supports jobs every Tuesday night. It is estimated that almost 700 local industry jobs including breeders, full-time and hobby trainers, kennel staff and race day attendants as well as those who supply the industry with pet food and so on will be lost on the Central Coast. This will cost the Central Coast's economy an estimated $74 
million a year. 
Records show greyhound races were being held at Gosford as long ago as 22 June 1946. Meetings are held every Tuesday. Approximately 200 people, including handlers, officials and punters, attend each race night. The death of greyhound racing will spell the end of decades of races run at the Gosford track, which is operated by the NSW Greyhound Breeders Owners and Trainers Association [GBOTA], the State's biggest club. Across the State, the Baird Government's move to shut down the $335 
million greyhound racing industry will potentially cost several thousand jobs and millions of dollars in annual wagering tax revenue. This will hit many communities across the State, particularly in regional New South Wales. Our leader, Luke Foley, stated the situation correctly when he said  
In no other field of life do we engage in collective punishment to punish all of the good people for the sins of the few, and it's just an overreach here for the Premier to outlaw an entire sport and industry, an industry that employs thousands of people, because of the sins of a few wrongdoers. 
He went on to say  
Let's give that— 
meaning reform— 
a try and, you know, what if it does fail? Well, the industry should be shut down, but it has to be given a chance first, which it hasn't been under the Premier's plan 
… 
Anyone listening to those speakers from the other side who have attacked our leader, Luke Foley, would have concluded that they are making the same argument. The argument they are using is the same argument he is using. As have many of the people who have contacted my office, I have been struck by the unfairness of this process—and, as we have heard, so have several members of the Government. I was particularly struck by the speech of the Hon. 
Peter 
Phelps in the other place, as well as by that of the member for Cootamundra. Their words should be heeded by their colleagues, and I commend them for speaking their mind on difficult legislation. I know that it is not easy—it is a place that I have been. [Extension of time] 
We on this side have been attacked for political opportunism for making these arguments. I wonder whether the same would be said about Michael McCormack, MP, the federal member for Riverina. He was quoted extensively in an article inThe Land on 7 July 2016. The article said  
Mr McCormack said there was no doubt the report was "damning" but rather than shutting down the entire industry, due to a "select few offenders" the NSW Government should have considered tougher regulations before revoking the sport’s "social license". 
He expressed concerns for the loss of economic activity and the employment and social benefits of country greyhound race-tracks in his Riverina electorate like at Temora and the interests of the majority of greyhound trainers who "treat their animals like members of their family". 
Mr McCormack said the NSW government should have conducted proper community and stakeholder consultation before making its shock decision. 
"Decisions made in haste are not good decisions," he said. 
"This decision is far too hasty and will send a shiver down the spine of anyone involved in the beef industry or growing and producing cattle for the live exports market. 
"Which industry will they target next? 
"Where does it start and where does it stop? 
"Will they investigate the trots or shut down thoroughbred racing?" 
"Little by little the minorities are winning and soon we’ll be left with a nation of do-gooders." 
Mr McCormack said he’d spoken to local trainers and industry stakeholders in his electorate and they shared his outrage at the ban being imposed on them 
He said the decision was aimed to appease left-leaning city-centric voters at the expense of those in regional NSW. 
"Keyboard warriors, latte-sipping, long sock-wearing elitists from the north-shore who live life through rose coloured glasses and have never been to a greyhound track, or would not know a greyhound trainer who treats their animals like a member of their own family, are cheering this decision on," he said. 
On Facebook, Mr McCormack said one of his first tasks working as a journalist in Wagga Wagga at The Daily Advertiser in November 1981 was previewing greyhound meetings, covering race-days or nights and penning a weekly column. 
He said across the Riverina he found a group of dedicated, animal-loving people existed who owned, trained and bred greyhounds and "these were hardy souls". 
"They walked their dogs, fed them well and cared for them as though they were part of their family," he said. 
"They looked after them well when the dogs’ racing days were over. 
"Such people received little financial reward from the sport but the money meant little anyway—they did it for the love of it." 
Mr McCormack said the Baird government’s decision would shock the entire racing industry, which had often come under attack from "noisy animal liberationists". 
He said NSW banned jumps racing in 1997 and "disgraceful" anti-racing protests were held each Melbourne Cup and had to be seen to be believed. 
"I do wonder about where we are headed as a society with decisions such as today’s edict," he said. 
"Governments are not there to shut industries down and put in place adjustment packages to ensure participants go on permanent welfare going forward. 
"It is acknowledged there are some involved in dog racing—albeit a very small percentage—who do not act appropriately or in the best welfare interests of greyhounds. 
"But why should the whole industry have to suffer the consequences?" 
Mr McCormack said more regulation was needed but not a blanket ban. 
"Surely tighter, independent and stricter monitoring would have been a better course of action than to forthwith stop a decades-old industry in which the vast majority of its stakeholders are good, honest, decent people who have only ever wanted the best for the dogs in their care," he said. 
I wonder if that is "political opportunism". Mr McCormack’s views accord 100 per cent with the arguments from this side of the House—and also with those of many members of the National Party who have put forward very similar arguments. Greyhound racing will continue in Victoria and Queensland, although Queensland Minister for Racing Grace Grace has said that the industry is on its last chance because of cruelty matters. Victoria's Acting Minister for Racing, Jill Hennessy said  
The Victorian greyhound industry under Bernie Carolan and Alan Clayton has taken great strides in reforming the industry. 
The Government has no plans to ban greyhound racing in Victoria. 
So why is the greyhound industry beyond saving in New South Wales but not in those other States? I acknowledge that in the past there were concerns, but the industry had started to reform. It was only in the early stages and then without warning, via Facebook, the Government announced the end of the industry. As Mr McCormack and many others on the other side of politics have said, this sets a disturbing precedent for this State. I repeat that I detest animal cruelty and support anyone engaged in such activity being prosecuted to the full extent of the law, but what industry will be next? What will happen to the people involved in this industry? 
What will happen to people in my electorate like Noel McCaskie who will lose not only his income but also the great love of his life? Financial compensation is only one consideration. There will be a range of other issues, including mental health issues, that cannot possibly be addressed in any compensation package. In this instance the Government has gone too far. It has attacked us for making this a political issue, but those on the Government benches who oppose the bill have used the same arguments. I acknowledge there are good arguments on both sides, but this bill should not be passed.

As members would know the Central Coast has a greyhound racing track located at Gosford showground. The Greyhound Racing Prohibition Bill 2016 will close that track and deprive the showground of its biggest user. There are 330 members of the Gosford Racing Club and 674 
locals who participate in the affairs of the club. I am advised by Greyhound Racing NSW that $8.7 million of expenditure occurs through the Gosford track. It is appropriate that I speak to this debate on behalf of the Labor Opposition on the Central Coast. I oppose the bill and support Labor's plan on the Central Coast to improve greyhound welfare and general animal welfare across the State. This bill can be traced back to 16 
February 
2015 when the Australian Broadcasting Corporation [ABC] broadcast theFour Corners program entitled "Making a killing" that revealed instances of live baiting in New South Wales, Queensland and Victoria. As the Special Commission of Inquiry into the Greyhound Racing Industry in New South Wales noted  
Hidden cameras captured graphic and disturbing footage of live animals—including rabbits, possums and piglets—being, in effect, mauled and killed by greyhounds at the command of their trainers. The animals were tied to mechanical lures before greyhounds chased, caught and savaged them. 
The act of live baiting, coursing and similar activities are unlawful under section 21 of the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act 1979. The conduct revealed by ABC reporter Caro Meldrum-Hanna had not been discovered by Greyhound Racing NSW, which is deplorable. Nor was it discovered by the RSPCA, and that is regrettable. It 
was discovered by animal rights activists using hidden cameras. Trespass by activists and community groups has often revealed wrongdoing by individuals and businesses, particularly when it comes to the treatment of animals. 
As a society we accept such civil disobedience if it is directed at unlawful or destructive acts by others. There is a direct link between theFour Corners program and the appointment by the Government of the Hon. 
Michael McHugh, AC, QC, on 6 May 2015 to inquire into the greyhound racing industry in New South Wales. The way in which this Coalition Government has reacted to the civil disobedience that exposed live baiting of greyhounds and animal issues is instructive. 
Three bills have come before this House in the past 12 months. These bills represent different and inconsistent responses to animal welfare more generally. These bills are the bill before us now, the Biosecurity Bill 2015 and the Inclosed Lands, Crimes and Law Enforcement Legislation Amendment (Interference) Bill 2016. On the one hand, the information obtained covertly by community groups and activists is used to justify a commission of inquiry into the closure of an industry and the ending of livelihoods. On the other hand, the sort of conduct that led to the information the Premier has relied on to establish the greyhound inquiry has been proscribed and declared reckless. The Biosecurity Bill 2015 has declared animal rights activists to be biosecurity risks. It creates a new offence of failing to discharge a biosecurity duty with a maximum penalty of three years imprisonment and/or a fine of more than $1 million. 
The Inclosed Lands, Crimes and Law Enforcement Legislation Amendment (Interference) Bill 2016 creates an aggravated form of offence of unlawful entry on inclosed land when that land is used for a business purpose and an increased penalty for doing so of more than $5,000. After reducing the ability of animal rights activists and others to reveal animal rights abuse, what has this Government done to bolster the enforcement powers of those whose job it is to police the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act 1979? The answer is not much. Police powers under the Act have not been enhanced by this Government. I note that the McHugh report recommends that they be significantly improved, but the Government has ignored that part of the report. The heavy lifting of animal welfare policing in this State is still primarily the job of a charity, the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals [RSPCA]. This Government has no welfare plan for animals in this State beyond this narrow gesture by the Premier. 
Greyhounds arrived in New South Wales on the First Fleet. Greyhound racing in the modern form was first introduced to New South Wales in 1927, when the first mechanical tin hare race meeting was held at Harold Park racecourse. The Labor Government of Jack Lang legalised greyhound racing in 1931 with the Finance (Greyhound Racing Taxation) Act. The McHugh report of the Special Commission of Inquiry into the Greyhound Racing Industry in NSW was delivered to the Government on 16 June this year. The first recommendation of the report was that the Parliament of New South Wales should consider whether the industry has lost its social licence and should no longer be permitted to operate in New South Wales. That is followed by a further 79 
recommendations aimed at maintaining and reforming the industry to reduce the number of greyhound deaths. 
The Premier immediately ignored the body of the recommendations and without reference to Parliament announced closure of the industry. This bill, introduced to the Legislative Council on 10 August, is the result. The 
object of this bill is to close the greyhound racing industry in New South Wales on 1 July 2017. There are some details not dealt with by the bill, and I refer to the second reading speech of the Deputy Premier delivered on 11 
August, in which he said  
Placing a bet in New South Wales on a greyhound race conducted in another jurisdiction will not be prohibited. The keeping of greyhounds for racing in New South Wales will be prohibited from 1 July 2017. This will not prohibit people owning greyhounds as companion animals, nor will it stop people from keeping greyhounds for the purpose of racing interstate. 
[Extension of time] 
The Government's position is that this industry, which is so bad and incapable of redemption that it must be closed, will, however, be allowed to keep its dogs as long as they race in another State. The Government appears not to have a plan for the welfare of those dogs in the meantime, yet people will be able to continue to have a bet on this "horrific industry", to use the Premier's words, as long as the race is not held in New South Wales. It is not a good plan for animal welfare. I have been contacted by a number of people from my electorate and further afield who are involved in the industry. 
Lee French, a greyhound owner in Bateau Bay in my electorate, lives with her 90-year-old mother. She 
has three dogs, two of which she races. I had a long conversation with her and her mother. These are people whose livelihood is based on their dogs. They are not involved in any wrongdoing, yet they will be unfairly affected by this heavy-handed bill. I was contacted by Phil Morgan, who resides in Newcastle. I knew Phil over five years when he was the union delegate for storemen at OneSteel's warehouse in Newcastle, next to the steelworks. We did not talk about greyhounds; frankly, it is not something that I am particularly interested in. Phil 
was a man whose word one could trust. He was honest and level-headed. He was a leader in his workplace and negotiated with his employer on behalf of his colleagues. I had a long conversation with him about this industry. He is not the sort of person to be involved in any wrongdoing. His livelihood and his pastime in retirement will be wiped out by this bill. 
I 
acknowledge my constituents who have written to me about this matter. I appreciate the strongly held views on either side of the argument. I undertake to write to each of them to let them know how I voted today and my reasons for voting the way I did. There is much more we can do to improve animal welfare in this State. This bill will do nothing to improve the welfare of the more than two million animals in New South Wales that are killed every year for medical research, experiments and surgical training. It will do nothing to protect livestock from cruelty. The RSPCA says there is still much we can do to improve the welfare of livestock in this country. This bill will do nothing for the welfare of caged hens. The RSPCA found just the other week that the poor welfare of battery hens is caused by their cages and cannot be overcome. It is said that Australia is falling behind the developed world in failing to end their use. 
The legislation will do nothing for the more than 24,000 dogs and cats euthanised in this State last year. A similar number will be euthanised in the coming year because we in the community do not care enough for animal welfare. The legislation will not stop horses being whipped at horseraces. It will not stop puppy farms. It 
will do nothing to improve the job prospects of people on the Central Coast. Only a Labor government has a plan for animal welfare in New South Wales. The endeavours of this House should be more properly directed to the welfare of all animals. We can progress animal welfare in a better way than through this narrow bill, this gesture by the Premier, who is a man of gestures but no depth. He has no feeling for the livelihoods of hundreds of people in this State.

text:
It is extraordinary to be here tonight debating the Greyhound Racing Prohibition Bill 2016. The die has been cast and the numbers have come up, so very little will change based on the merits of this debate. If nothing else, bringing this matter to a head today and having it completed tonight will bring about certainty for all sides of the debate. Those who support the bill will have the certainty that in time greyhounds will not be subjected to cruel practices and animals such as cats, possums, rats and others will also not be subjected to cruelty from greyhound racing, at least not in New South Wales. Those who staunchly oppose the bill will have their lives changed as they lose their hobby and employment. Many will lose not only their income but also their financial investment in an industry they thought would be ongoing. 
I have read the report of the special commission of inquiry. As a matter of fact, I read it while on holiday with my grandchildren. It was a harrowing thing to do. I have spoken to many opponents as well as supporters of the bill. I formed an early position that I would lean towards supporting the Government, though I always had strong concerns about the process. The issue has divided the community and it is my guess that, given the option of business as usual or a complete closure of the industry, the community would overwhelmingly support the closure. Given a middle option as provided for in the recommendations of Justice McHugh, most seem to support significant changes and greatly increased regulation. For the record, I am not and never have been keen on greyhound racing or, for that matter, horseracing. It is many years since I attended a race, although I used to as a young man. Do I believe that greyhound racing in itself is wrong? No, I do not. 
Indeed, these dogs love to run, and chasing or racing is a natural behaviour—a natural behaviour relied on by the industry and one that has, unfortunately, been gamed and exploited by some. As I have mentioned, I 
have deep concern about the process of this decision. At least some Government members—some of whom have spoken in this debate—are very upset by being trapped in a position due to an announcement of great magnitude on social media without the courtesy of consideration by the party room. It 
would have been great if this was brought from the Cabinet to Government members, the Opposition and the crossbench without a pre-determined outcome. It is a conversation that should have been had. I note the presence at the table of the Deputy Premier and I pay respect to him. He knows I respect him, but I have to say that this was an opportunity for this Government to change the paradigm of how business is done. 
I hear the Premier, whom I also respect, saying to the Opposition that this is an opportunity to be bipartisan. How can anyone be bipartisan if they are not brought into the tent? That is not how bipartisan agreements come about. They are not about somebody making an announcement and then the Opposition falling in line. It does not work that way. So I am not surprised that the Opposition took an alternative approach. Of 
course, that approach was very similar in that in a very short time a decision to oppose was taken. However, 
I 
think that the Opposition possibly came up with a more nuanced and better outcome in the proposed bill of the Deputy Leader of the Opposition. I truly believe that this could have been an opportunity to change the way we do business in this House. But then it would be great if greyhounds were not bred for gaming or viewed by some as a commodity. That is just my personal opinion—it is just how I feel. 
It is impossible to separate the issue of greyhound welfare from money and from gambling. Clearly the more money on offer, the higher the likelihood that someone will look for an edge by way of doping, blooding or perhaps other measures—just to get that extra edge. I have no doubt that the growth of the industry—with its demand for dogs to service the many tracks, meets and races and the money involved—has been a factor in bringing us to this point. On that I have to ask  Where have successive governments and respective responsible Ministers been for many years? They have also failed the industry and the community. How has it got to this point without their knowledge or more direct interest? This bill, in closing down an industry, will have far-reaching ramifications on the lives of many people—not just trainers and breeders but also vets, ground attendants, track workers, those who like to own a dog or two, those who enjoy the spectacle and those in associated industries such as pet and racing suppliers. 
Clearly the greyhound racing industry has been plagued by a shocking litany of abuses over many years. Equally I have no doubt that there are many people working in the industry who have not only always followed the letter of the law but also cared for their dogs beyond the minimum requirements of the rules and regulations. The report of the special commission of inquiry, the McHugh report, confirmed many of my long-held views about the greyhound industry. It is an industry that clearly has a dark side to it that many knew about, even those who did not participate in reprehensible activity. The commission of inquiry has shone a light on the industry's very serious shortcomings over many decades and cast considerable doubt on its ability to overcome those shortcomings in the future. It did not, however, sign the death warrant for the industry. We are doing that tonight. 
I have had many conversations with greyhound industry groups over the past month. I understand and accept that their efforts are well intentioned, but in some ways they have come frustratingly too late. We should not have had to wait for theFour Corners report, the McHugh report or the Government to get to this point. As 
an industry, it has failed in so many ways, particularly the body most would have thought could be relied upon—that is, Greyhound Racing 
NSW. How wrong we were. A large part of this industry knew of its dark underbelly. These people, who knew what was happening but did not speak out or take action, are also to blame for the grubs in the industry getting away with things which are clearly outside the realms of social acceptability and outside the law—those actions that saw the industry lose its social licence. 
Having said that, I believe the industry is likely salvageable. I believe it has reached a point where it has displayed a genuine desire to reform and take the drastic measures needed, even if that has come about as a measure of self-preservation. Greyhounds like to run. Exploiting natural behaviour for our amusement and gaming purposes in ways highlighted by the McHugh report is, however, more questionable and goes to the difference between this industry and others that also experience wastage. Many figures are being used, and contested, by both sides of the debate to support their arguments, but the Greyhound Racing Industry Alliance has given me an undertaking that it could reduce the number of dogs bred each year to 2,000, down from the current 6,000 
estimated by Commissioner McHugh. [Extension of time] 
If the industry were to survive, there would need to be total life cycle management of all greyhounds. I 
note that the industry did introduce such a system for all dogs bred from 2015 onwards. In my opinion, the industry has grown too big, with too many tracks and too many meets requiring too many dogs to be whelped each year to service the racing schedule. I believe every dog whelped should have a reasonable expectation that it will be able to see out its natural life. That would also mean that tracks and procedures in racing should change to reduce track-borne injury. With reduced races and dogs racing for longer—that is, perhaps, age group racing—the number of dogs needed should allow for all to be rehomed for their retirement. If that cannot be done, the industry should be closed down. 
Animal cruelty has no place in our society and we need the best regulation and supervision possible to eradicate it altogether. There should be zero tolerance for the barbaric acts shown byFour Corners. There needs to be ongoing cultural reform within the industry and harsh penalties for those who breach the code of practice, and all costs associated with that reform should be drawn from wagering revenue. I accept that Commissioner 
McHugh has made a number of changes to his initial report following responses from those in the greyhound industry. After discussions with some of those industry representatives and local enthusiasts, I also accept that some of the figures used in his report are not as clear-cut or as accurate as they may have first appeared. I speak on behalf of The Greens on the Greyhound Racing Prohibition Bill 2016. I appreciate the considered discussion that has been had in the House this evening. I 
acknowledge the difficult decision members are making, particularly those who intend to cross the floor, because I know that it has involved a great deal of heartache. I have had the pleasure of having Wentworth Park Sporting Complex in my electorate, which has been used as a greyhound racing track. I have visited the complex and I 
have fond memories of greyhound racing. My father worked in a car wrecking yard for many years, and his colleagues' oft-spoken refrain was that one should never trust any race involving a jockey. I will always remember their support for the greyhound racing industry and their affection for the dogs. 
More recently we have been witness to revelations about the endemic and systemic problems in the industry. That is not only a failure of the industry but also of government. Members have mentioned the special commission of inquiry report, which was tabled on 16 June. The key findings are very difficult reading. Those who have read the report would acknowledge the harrowing detail it provides. It states that of the 97,783 
greyhounds bred in the past 12 years, between 48,891 and 68,448 were killed because they were deemed uncompetitive as racing dogs. That equates to a wastage rate of between 50 per cent and 70 per cent. The report also states that by reducing the number of races to the minimum required for the industry to remain viable—that is, 593 races—at that wastage rate, between 2,000 and 4,000 dogs would be killed prior to reaching racing age each year. 
The report also indicates that the evidence of live baiting goes back to as early as 2009. The commission concluded that there is endemic support for the practice and that Greyhound Racing NSW knew about it but effectively did nothing. Deaths and injuries also went unreported to Greyhound Racing NSW, even after aFour Corners report broadcast in February 2015 exposing live-baiting practices and the establishment of the special commission. I 
now draw members' attention to the history of the greyhound racing industry. People ask why this industry is different from other industries. I can detail a history of ongoing noncompliance, corruption, scandal, and animal cruelty. Dr John Kaye gave a speech in 2012 in the other place noting that corruption, scandal and animal cruelty were endemic to the industry. 
He spoke of the overwhelming evidence that the industry was unwilling and unable to address those problems and neither Labor nor Liberal governments were prepared to intervene. He presented a history of corruption and cruelty in the industry that dated as far back as 1995 when allegations of corruption and doping finally brought about the well-known Independent Commission Against Corruption [ICAC] investigation in August 2000 that found corrupt behaviour, including by the chief steward and five other people. A number of individuals were charged, yet there were no broad-ranging and systemic reforms to really transform accountability and probity within the industry in order to eradicate doping and corruption or to reduce the toll of the thousands of dogs that were euthanised each year. 
I also note that it got worse in 2009. Why was 2009 significant? That is when Labor introduced its legislation that effectively privatised the regulation of the greyhound industry and created the autonomous, independent body Greyhound Racing 
NSW. That removed the much-needed direct government oversight and also removed the ability of the Independent Commission Against Corruption to expose corruption in the industry. In hindsight, we can now see how lacking Greyhound Racing 
NSW has been as a self-regulating body, but do not accept just my word for it. 
Members may recall that former Ombudsman and Chief Magistrate of New South Wales David Lander resigned as the integrity commissioner for Greyhound Racing NSW, saying in 2012, "Nowhere in the world would the gaming industry be allowed to self-regulate like this." The 2009 decision by the former Government to effectively privatise the regulation of greyhound racing let down not only the people of New South Wales but also the industry. That has led to this industry failing to act. When more allegations of animal abuse surfaced in 2013 a parliamentary inquiry was formed with Dr John Kaye as Deputy Chair. In tabling the final report, Dr 
Kaye stated  
The reality from the submissions and the evidence presented to the committee is that a large number of animals end up in appalling conditions. From the admissions of Greyhound Racing NSW, at least 3,000 dogs each year are killed before they reach their natural age of death because of massive overbreeding in the industry. This industry has failed time and again to get control of breeding more animals than are needed for the racetrack. This industry has failed to deal with the simple processes of genetics and has opted for large numbers of breeding events, rather than trying to reduce the number of breeding events and increase the rate of animals suitable for racing. 
Dr Kaye went on to say  
... reforms flagged by the Baird Government will fail to address inherent conflicts of interest created by the single body being both regulator and promoter. What will emerge is a body that still has little accountability and virtually no transparency. Greyhound Racing 
NSW will continue to operate well outside basic expectations of animal welfare, integrity and fairness to participants in the industry. 
That is at the heart of the crisis in the industry. It is clear that the industry has endemic and deep-seated problems that have been made worse by government inaction and decisions as well as the failures of the industry. I refer in particular to the ICAC investigation and the recommendations of corruption charges as well as the animal welfare issues. I must also highlight my concern about the Labor Opposition's position on this bill. We know that it is a controversial issue, but I feel this is complete opportunism by Labor because the position of the Leader of the Opposition was clear in the animal welfare industry. He has not said, "I have looked at the evidence. I thought we should ban it but now I have changed my mind." The position he has taken lets down the community and all those who care about animal welfare. 
I have taken this matter up in my electorate by issuing an open letter asking people for their support. I acknowledge that the way it was done came as a shock to them, but I take what the Premier said at face value that he and the Government leadership were so horrified by the report that they felt they had to act. I also acknowledge that people who have approached me with concerns feel that there is a lack of certainty around the transition plan. 
Of course I urge the Government to expedite that plan, but the bottom line is that we believe and we think the evidence supports that this industry cannot be allowed to continue. On that basis we support the Government's bill and we acknowledge that the years and years of work to try to achieve industry reform have failed. We acknowledge that the parliamentary inquiry, the Independent Commission Against Corruption investigations and the special commission report all identified the key problem. Based on the evidence gathered, the key recommendation from the report was  
Given the findings of the Commission concerning the management and governance of the greyhound racing industry, the Parliament of New South Wales should consider whether the industry has lost its social licence and should no longer be permitted to operate in NSW. 
So we are here today having this debate, and it is disappointing that we have to have it. This debate will have far-reaching ramifications for many in the industry, but we believe the time for this debate has come. The industry has been on notice for many years but it failed to act. Sadly, governments of both political persuasions have failed effectively to regulate the industry not only for the prevention of animal cruelty but also to protect against corruption. On that basis The Greens will be supporting the Government's legislation and look forward to the transition in the future which will ensure that people in the industry are well supported, that places such as Wentworth Park are open to the community for public participation, and that animal welfare is at the centre of any government decisions rather than seen as waste or a by-product of a gaming industry.
