I speak in debate on the Greyhound Racing Prohibition Bill 2016. I too acknowledge those in the gallery who have been here since 2 o'clock this afternoon listening to us debate this important topic. When I was younger, I was a student at the University of Wollongong.    The member for Lane Cove also went there. It is a great university. I used to do my electives at Dapto High School. One Thursday night we decided to go to the Dapto dogs for a bit of fun. A few members have spoken about the Dapto dogs. Although it was a good night out, it was the only time I went to the dogs. However, on that particular night I saw some wonderful things; I saw the community come together. I was a visitor on this occasion, but I could feel the strong sense of community at the Dapto dogs. In many ways it became a touchstone for those people because it was their one outing for the week that gave them a chance to touch base with others. If we want to talk about building communities, then we should start with community events. I experienced a community event on that Thursday night at the Dapto dogs. 
All members acknowledge that animal cruelty is abhorrent and no-one condones it in any shape or form. The Labor Party made it clear that it will stand up for two things  We want to see the industry cleaned up but, most importantly, we want to see it kept alive so that the vast majority of people who are doing the right thing are not punished for the actions of a few. Like me, many of my colleagues read Justice Michael McHugh's report on the Special Commission of Inquiry into the Greyhound Racing Industry in NSW, which raised 80 
recommendations. All bar one were ignored. The primary recommendation allowed for a drastic restructure of the industry. The member for Ballina commented that regulation makes a difference, which is the whole idea. Let us regulate greyhound racing instead of it cutting it out completely. Let us give people an opportunity to redeem themselves. 
One recommendation in particular states that the Parliament should consider whether the greyhound industry needs to be banned. That recommendation never made it to Parliament. Instead, an announcement was made on social media, which has been raised by many members. The recommendation was also not made in consultation with members within the confines of Cabinet circles. Many of the other recommendations suggested ways to regulate the industry rather than close it down. Many involved drastic measures but were quite sensible. I will cite a few of the recommendations that I think stand out. Recommendation 2 states  
The Greyhound Racing NSW Rules of Racing should be amended to provide a penalty of disqualification for life for any person found to be involved in the practice of live baiting. 
I definitely do not disagree with that. That has been our position, as we have made very clear. Recommendation 14 states  
The Greyhound Racing Act 2009 (NSW) should be amended to include a provision that requires Greyhound Racing NSW and its stewards to report any serious or repeated breaches of an animal welfare-related rule or standard to RSPCA NSW or the Animal Welfare League. If a new regulator is established this should be included in the Act establishing the new regulator. 
Recommendation 34 states  
The enforceable Code of Practice should require Greyhound Racing NSW or any new regulator as well as industry participants to maintain complete lifecycle records. The record should travel with the greyhound throughout its lifecycle. 
There has been much discussion about self-regulation and that perhaps the Government should be forcing regulation and enabling things to be done in a particular way. Recommendation 65 states  
The regulatory and commercial functions of Greyhound Racing NSW should be separated. A separate regulator, the NSW 
Greyhound Racing Integrity Commission, should be established. It should not be independent of Government but it should be independent of Greyhound Racing NSW. 
That is a pretty sensible recommendation. Most importantly, recommendation 73 (b) states  
[The powers of the NSW Greyhound Racing Integrity Commissioner should include] the power to investigate the conduct of any racing official in respect of the exercise of functions relating to greyhound racing. 
I think that is pretty fair. There are 80 recommendations in the report and the Government chose just one. I have read out just a small selection of recommendations that make sense—things Parliament could achieve with a little courage. I have said that I am not an expert on greyhound racing but I am looking at the bigger picture. We build a redemption factor into every element of our society. For example, schools teach and practice natural justice. I 
struggle to see natural justice in this legislation. Why is natural justice so important? It is because it allows for consequences but in a fair manner. That is what our society is built on. 
There is injustice in this legislation. The commission's report identified that between 10 per cent and 20 
per cent of people involved in the greyhound racing industry have done the wrong thing—some have done abhorrent things. But, according to my calculations, it means that between 80 per cent and 90 per cent have done the right thing. So why are we penalising the whole lot because of the actions of a minority? Eighty per cent to 90 
per cent of people in the industry are being tarred with the same brush. That is what makes the bill unjust and why I talk of natural justice. Collective judgement is wrong. 
Most significantly, this legislation strikes at the very heart of a fair and just society. People have been critical of Labor's position on this issue. We have heard comments from Government members in this place and from different areas across the board—obviously we are open to receiving comments through the mail and via other means—but it is interesting that, of all the accusations, the worst have been about the position we have taken. We have said get the regulation of the industry right, but that has been taken to mean that we support animal cruelty. We do not support animal cruelty. I make that very clear; every one of my colleagues has said we do not support animal cruelty. We support an industry that has an opportunity to regulate and that is given a chance to redeem itself. If someone in the industry does something wrong they should have the book thrown at them; they should be banned for life. But an entire industry should not be shut down in one fell swoop based on a report that, in itself, has a few problems. 
Every sitting week in this place we hear read a petition calling for a ban on the sale of animals in pet shops. The Government has taken no serious position on puppy farming or puppy factories. If the Government were fair dinkum it would be addressing that as well. It would not be addressing one particular issue; it would be addressing the whole lot. The decision to introduce this bill was made without considering that it might be opposed. Sadly, the Premier spoke today about an individual or two who had had bad experiences—who had witnessed awful, abhorrent acts. He spoke about one person who had seen things as a youngster and one person who was a vet. But juxtapose those cases with the case that the Leader of the Opposition, Luke Foley, raised. He talked about the life experience of a young lady who had suffered great difficulties. The one thing that made her happy was the chance to raise dogs. I do not imagine that she was treating her dogs in a cruel or miserable manner. Hers is a human story. 
There are two sides to every argument and we must be careful that we do not tar every single person with the same brush, over and over again, because of the actions of the 10 per cent to 20 per cent. The Opposition does not accept that kind of action. This legislation will affect people, so we cannot throw the baby out with the bathwater, as the Government seems to be doing. The issue is complicated and the decision is not a simple one. It is, sadly, easier just to say, "We are going to cut the industry," but that is not the right decision. We are here to make the right decision, as best we can. We are in this place to have a proper debate and to look at all sides of the argument. The decision to ban greyhound racing will have incredible impacts across society. It will be felt well beyond the industry. The industry contributes more than $300 million to the economy, but let us not forget that $30 
million of that goes to the coffers of State revenue. [Extension of time] 
In this debate we have heard about the number of racetracks in rural areas as opposed to the number in metropolitan areas. Race days do so much more than bring the community together. We have heard about local businesses that rely on the industry. That was well articulated by the member for Cootamundra, who spoke so passionately earlier this evening. The member has highlighted the way in which the Temora Greyhound Racing Club's activities support the community. I will read some of the things that were highlighted through one of her social media posts—things that may not have been taken into account in the report. 
The Temora Greyhound Racing Club raised money for charities, including $50,000 for cancer organisations; $5,000 for cystic fibrosis organisations; $30,000 for the Temora District Hospital humidicrib; and $30,000 
for Red Nose Day. The club runs Work for the Dole and community corrections schemes. The club has 40 trainers, 300 race dogs and employs 32 workers. Clubs like Temora are the experts in this area—they live and breathe these issues, and I will listen to them any day. The member for Cootamundra argued that if the greyhound industry closes it will affect the economy not just of Temora but of surrounding communities. It will affect the lives of trainers, families and their friends. The unemployment rate will rise in the community. If we ever needed an economic argument for the industry, that is it. 
Let us consider those who are doing it tough. Maybe the one race meet a week is a chance to make a few extra bucks here and there. I am talking about the people—they may be selling from coffee carts; they may be parking attendants—who have part-time jobs to supplement their incomes to help them eke out a living. We should think about those people and what they will be missing out on. Then let us look at why the introduction of this bill seems so cynical. The announcement was made just after the election. It was effectively a captain's call by the Premier. The Premier has been critical of the lack of bipartisanship. How can he talk about bipartisanship when he made a decision without even consulting his own party? If he brings people to the table he will be able to make a decision. He should not make those sorts of comments or an announcement on social media. He should be doing these things in the right way. The Premier knows how to do things the right way; he has done it before. We expect him to do the right thing this time. 
There is always the possibility, of course, that the Government will use the land in a fire sale. It does have a history of—and I would say almost an obsession with—selling assets. Let me turn to some of the things that were a major concern such as so-called "Ernie" in the United States, who appeared in a report that was commissioned in Canada. I can see a relationship. Let me turn now to the $1 million-plus spent on a government‑funded propaganda program before the bill was even debated in Parliament. There is also the concern we heard today that the submission of Percy Allan, the highly respected former senior public servant, an economics expert, was ignored. My colleague the member for Kogarah alluded also to the so-called compensation adjustment package. We are told to trust the Government on this but the member for Kogarah is absolutely bang on with this. We are told to trust the Government but where is the detail? Taxidrivers were told the same thing but all they got was twenty thousand bucks. That is not real. If the Government were genuine it would be up front about this but there is just not that level of trust at the moment. 
The bill is more than just about the greyhounds. It strikes at the very heart of a fair and just society. I 
have used that phrase often and on purpose. It may start with a ban on greyhound racing but where does it end? When did we begin to accept collective punishment as a way to go when penalising the 80 per cent to 90 per cent of people who are doing the right thing? I say over and over again  the actions of some have been absolutely horrific and live baiting is completely unacceptable. However, we do not serve our society well when we do not allow for redemption, for regulation and for an opportunity to allow people to prove themselves and do things right. There is an opportunity here to do things right; for us to argue for things to be done right. I accept there have been some horrific practices but surely this opportunity for redemption must be something to put on the table. I have only been to the dogs once. I am no expert on greyhound racing nor do I profess to be. But I do know one thing  Australia is built on the notion of a fair go. The Executive Director of the Greyhound Breeders, Owners and Trainers Association, Brenton Scott, said  
All we ask for is a fair go. The industry believes that it is only fair to be given the opportunity to prove that it is adaptable and capable of change. 
The notion of a fair go is the very foundation on which our nation has been built and it is sadly missing from the proposed legislation.

I speak in debate on the Greyhound Racing Prohibition Bill 2016. This bill prohibits the keeping of greyhounds for the purposes of racing in New South Wales as of 1 
July next year and makes it an offence to race greyhounds anywhere within the State. It also makes it an offence to conduct a meeting for the purposes of greyhound racing or to bet on greyhound racing or to operate a greyhound trial track in New South Wales. Like most members in this place, I have received countless emails, phone calls and visits to my office over the past few weeks including from some four-legged constituents about the Government's proposed ban on greyhound racing in New South Wales. 
I begin by sincerely thanking each and every one of those residents who took the time to reach out and share their views. Many of them told me it was the first time they had contacted their local member of Parliament but that they were moved to do so because they felt deeply about this issue. This is a highly emotive and complex issue, with proponents and opponents of the ban both passionately putting their case. What is clear is that, whether Parliament chooses to ban greyhound racing or reform the industry, we can no longer turn a blind eye to the cruelty revealed in the media and in the McHugh report. 
We must put an end to the appalling practice of live baiting, where animals are tied to mechanical lures to train and blood dogs; we must end the termination of tens of thousands of underperforming dogs in what is callously referred to as "wastage"; and we must put an end to the culture of cruelty that persists in the industry despite attempts to clean it up. What is also clear is that if Parliament chooses to ban the industry we must act now to assist the communities and families impacted, to properly resource greyhound rescue organisations and the RSPCA, and to keep racetracks like Wentworth Park in public hands. 
Animal welfare is at the heart of this debate. It is something that has motivated and moved me throughout my career. I strongly believe that treating animals ethically and with dignity is vital to our wellbeing as a civilised society. We must always strive to do our best when it comes to the way we treat animals—to care for the animals we share our homes with, to be respectful of the native wildlife all around us and above all else to be good custodians of our planet. Gandhi once said that you can judge a country by the way it treats its animals. I am the first to admit that this is not a simple issue. We cannot fall into the trap of saying that on one hand there are people who care about animal welfare and on the other hand there are people who support greyhound racing—it is not that simple. 
I accept that animal welfare is just as important to a farmer who raises animals as it is to a family living with a dog in Summer Hill. Similarly, I accept that animal welfare is important to many of the owners and trainers of racing greyhounds even though I disagree with the industry. I do not doubt that many animals within the industry are respected, loved and cared for. It is unfair to tar all trainers, greyhound owners and opponents of the ban with the same brush, but it is also unfair to dismiss those supporting the ban as elitists or radicals. This is a complex debate requiring complex consideration and the simple truth is that there are no simple answers. The fact remains that the McHugh report details significant abuses that must be heeded. What is clear is that both sides of this place categorically condemn animal cruelty. 
Over the course of the past few weeks I have been visited by many owners of rescued greyhounds undoing the damage caused by the industry. I have listened to haunting stories about the trauma inflicted on these dogs and I have had the chance to meet some of them. Natalie and her greyhound, Rosie, dropped by my office to visit a few weeks ago. Rosie is a beautiful, little, black greyhound, gentle and open-hearted. She has an unusual past for a greyhound. She was the runt of her litter and was bottle-fed as a puppy. She only ran five races and ran dead last or close to last every single time. She was handed over to the Greyhound Adoption Program and experienced two failed adoptions before spending some time as a support dog at the John Morony Correctional Centre in Windsor. After a period spent as part of a cell-dog program with female inmates, she found Natalie and Natalie gave her the second chance we know many dogs do not get. 
I have listened to stories about dogs who seemed calm and perfectly fine until they were triggered by something that reminded of them of their time in the industry—dogs who are fearful and anxious and require months and years of patient retraining and compassion; the happy, self-assured dog who would cower and yelp when someone lit a cigarette because the trainer who had beaten it had smoked; or the dogs left permanently injured and affected after racing accidents, including lacerations, amputations, skull and bone fractures and muscle injuries. My constituents have also raised with me the media reports of mass graves and the destruction of "wastage" in the industry. This kind of abuse cannot be tolerated. It is clear that things cannot continue as they have. 
I have seen something like this before. I worked for former Prime Minister Julia Gillard when she suspended the live export industry following similarly ghastly revelations of animal cruelty onFour Corners. The program exposed systemic cruelty, with three-quarters of Indonesian abattoirs processing Australian cattle failing to meet international standards. In response, former Prime Minister Gillard and the then Minister for Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries, Joe Ludwig, took the decision to suspend live exports until safeguards could be put in place to ensure the humane treatment of those animals. This was the correct response—one that I note was steadfastly opposed by the Coalition at the time. 
We must remember there had been precedent—former Prime Minister John Howard suspended live exports to Egypt in 2006—but still the Government weathered criticism from the live export industry. I recall hundreds of emails to Prime Minister Gillard's office, ferocious media attacks and accusations. Then, as now, there was intense feeling on both sides. Former Prime Minister Gillard and former Prime Minister Howard were keenly attuned to the fact that animal welfare must be balanced against the livelihoods of people, particularly those in regional areas. They acted to ensure that there were substantial industry packages to assist farmers and to protect livelihoods. 
The Gillard Labor Government provided a $5 million welfare contingency fund for cattle stranded in export holding yards, the $30 million Live Exports Assistance Package for primary producers and related businesses, a subsidised interest rate on new loans for affected businesses, grants for obtaining financial advice, and a Northern Territory Government freeze on pastoral lease rents. The Government must take a page from that book and deliver a strong, fair and clear industry package to help those impacted by any ban. I share my colleagues' concerns that the Government's commitments in this respect have been vague and minimal at best. 
Whether or not you support the ban, we must not underestimate the devastation for families told that their business and way of life is to be taken away in less than a year and with no clear sense of what transitional support is going to be provided. There is confusion about what support might be offered, and this Government has weakened many of the other supports for people whose careers are in transition—including ripping $1.7 billion out of TAFE, sacking 4,600 TAFE teachers and flagging 27 TAFE campuses for closure. Again, whether or not you support the ban, it is hard to overstate the rank irresponsibility of this Government's decision to leave working families and regional communities in limbo. 
My constituents have also called for greyhound rescue organisations to be funded properly, especially the RSPCA but including the Greyhound Adoption Project, Greyhound Rescue and others. This is the only way to ensure that those dogs who can be adopted are given a second chance, just like Rosie was. I note that the Victorian Labor Government announced recently that it would ban the sale of puppies and kittens in pet shops. At the same time it has committed $5 million in funding to the RSPCA to assist with investigations and rehoming of animals. The Baird Government must act similarly to protect as many dogs left behind by a potential industry closure as is possible. [Extension of time] 
Organisations like the RSPCA do amazing work on the smell of an oily rag. While I am sure they welcome the news of a ban, they need proper financial support to meet the challenges ahead. When the news of the ban was announced, many of my constituents were understandably sceptical of the Premier's newfound passion for animal rights. After all, this Premier has refused to join his Victorian counterpart in banning puppy farms and restricting the sale of puppies and kittens in pet shops, he has not acted on the insidious practice of testing cosmetics on animals, his Government walked away from better regulation of free range eggs to improve the quality of life for chickens, and, perhaps most importantly, this Premier is responsible for proposed land-clearing laws that would have a catastrophic impact on biodiversity and native fauna. 
Many inner west residents think instead that the Premier has his eye on Wentworth Park and other racetracks across the State. That is fair enough, because this Premier has form when it comes to selling off public assets and public land to developers—mass rezonings along the Sydenham to Bankstown corridor, the Bays Precinct and the Parramatta Road strategy, for example. Premier Baird is turning the inner west into a developer's paradise, no matter what the impacts are on the community or the environment. 
If further prove was needed, as the Hon. Mick Veitch noted in the other place, just weeks before the announcement that the greyhound industry would be shut down, the community trust board of Wentworth Park was disbanded and a handpicked administrator installed, only for Wentworth Park to appear on UrbanGrowth's plans for the Bays Precinct shortly thereafter. Labor moved an amendment in the other place to ensure that the racetracks would remain in public hands, and disappointingly The Greens and the Coalition voted together to block it—an interesting alliance given The Greens' regular campaign rhetoric about retaining public assets. The Greens voted against the protections afforded by Labor's amendment despite claiming to protect public lands. A 
quick Google search has revealed that The Greens' public lands policy is "under review". It would have to be under review given that The Greens have entrusted the Premier with Wentworth Park on nothing more than a wink and a nod—Premier Baird has never seen public land that he would not like to sell. 
Last week the Premier chose to make hay of my response to constituents in this place but he was selective in what he quoted. It is true that I am a passionate advocate of animal welfare and that the evidence in the McHugh report is clear. I do not support greyhound racing and I fear for the welfare of the thousands of dogs caught up in the industry. But I also said that we need a transition package that is fair, clear and immediate if we are to ensure that the communities and families affected by this ban are supported through what will be a very difficult time. This Government has failed to deliver that. We must act to resource properly the organisations that are managing the adoption of greyhounds and preserve these racetracks as public land. I have listened to my constituents. I will continue to make the case strongly for animal welfare both in this Parliament and in my party room, of which I 
am a proud member.

text:
Like others on this side of the House, I oppose the Greyhound Racing Prohibition Bill 2016. On 7 July, together with many other people, I was shocked at the Premier's surprise announcement to end the greyhound industry in New South Wales. In one Facebook post, the Premier unexpectedly declared the greyhound industry over and wiped out 90 years of working-class tradition. He has no idea how many lives he up-ended in that one comment. On 16 June, former High Court judge Justice Michael McHugh provided his report on the Special Commission of Inquiry into the Greyhound Racing Industry in New South Wales. The report details 80 recommendations, 79 of which the Premier has completely ignored. 
The first recommendation asks the question  should the greyhound industry continue in New South Wales or not? To respond to this, the Liberal-Nationals Government drafted legislation, had it introduced into the other place—which is a House of review—and brought on a second reading speech with no opportunity for members of that place to look at the legislation prior to its debate. What other industries have been shut down in this manner? It is quite astounding that the Government would choose to act in this way. 
Justice McHugh's 79 other recommendations provide a roadmap detailing a drastic restructure of the greyhound industry and improving animal welfare. The Premier does not understand the real impact of his decision to unilaterally shut down greyhound racing in this State because it does not affect the people that he and the Liberal Party represent. He does not understand the importance of the greyhound racing industry to the working class of this State. Therefore it is not really surprising that the Premier would make this out-of-touch call. However, it is surprising that at the announcement the Deputy Premier and Leader of The Nationals was standing right by the Premier's side. 
Since the Premier's announcement that he was abolishing the greyhound industry in New South Wales I 
have been contacted by many in the greyhound industry, many greyhound owners and many animal rights activists. Let me be clear  The greyhound industry is in need of reform. There is no place for animal cruelty in the greyhound racing industry or in our society. Animal cruelty is abhorrent. TheFour Corners footage aired in February last year was highly disturbing and such animal cruelty must not be tolerated. For too long greyhound racing has been under policed and under regulated. 
Labor supports severe punishments for people who are guilty of animal mistreatment, including life bans from the industry and jail terms; Labor believes the commercial and regulatory functions of the sport should be clearly split; and Labor believes there should be a new greyhound racing industry regulator with a mandate to implement the highest standards of animal welfare. There are many industries in our society that need change and reform  the banks, the tobacco industry, the churches, the casinos and the horseracing industry, amongst others—some might even say that this Parliament needs reform. I make a contribution to debate on the Greyhound Racing Prohibition Bill 2016. From the outset, I note that many good people in the industry will be impacted by this decision, including people in the gallery tonight, and men and women in my electorate of Monaro and the city of Queanbeyan, whom I have met in relation to the greyhound industry. I have grown up with these people; some are mates and some I have had a punt with. I genuinely feel for the many good people in the industry who will pay a high price with the likely passing of the legislation and the ending of greyhound racing in this State. 
However, it is important that members explain to their constituents and those affected why the Government has taken this action. As a Cabinet Minister, I supported the decision to end greyhound racing next year but it was one of the toughest decisions I have made. It was a torturous decision that challenged one's role in government and the legacy we leave for our communities. That is why this has been a tough, challenging time. The Leader of the Opposition said that theOld Testament recognised that greyhounds were a noble dog, but that is the principle of this bill. A noble dog deserves a noble life and we seek to achieve that with this bill tonight. The Leader of the Opposition referred also to Catherine the Great having a pet greyhound. However, she ruled at a time when there was slavery. Since then decisions have been made by governments to end slavery. The decision of this Government will, in time, be judged as to whether it was right or wrong. I genuinely believe it is right. 
The decision is based on the need to stop animal cruelty and to assist society to change its attitude to animal welfare. The Government has decided to end greyhound racing on 1 June 2017. My job as a Minister and local member is to put in place the support package that allows for an orderly transition. This decision will have economic and social impacts on some regional communities. For some individuals within the racing industry, the Government's decision has taken a significant personal toll. The Government cannot and will not forget those individuals and their communities. 
The Government has moved decisively to appoint Dr John Keniry, AM, as the Greyhounds Transition Taskforce Coordinator General. Dr Keniry has consulted with people working directly or indirectly in the industry in order to guide the industry to a compassionate and orderly closure. Dr Keniry has publicly reassured the greyhound industry that direct financial assistance will form part of the package developed for government consideration. The media has reported that revenue from wagering taxes will be used to fund the transition plan. A training and skills program will be available to help people within the industry find new jobs. Businesses affiliated with the greyhound industry will be given access to business assistance through an expanded Small Biz Connect program. There will be financial support to cover immediate greyhound welfare costs. 
People who are affected need to know what will be available so that they can plan for the future. The Government commits to announcing its assistance package within three months of the passing of this legislation. To ensure that as many views as possible form part of his report to government Dr Keniry will be visiting several regional centres across New South Wales to hear first-hand about the issues people are facing due to the industry's impending closure. While the legislation sets a 1 July 2017 closure date for greyhound racing, there will be transition periods for other aspects of the greyhound racing industry. 
The task force will provide advice to the Government based on discussions with the industry on the most effective way to phase out other activities such as training, breeding and ownership of greyhounds. Consideration will be given to the supply chain of businesses and people supporting the industry. The Government will then decide what assistance will be available to people affected by the industry's closure. This is expected to be announced in late October. A new round of community consultation will inform people about what is available to them. Greyhound racing in New South Wales will end on 1 July 2017. In the meantime, owners, breeders, trainers and all those affected by the closure are encouraged to consider carefully any decisions concerning their future circumstances and the welfare of their dogs. The Government wants to avoid subjecting the industry to months of uncertainty. 
In addition, allowing a staggered wind-up of the industry will provide the best possible chance for greyhounds to enjoy the best quality of life. It will take into account the life cycle of a dog and the ability of breeders and trainers to receive a return on investment. If the wind-up of the industry requires three or four years to allow an orderly transition then that will be considered. Allowing a staggered wind-up will ensure that greyhounds have the best opportunity to be rehomed with quality of life. Welfare assistance measures for greyhounds may include support from organisations such as the RSPCA to ensure that greyhounds are treated humanely following transition out of the industry. There will be support for the RSPCA to coordinate rehoming efforts. The legislation banning greyhound racing in New South Wales needs to be dealt with quickly and clearly so that people can establish clear plans for their future and their dogs' future. 
I have spoken to breeders and trainers in my electorate. The Leader of the Opposition said that no other jurisdiction has made this decision, but he is incorrect. The Australian Capital Territory Labor Government has also announced the end of greyhound racing. That decision shows this issue crosses the political aisle and is based on animal welfare. This industry has had years to self-regulate. Live baiting has been banned for 60 years yet there are examples of live baiting today. The community has been asked to trust that the industry can change. Reputable greyhound owners, breeders and trainers in the industry should be angry.    They should be angry with those who have governed this industry and allowed it to deteriorate to this point. I spoke to a breeder in my community in Braidwood. I asked whether he believed the McHugh report had been exaggerated. He said he was angry with the Government's decision but that the McHugh report is not exaggerated—if anything, it is probably the tip of the iceberg. Many within the industry have been aware of cruel live-baiting practices in the industry but have sat idle and not voiced their concerns. Today the industry has to pay the ultimate price for that silence. 
The good people will pay a high price, and it is the Government's role to ensure the assistance package works to transition the industry in an orderly manner. As the member for Monaro, with a 2½ per cent margin, I 
accept that this is a tough decision. Governments regularly make tough decisions. Those opposite have criticised Government decisions concerning death and disability benefits for police, the poles and wires issue, and workers compensation. The member for Blacktown used to throw grenades and say, "You are gone in 2015". I 
remind the member that I was returned to Parliament with a swing in my favour. 
I have articulated to my community the benefits of being in Government and that honest decision-making processes are delivering for communities that were left behind by Labor. In Cooma, Rosi Schenkar now receives dialysis locally and does not have to drive six hours to access treatment. The Queanbeyan bypass was promised by government after government, including by Bob Carr, but was delivered by this Government and my community no longer has to endure incidents such as a citizen being hit by a truck and g dragged down the main street. Things such as these are possible when a government makes tough decisions and runs a good government. At times governments have to take tough decisions, and this is one of those times. This is the correct decision. For the reasons laid out in the McHugh report and the previous upper House report, I stand by the Government's decision.

I make a contribution to debate on the Greyhound Racing Prohibition Bill 2016 and state at the outset that I am not a fan of the way the greyhound racing industry conducts itself and I am incredibly concerned about animal welfare. But greyhounds like running, and they like running fast. There is nothing inherently cruel in dogs racing each other, yet the evidence before the McHugh inquiry and recent media reports are damning. Grotesque acts of animal cruelty are being perpetuated purely for commercial gain and that cruelty must stop. I believe the way the Government has gone about banning greyhound racing without any sort of strategic direction or transition plan is wrong. 
After very careful and difficult consideration I would prefer to give the industry one last chance to change the way it operates and to work with the industry to ensure this happens rather than implement a half-baked solution that I fear will result in most of the 10,000 or so greyhounds in New South Wales being put down rather than rehomed, as it is just not possible to retrain and rehome that many dogs in a year. It is also not fair to people who work in the industry not to provide any support or retraining to find employment after the shutdown. 
I also strongly support Labor's amendments to require that public lands used for greyhound racing cannot be sold or disposed of without an Act of Parliament and to require a timetable and reporting on the assistance plan, the details of which we are all waiting to hear. Constituents in my electorate have mixed views about the ban and it is not as big an issue in the Granville electorate as many others, such as the reforms to the taxi industry, which affect the livelihoods of hundreds of people in my electorate. But there are some people involved in the industry, many who have knowledge of the industry and many others who are rightly concerned by the utter disregard for animal welfare shown by some in the industry. Labor supports implementing the recommendations of the McHugh inquiry. They are strong recommendations that I believe will go a long way towards improving the industry. 
I am not sure whether they go far enough, but only time will tell. What I am sure of is that the current industry structure and self-regulation does little to inhibit, deter or prevent animal cruelty, should participants decide to engage in animal cruelty to increase the chances of their dog winning, or to dispose of slow dogs. Labor 
wants to separate the commercial and regulatory governance of greyhound racing and improve the oversight of the industry for greater animal welfare. This is an important and overdue reform. The industry is coming off a very low base. Maybe it will not be enough, but it may be worth trying before considering banning greyhound racing altogether. We want stronger laws against animal cruelty in industry, including lifetime bans for live baiting. I believe more broadly there must be greater capacity for the enforcement of the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act in New South Wales, which largely now rests with underfunded charity organisations. Whether or not greyhound racing is banned, this must happen if the Government is serious about stopping cruelty to animals. 
In providing my support to those reforms, I call on the industry to take reform seriously. Every few years there is a scandal about greyhound racing, whether it is about the continued use of live baiting, doping or the obscene numbers of perfectly healthy dogs that are being killed for being slow. Each time, the industry promises to reform and then nothing happens. This time it must be different. Too many people have turned a blind eye to the worst excesses of the industry on the basis that they are not party to it. I say to members of the industry that the standard they walk past is the standard they accept. Stop turning a blind eye to live baiting. I know that the overwhelming majority of people involved in the industry do not do it, but if people know it is happening, they should report it and stop it. It has been illegal for decades, and for good reason. It is a cruel and abhorrent practice. It is entirely morally unacceptable. That it occurs at all and the participants have remained in the industry reflects on the entire industry. 
The same goes for doping and injuries sustained in racing. Stop turning a blind eye to those things. Many in the industry say that they love their dogs, but if they love their dogs, please let them get old. They should stop breeding so many dogs that they cannot afford to keep, or for which they cannot afford to find homes if they are slow. I know some people in the industry keep failed or retired greyhounds as pets or have them rehomed. I am glad that there has been a massive reduction in the number of pups bred in the past 12 months to reduce wastage and increase rehoming, but it is not yet enough. It is nowhere near enough. Euphemistically calling it wastage or euthanasia does not change it  Killing healthy dogs is morally wrong and it needs to stop. Greyhounds are no different from other dogs. They are lovable and deserve a happy and full life, running around or living on the couch doing nothing. I say that as someone who has adopted a number of dogs that other people did not want or could not keep—great pets that I have never regretted taking on, even if I did not have them for as many years as I would have liked. 
I also grew up on a farm. My dad, like all our friends and relatives, always had some lovely old retired working dogs living around our house. Once they could not get up on the ute anymore, they retired to live out their days being spoiled at the farmhouse. Greyhounds deserve the same—not to be killed for not being profitable. I speak on the Greyhound Racing Prohibition Bill 2016. The decision to ban greyhound racing in New South Wales has raised many diverse views in my electorate. It has caused a great deal of conversation from all corners. The views that have been expressed to me, both for and against, have been taken on board. I have listened carefully and considered each and every one. I have raised those views with the appropriate Minister and I thank those who have contacted me. 
I note that people from the industry are present in the gallery this evening, including the President of the Greyhound Breeders Owners and Trainers Association, Mr Geoff Rose, from my electorate. I have had extensive discussions with him and others about the problems the industry now faces. We also discussed what I now have to do to help. It is well documented that following a parliamentary inquiry in 2013-14 and a 12-month special commission of inquiry there was very strong evidence to suggest that in many aspects the greyhound racing industry, by its own admission, was in decline. It did not have a long-term future. For various reasons, including systemic animal cruelty, it was not fit to continue. As a result, a decision was made. 
When the decision was announced many, like me and those in the industry, were taken by surprise. As a result, I have had many conversations with people from all walks of life, who are either for or against the decision. Many of them have nothing to do with the greyhound racing industry at all. However, many were unaware of the evidence being considered by the Government that led to this decision. There is so much more to this than people realise. It is very complex. After a long period the industry had failed to convince the Government and the community that it could reform in areas such as breeding, racing, the number of races, the number of tracks, animal welfare, financial matters, rehoming and much more. 
The industry is self-regulated and in many aspects it is a closed shop. Those who are not involved in the industry know little about it, apart from the races we see on television or when making the odd visit to the track. The decision is very hard to accept. It took a long time for me to form any other view. Greyhound racing has been part of the culture in New South Wales for a very long time. The community's perception has changed; the community's expectation of the treatment of animals has also changed. I acknowledge those who have had greyhounds in their families for generations, and I cannot begin to understand how they feel. 
The decision has been made and so now, as I have discussed with many in my electorate, we need to ensure that there is a smooth transition. My office has had contact with the Coordinator General of the Greyhounds Transition Taskforce, Dr John Keniry. I am pleased that he will be in my electorate in the next few weeks to meet with trainers, owners, breeders and businesses to discuss a way forward. There will be a transition package that can help overcome some fears of the people in my electorate. My door has always been open. I will continue to do my very best to help those who need help.

I put on record the reasons that I cannot support the Greyhound Racing Prohibition Bill 2016. I do so with some degree of discomfort and with no pleasure at all that I need to take a stance different from that of my party. I do not for a moment doubt the sincerity of the Premier and the Deputy Premier in their opposition to cruelty to animals. It is an opposition that I share, as indeed all members do. I also respect their preparedness to make decisions that they believe to be necessary despite the likelihood of opposition from some within the community. I cannot, however, bring myself to support them in this instance. That courage on the part of the Premier and the Deputy Premier has led to much positive change in New South Wales. 
It has been overwhelmingly good for the people of this State in many other instances. But, in this case, I 
do not believe this is the right response. I will explain why this is so and then, as I cannot in good conscience support the bill, I will abstain from voting on it. A good number of the constituents of the electorate of Riverstone have an interest in greyhound racing—as owners, trainers, breeders or just as spectators or punters. Some have businesses that serve greyhound owners. It is my understanding that in fact Western Sydney collectively has the largest number of followers of this sport of any region in New South Wales. Near my electorate—actually in the seat of Londonderry—is the track at Richmond, which is a significant hub in that community. 
I am convinced that the vast majority of people within the electorate of Riverstone and across Western Sydney are decent, law-abiding people who are not in any way responsible for the incidents of cruelty to animals identified in the McHugh report. Indeed one local made representations to me a few years ago, before the infamousFour Corners program, seeking government support to address integrity concerns held about the past management of greyhound racing in New South Wales. I sought to assist that whistleblower in their quest to improve the industry. I cannot stand by and see all these people tarred with the same brush because some in their industry have done the wrong thing. It is for these people that I stand here tonight doing what I would much rather not do. 
While much has been wrong in the industry, it is my view that the participants in greyhound racing should have been afforded the benefit of natural justice in various respects. Natural justice would have afforded them a chance to challenge the assertions made by interest groups to the commission of inquiry, it would have afforded them a chance to respond to the findings of the McHugh report before a decision was made, it would have afforded them a chance to demonstrate whether the reforms that were commenced in 2015 could have led to the industry meeting current community standards, and it would have afforded them the opportunity to be judged according to the law and standards of the day, not according to a new, unarticulated standard applied retrospectively—which is what I believe the concept of "social licence" amounts to. I will return to that later. 
The key element in the McHugh report was wastage. Euthanising animals no longer needed by their owners was not illegal in the period reported on in this inquiry. In fact, it is not illegal today; it is practised in many fields of activity yet only one activity—greyhound racing—is subject to prohibition. It remains legal and need not be cruel if done properly by a vet. So what standard was being applied when the commissioner came to the conclusion that the social licence was lost because of the issue of wastage? It appears that he moved from concerns about cruelty to animals such as live baiting—about which we would all agree—to a focus on animal rights, which is a different proposition altogether. 
It has been argued that there was no choice but to close the industry based on the McHugh report but the commissioner found that there was a choice—one that Parliament should make. I have no doubt that this has been a difficult choice for the Government. The documented instances of cruelty to animals, substandard practices and poor governance have to be taken seriously; I share the intent of my colleagues to see these wrongs brought to an end. However, the gravity of the effects of prohibition on many people demands that the case for choosing that response should be overwhelming. This is particularly so given that the alternative of a setting a period to allow the industry to demonstrate its capacity to meet community standards would not have precluded eventual prohibition should those standards not be met. 
A good deal of comment has been made about the concept of social licence in the report. I 
reject this concept. In a democratic society based on the rule of law Parliament alone determines if and when a person's right to pursue an activity needs to be curtailed, limited or prohibited. If law-abiding citizens need to watch over their shoulders for some rival source of authority that may capriciously deny them the opportunity to pursue their plans, efforts and investments, then we would all suffer from the loss of certainty and safety that such an unsatisfactory state of affairs would bring. It seems to be no coincidence that supporters of the concept of social licence tend to be people who want to ban things. 
I, like other members, have been contacted by constituents on both sides of this issue. In the main, their views were put respectfully and I take them all very seriously. In conclusion, I acknowledge that the considerable animal welfare challenges highlighted in the McHugh report demand a government response. In fact, it makes the motivation behind the bill understandable. But it is the wrong response. I would have chosen to reform the industry rather than close it; to prosecute those who do wrong rather than deny all participants the opportunity to pursue their sport; and to set clear rules and standards in advance for the industry to meet rather than condemn a sector of the community for failing to meet community standards that were never articulated in advance by this Parliament or the government of the day. For those reasons I will not be voting to support the bill.

I state at the outset how unhappy I am that we are being required to make a decision on the Greyhound Racing Prohibition Bill 2016. couple of weeks ago I spoke to David Lee. David is an owner and trainer. He used to be in the horseracing industry but was unable to continue in that industry after suffering significant injuries. He is now on a disability support pension. He has four dogs and he absolutely loves them. If we were to look at the condition of his dogs and the receipts that show the amount of money he spends on looking after his dogs to keep them in top condition, it is evident that David is committed to his dogs, because he loves them dearly. 
I met with Kate Lord from Kankool Pet Foods in Willow Tree in my electorate. She wrote to me as well as to the Deputy Premier and the Deputy Prime Minister. Her letter states  
We are a family owned pet food abattoir located at Willow Tree in the Upper Hunter electorate. We designed and built this facility ourselves and have invested a very large sum of money into building and maintaining this business. 
We currently employ eight people on a permanent basis and three casuals, and as such are a significant employer in this area. Four of the people relying on this enterprise for their livelihood are over the age of 55. 
Our current pet food sales are comprised of approximately 99% greyhound owners and trainers and 1% pet owners. 
In her contribution the member for Wallsend mentioned a man by the name of Steve Whalland. Steve, a good mate of mine, is listening to the debate tonight. He has been involved in the greyhound industry for a long time, as was his father before him. Steve takes photos at the finishing line and was planning on running his business for at least another 10 years. I have known Steve for approximately 35 years. He is a man of integrity who has owned and trained dogs. He will be another casualty of the ban on greyhound racing because he will not be able to follow through on his business goals. The now deceased Maurine Gray, who was President of the Muswellbrook Greyhound Race Club, would be turning in his grave wondering what the hell has happened. He loved the industry and the dogs. For decades, he did a lot for the Muswellbrook Greyhound Race Club. 
I have also spoken to industry representatives. I acknowledge Mr Scott, who is in the gallery, as well as members and supporters of the industry who are keen to continue supporting the greyhound industry. I thank them for their honesty and pragmatism in the discussions I have had with them. Prior to becoming a member of Parliament, I was a financial planner. My contribution will focus on the economic aspect of the industry and the problems that are associated with it. I quote from the 2013-14 report of the Legislative Council Select Committee on Greyhound Racing in NSW. Chapter 3, entitled "The economic viability of the greyhound racing industry", covers the sustainability of the greyhound racing industry in New South Wales, and states  
3.1The sustainability of the greyhound racing industry can be considered from the perspective of a greyhound racing participant or from a broader industry-as-a-whole perspective. The sustainability of the industry is largely affected by the costs of running the industry and the returns from wagering; however, it is also reliant on the ongoing involvement of greyhound racing participants, such as owners and trainers. For industry participants, viability is mainly influenced by the cost of owning, training and racing greyhounds and the returns received in the form of prize money. 
3.2The Committee heard that the industry is not viable in the short to medium term and not sustainable in the long term. This view was expressed by Mr Brent Hogan, Chief Executive, Greyhound Racing NSW  
It is the view of the industry that the New South Wales greyhound racing is not viable in the short to medium term and certainly not sustainable in the longer term. This is the collective view five bodies included in the joint industry submission and merely expands upon the conclusions of Alan Cameron in his 2008 review of wagering and racing in this State. 
The next section of the report states  
As noted by Mr Hogan, this view was shared by the five industry bodies that signed off on the joint industry submission, namely  GRNSW, the NSW Greyhound Breeders Owners and Trainers Association (GBOTA), the Metropolitan and Provincial Greyhound Clubs Association, the Greyhound Racing Clubs Association and the Greyhound Action Group. Together these groups represent a substantial number of the clubs and participants in the greyhound industry. 
The alternatives have been discussed. I brought them up with the Minister and Deputy Premier, and the Premier but I have chosen to make my discussions far less public and much more meaningful directly to the source. To 
implement the other recommendations in the McHugh report, as has been suggested, would cost $20 
million a year, which equates to approximately $1,700 per dog per year. That will add a burden to the cost of owning the dog, racing the dog, looking after the dog and everything else that goes with it. In relation to costs and benefits, in the 2013-14 report of the upper House Select Committee on Greyhound Racing in New South Wales, table 5 on page 20 states that the average revenue across the industry—all breeders and trainers—was $4,041 and the average cost was $22,936. Earlier this evening I asked what was the average racing life of a dog. The average racing life of a dog is somewhere between 1½ and 2½ years, but let us say, for the sake of this exercise, that it is two years. [Extension of time]

I am not sure that it is because I believe it would substantially add to their burden. But the Government has announced that it has put in place a transition task force which is designed to provide financial assistance. It has begun planning and, following the announcement, the Government appointed Dr John Keniry as the Coordinator General of the Greyhounds Transition Taskforce. I know that Dr John Keniry has been out and about already seeking information from industry participants and that he will continue to do so. I speak on the Greyhound Racing Prohibition Bill 2016 that is before the House today. Labor's position will allow the greyhound industry to survive but supports significant reforms that would provide a highly regulated and monitored greyhound racing industry with the highest standards of animal welfare. Labor has released a plan that would provide a means of regulating this industry to bring about an end to animal cruelty and unethical practices. 
The Special Commission of Inquiry into the Greyhound Racing Industry in New South Wales was undertaken by Justice Michael McHugh and provided 80 recommendations. We all agree that the greyhound racing industry needs to be reformed, but I am not sure if the Premier is aware of or cares about the consequences of banning this industry. The ban will mean massive job losses and cause people to lose their livelihoods. 
In some cases, people may have only two or three dogs in their backyard; in other cases, people have invested their life savings in the industry. The ban will mean bankruptcy for those people, and who knows what else? Perhaps it will result in mental problems and marriage breakdowns. The ban will also result in an abundance of greyhounds that were once involved in this industry. dogs have been rehomed by Greyhound Racing 
NSW since 2007; during the 2014-15 financial year only 585 
greyhounds had been rehomed. Some dogs will be rehomed as pets in New South Wales. Others will be sold interstate. But the new owners will only want the good dogs; they will not want the dogs that cannot perform, and those dogs will be euthanased. 
Based on recent figures, the rehoming of thousands of greyhounds over the next year is wishful thinking on the part of the Government. There are some 12,000 greyhounds that need to be disposed of—rehomed, got rid of or sold interstate. Many years ago there were bone trucks that picked up carcasses when the butcher was finished with them. The bones would be tossed on the back of a truck and taken off to factories to be ground down to make blood-and-bone fertiliser. I am afraid that this is the kind of thing that will happen to a lot of these animals. The 
carcasses of these animals will be taken away and buried in some landfill or taken to factories where they can be made into fertiliser. I do not want that to happen; I would hate to see that. 
When I was young I found it confronting to see animal bones—legs, et cetera—hanging out the back of those trucks. Those trucks probably still go around to butcher shops in country areas, collecting bones. I 
hope that that will not happen to some of these greyhounds. But how else are people going to get rid of them if nobody wants them? As I said, there are 12,000 greyhounds that need to be rehomed in loving families. I do not think we will be able to rehome that many, and the greyhounds that are left will be killed or disposed of in some other way. It is absurd that on the one hand the Government is advocating for the rights of greyhounds—expressing concern about the killing of greyhounds that have been deemed uncompetitive—but on the other hand it is supporting a bill that will result in the deaths of thousands of these animals whose unemployed owners will have little choice but to euthanase their dogs.

million-a-year industry. The ban will prove to be devastating for the New 
South Wales economy, particularly in regional areas, which will bear the brunt of the impact. It seems that the Premier has ignored the widespread impact of this decision. Instead of showing leadership on this issue, he has placed it in the too-hard basket and decided to ban the industry all together, regardless of the social and economic impact it will have. This is policy on the run at its worst by the Premier and his Government. By 
providing strong regulations for this industry and significant reforms, the Labor Party will treat animals in a way that protects them from inhumane treatment by unscrupulous people. 
Labor will fight to prevent the loss of thousands of jobs for the people of New South Wales and give the industry a chance to improve its conduct. Only Labor will provide this $300 
million industry the chance to rectify the unacceptable practices of a minority, before taking extreme action such as this Government has taken. In Queensland and Victoria, the response of the respective governments has been to provide a clear warning to the industry and stronger regulation to protect the animals involved in the industry. Indeed, Labor is not alone in its opposition to the banning of the greyhound racing industry. 
The Premier should listen to the concerns of members in his own party room, some of whom have publicly raised concerns about the selective nature of the ban. The Deputy Premier's Federal leader, the member for New England, Barnaby Joyce, has called for this Government to consider the implications of its decision, including the widespread human consequences. However, it seems that for this Government political expediency has won the day. Labor will support the greyhound industry and advocate for stricter regulations in the industry. The bill before the House will end an industry that employs thousands of people and will bring an end to the livelihood of so many. That is why the Labor Opposition will oppose this bill.

In speaking in this debate on the Greyhound Racing Prohibition Bill 2016 I realise that this will not be the biggest issue our Government will face during its tenure. Our Government will long be remembered for delivering the infrastructure this State desperately needed. Our record investment in roads, rail, hospitals and schools will be our legacy.

Phar Lap united this country during the Great Depression. Tulloch did the same following World War II. So it was not surprising that, when the time came for recreational activity in the new colony back in the early 1800s, pitting horses against each other  to see which horse was the fastest, quickly became an aspect of Australian life each which everyone could relate to. South Wales. And it is therefore appropriate that I put on the record my reasons for supporting this bill. It certainly does not give me any pleasure that one code of racing in this State will be lost as a result, but there are important reasons it is being done.

Statements made by witnesses who appeared at the commission headed by the Hon. Michael McHugh bear testament to this. Current registered greyhound trainers who have visited my office since the announcement that we would close the industry in July 2017 have also endorsed our Government's actions, stating, "Live baiting is rife right across the industry with those directly involved with the education of greyhound dogs and it should be closed down."

greyhound is eligible to be registered when it is 12 months old. Some pups that were whelped in the last 18 months may be within litters, being reared, broken in or in pre-race training and not registered. However, even assuming that none of these juvenile animals (approximately 10,253) has been destroyed, where are the remaining 80,721 greyhounds? What has happened to them? 
The question posed by the commission is simple  Where are those 80,721 greyhounds? Acknowledging that a 
small number of greyhounds have been transferred interstate or overseas, the real answer is that a large number of those 80,000 greyhounds are missing, presumed dead. If they were not dead, they would be easily accounted for, but they are not. That is the unmentionable truth and wastage about which the greyhound industry will not speak, nor has it dealt with it. Indeed, it had no intention of dealing with it until the announcement of the potential closure of the greyhound racing industry. That attrition rate, combined with the large number of small, innocent animals that are used in the inherently cruel live baiting activity, is the fundamental reason that the New South Wales Government has introduced this legislation to close the greyhound racing industry on 1 July 2017. 
The training of greyhound dogs involves getting them fit and teaching the animal to jump out of starting boxes and to run as fast as possible over a chosen or suitable distance. There is no more effective way to extract the ability and natural speed out of a greyhound dog than to tie a small live animal on an armature which is then pushed at speed along a track and allows the greyhound dog to chase it, catch it and then tear it apart—all while the small animal is tied down defencelessly and killed. It is an activity known broadly by the term "live baiting". This is a tried and tested method that has been used for more than a century in the education of greyhound dogs. This widespread and cruel practice continues to be used widely to this day despite being illegal in this country for the past 60 years. 
Trainers and people educating dogs are on the record as stating that the practice is widespread and they will never stop using it as they believe it is fundamental to the training and educating of high-performance greyhounds. The small animal of choice is usually a rabbit but, as was seen onFour Corners, small wild piglets and possums and several other animals have all been used in the practice. One greyhound trainer once advised me, "Anything that is small, breathes and squeals has been used, including cats and even chickens thrown into cages to blood these dogs prior to a race." It is inconceivable that anyone with even an ounce of civility or humanity could condone this widespread practice continuing. It is certainly not our Government's intention that it will. As I said, many people who participate in the industry are largely unaware of these practices. The sad fact is they do happen, whether participants in the practice acknowledge it or not. 
The other abhorrent cruelty involves the destruction of the greyhounds themselves. In my local area one veterinarian has offered his services to euthanise dogs for decades for next to nothing given that he is so sickened by the cruel way greyhounds are disposed of once their lack of speed or racing ability is known. Once a dog has been tested and found to be too slow to earn its keep the dog is destroyed, sometimes in the most brutal of manners. As has been recently reported, sometimes the dog's head is bashed in with a hammer and then it is buried. The question is  how many of the large number of 80,721 dogs that cannot be accounted for today have met similar fates? 
That huge number of dogs is conveniently referred to as "wastage" by the industry—discarded in the name of sport—and they are not even given the courtesy of a humane ending, which is something that I cannot forgive or condone. To his great credit, the vet I have referred to is none other than Rob Zammit, the 2GB 
Pet Vet, a noted veterinary practitioner and past participant in the greyhound industry. Together with his brother, he has tried valiantly to reform the industry, but to no avail. When noted people like Rob Zammit, who have undeniable knowledge, over many decades, of the inherent cruelty contained within the industry, are calling for a complete ban of the industry, it is hard to understand how those who protest against the prohibition can raise a viable argument against its closure. I commend the bill to the House.

I am delighted at 2.02 a.m. this Wednesday morning to be able to contribute to this very important and lengthy debate on the Greyhound Racing Prohibition Bill 2016. I 
inform the House that I support the Opposition's position not just because I am bound to but because it is right. I, like any right-thinking human being, was mortified when I saw the ABCFour Corners program "Making a Killing" in February 2015. I could not believe that any human being could treat animals in the way I witnessed on that television program. In fact, those images are firmly placed in my mind. 
Preventing cruelty to animals and the protection of animals is one of the very fabrics of mankind—if that age-old expression is still politically correct—because one can go back to biblical times 3,500 years ago to Genesis where the biblical writers enshrined the laws of mankind for the protection of animals and the prevention of cruelty to animals. In fact, the protection and welfare of animals was quite strict in biblical times; animals could only be slaughtered for human needs and they could only be slaughtered in a particular humane way for human needs—a practice that is still followed by the Muslim and Jewish faiths. Animals also had to rest on the Sabbath, just as human beings were required to rest on one day out of seven. Human beings have, for a lengthy period of time, advocated those principles. And those principles are enshrined in our modern-day laws. The actions which I saw on theFour Corners program clearly represent an offence under section 530 of the Crimes Act, which carries, as far as I recollect, five years' jail. So laws are in place to protect animals. 
After the February 2015 ABCFour Corners program there was a parliamentary inquiry, and then an inquiry by the Hon. Michael McHugh, QC. Michael McHugh is a working-class Newcastle boy who studied law part time through the Solicitors Admission Board and rose to become one of the greatest jurists this country has ever produced and a Justice of the High Court. Known to be a black-letter lawyer—much to the chagrin, I suppose, of many of us who were more progressive—his credentials are beyond reproach. Following his special commission of inquiry he recommenced, and this fact was important for me in coming to a determination with respect to this bill, that it was for Parliament to determine whether or not the industry had lost its social licence as a result of some terrible matters that had been exposed during his inquiry. He handed it over to Parliament to make that decision. 
The Hon. Michael McHugh then incorporated 79 recommendations for Parliament to consider if it was of the view that the industry should continue. There is nothing new about the expression "social licence". The CSIRO website uses the expression to refer to whether mining should occur in a particular area. The Hon. Michael McHugh used the expression because whenever there is a failure of an industry—whether it be the atrocities of a section of the greyhound industry or any other industry—the responsibility can be traced back to the regulator; it can be traced back to the government of the day. 
What was witnessed on theFour Corners program, and in some of the evidence that was disclosed in the special commission of inquiry, was the failure of the government of the day. This Government has been in office since March 2011. How many people have been prosecuted for criminal offences under section 530 of the Crimes Act, and how many have been sent to jail? How have some sections of this industry, in the 5½ years of this Government, been able to get away with what they have got away with? The reality is that it is the fault of the Executive Government. That is why the Hon. Michael McHugh said that Parliament should make the decision. 
In this case, the Executive Government was at fault for what we discovered, yet it then decided that this industry should close. Why could the matter not have gone to some joint committee? There will be horrendous consequences from the closure of this industry—not only to the economy of New South Wales, particularly regional New South Wales, but also to people's jobs. What is going to happen to the estimated 12,000 greyhounds on the closure of the industry? A balance needs to be struck between the cruelty to the animals that have been affected by the industry and the economy of New South Wales and the regional communities. That balance can best be reached through a collective decision-making process of the Parliament. I did not come to my final position in relation to this bill—the view that the Opposition position is right—until I heard a debate by my colleagues in the party room. 
I had read the McHugh report and the library research paper; I must confess I did not read the annexures. I did not know the correct decision to make until I heard the differing views and opinions of many of my colleagues from different parts of the State. I reached my opinion through a different source and different mode of reasoning that I have already articulated. I would have thought that in view of the serious consequences and the report exposing a failure by the Executive Government, which has run this industry for 5½ years through boards or other people, the decision should have been left to the elected representatives of the Parliament to collectively decide the appropriate balance. That has been taken away from us all. 
This was not an ordinary public policy position. This was not an ordinary decision of the Parliament to change the laws to be more effective or to change the administrative structure. This was a special commission of inquiry that exposed the failure of the Executive Government, which is accountable to this House, yet the Government's response was simply, "I am going to shut down this industry because I have failed to properly protect the greyhounds and other animals associated with this minority industry." 
It is the process by which the Government has reached this position for which it stands indicted. The Government stands indicted by the Hon. Justice McHugh's report for its own failure and it stands indicted for putting up its hands and saying, "I don't think we, the elected Government of New South Wales, are capable of stopping the heinous criminal offences that have occurred by the way in which animals have been treated in this industry". As a result, innocent people across the State whose livelihoods depend upon this industry will be affected by the Government's own failure. That is why the system is broken and that is why this House should reject this bill.
