I too acknowledge those present in the gallery—representatives from the greyhound racing industry and representatives of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals [RSPCA]—who have been here for a long period. Obviously I will oppose the Greyhound Racing Prohibition Bill 2016, but I will outline how I come to this debate and what has brought me to a very clear conclusion. I grew up in arguably the world's most famous greyhound racing destination, which is Dapto—an area that is famous for the Dapto Dogs on a Thursday night. The area is famous for a lot of other things, but it is certainly famous for the Dapto Dogs. 
I was shocked at the decision made by Premier Mike Baird, but I will address the manner in which he announced the decision in a moment. On the weekend when the announcement was made, I did what I assume most of us did that weekend and have done since  I read the report in detail. Some Opposition members believe in the premise that policy questions are worth reviewing and debating. We are not simply handed scripted pieces of paper from central casting that we read in this House. Like many others, I read the report that weekend. In addition to that, I met with people such as Darren Hull from the Bulli greyhound track, which is in the Keira electorate, and people associated with the track at Dapto, which is the largest and one of the most famous tracks, not just in this country but across the globe. 
I believe that all members in this place deeply oppose animal cruelty. I come to this debate with a clear position on animal cruelty but not everyone in my electorate supports my view on this issue. As a backbencher and shadow Cabinet Minister I have always stated that I will be up-front with my community. Hopefully, following this discussion they will understand my position. As the shadow Treasurer, I will talk about the financial impact of this bill. It has not been the focus of the debate but is something I will take into consideration when reviewing any legislation. According to consistent reports the industry injects $350 million into the economy. That is not something to be sneezed at or joked about. It is a substantial sum. 
Critically, a large portion of that money is generated in regional and rural areas. Those of us who live outside the global city know that downturns in industry will hit rural and regional areas hard. This industry supports 10,000 jobs and many small businesses. I extend this warning to those opposite  From now until 2019 
Labor will not cop any assertion by Government members that they believe in small government. That is gone. Government members will not refer to it and if they do the Opposition will knock it out of the ballpark. The 
Opposition will not accept references from Coalition members that the Government gives a damn about small business. The only Government members who have the right to say they give a damn about small business are those who have the guts to cross the floor tonight. 
Government members give stupid pre-prepared speeches issued from level 8 that argue the Government champions small business, small government and liberalism. It is garbage. The Opposition will not hear it said in this place by Government members that they give a damn about regional and rural New South Wales. The Opposition will not cop it. Those in Dapto or Dubbo, Broken Hill or Bankstown will not cop that members opposite give a damn about anyone outside the Sydney central business district. Last but not least, I do not want to hear Government members say they give a damn about jobs. That stops today. There are 10,000 
jobs, many small businesses and regional and rural communities that the Government will damage in the next couple of hours through the passage of this bill. Each and every time a Government member gets up from the green leather bench to make a prepared speech about how the Coalition believes in jobs, small business or regional and rural communities the Opposition will remind their constituents about what they did tonight and the hypocrisy of their words.    Are you crossing the floor or not?    How did the Premier get to this point and what could he have done? The Premier got to this point by announcing it on Facebook. Just so we are clear, the way we treat the men and women going about their business in New South Wales and enjoying something that the Premier may not enjoy on the Manly Corso is by announcing the complete destruction of an industry. This announcement was made not following consultation, not following bringing in industry, not following a discussion with members of Parliament—heavens above, not following a discussion with Cabinet, as I understand it and we are tracking this, or in the party room—but in a Facebook post. The next time those opposite come into this place and say they care about people, I will remind them of this Facebook post. 
No-one doubts the report of the commission of inquiry was damning. Anyone who has taken the time to read the report will say that it was difficult reading, and I think I can say that for all of us. But no-one shuts down an industry via a post on social media. What sort of individual refuses to listen to industry representatives who most recently have tried to reform the industry? What sort of individual refuses to listen to experienced members of his own team about their concerns? What sort of individual refuses to listen to people about the impact that this ban will have on regional and rural communities? That person is a premier who is simply out of touch. [Extension of time] 
What could the Government have done? Firstly, we operate in a Westminster system of parliament. I 
understand that Premier Baird thinks that all the knowledge exists in a corner office on level 8—I get that. It is a very small room with the occasional adviser who may not live too far from the eastern suburbs. Would it not have been smart to say, "I have real concerns about this. I am leaning towards banning, but do you know what I 
am going to do? I am going to do something really out there. First, I am going to involve The Nationals." Members know The Nationals; most of them are Liberals in R. M. Williams, but they are still members of a separate party. "I 
will involve them in the discussion because most of the tracks are in regional and rural areas." That could be point 1. Point 2, the Premier could put the industry on notice and give it time to reform. In conjunction with the Opposition the Premier could say that this Parliament would give the industry a time in which it needs to reform. We could increase the policing of the industry to ensure greater transparency because all of us, including the industry, want to make sure that those who do the wrong thing are out. We do not tolerate the barbaric behaviour that happened in the past. 
We have to remember that the Federal Coalition supports live animal exports. Just so we are clear on this, those opposite support live animal exports—they can nod their heads and say that that policy is strongly supported by The Nationals. They had better check their policy platform. What else do they support? Obviously, they strongly support the sport of kings, horseracing. I assume they support farming and other types of industry that have had serious animal welfare issues in recent years, and no doubt will continue to have those issues, but have been managed by governments of all persuasions through appropriate policing and regulation. 
The people of New South Wales expect us to govern. Governing means at times implementing regulation and reform rather than taking the cheap and easy way out by saying, "It is all too hard," and shutting an industry down. I say loudly and clearly that the Opposition will not be supporting this bill. Nor will it allow members of the Coalition who support the bill to continue to say in this place that they are the champions of small government, of business, of jobs and of rural and regional New South Wales. Those days are over. I thank the Leader of the Opposition and the shadow Minister, who have led the debate for the Opposition, for their conviction. I thank them for the way in which they have ensured that Labor members have been able to express their views. I thank them for taking a brave decision but the right decision. It is a decision that Government members need to think through.

In this Chamber last Thursday we debated a 37,000‑signature petition created by my office to save the greyhound industry, jobs and Wallsend cultural history. They are 37,000 people wanting their voices heard and wanting the industry to be given a fair go. Those 37,000 
people want all the recommendations of the McHugh report implemented, not just the ones that suit the Premier and Deputy Premier and their limited agenda. They want to be supported, not have their livelihood annihilated. I have been overwhelmed by the number of people who support a reform process. They have a gamut of reasons. They want a sense of fair play for people who have spent decades in the industry and require more than 12 months to reorder their lives. 
The industry should be able to continue to reform its sport and its image, as it was doing prior to the McHugh report. The majority of recommendations in the McHugh report call for an expansion of the legislative and regulatory guidelines governing the greyhound industry and harsher penalties for those who are found guilty of violating them—in other words, greater enforcement. That has been agreed by the industry and supported by the Opposition. The Premier's announcement to ban greyhound racing within nine months has, by the Government's own admission, sounded the death knell for nearly 3,000 jobs across the State. 
The majority of job losses will be in rural and regional New South Wales, where unemployment rates are already staggeringly high. The rate in the Hunter Valley is almost 7 per cent, which is well above the State average of 5.4 
per cent. The Gardens is the local track in my electorate, hosting more than100 race meetings every year that are attended by 157,000 people. In one way or another, 6,010 individuals participate directly in the sport. That is one in every 80 people in the Hunter region. That is growth that the Premier will be denying the region. The immediate effect of the closure of The Gardens will be an estimated annual loss to the Wallsend economy of $17.69 
million. Three full-time workers and two part-time office staff will lose their jobs immediately, with almost 500 
people losing their jobs in the longer term. Race-day workers who will lose work include a judge, a photographer, a lure driver, a race meeting manager, a starter, a kennel supervisor, kennel officers, kennel attendants, a maintenance crew, pen operators, a kennel cleaner, a general grounds cleaner, two snack bar staff, bar staff and others. 
The popular restaurant at the racetrack, Angsara Wok, which is owned and operated by a lovely group of locals, will have to close. Redden Video will have to close. Steve Whalland Race Images, the course photographer, will close. That will put two photographers out of work in Wallsend. Then there are the other race-day employees  three Greyhound Racing NSW stewards and a vet, as well as the TAB staff. Remember, this is every race day, two or three times every week. I have mentioned only the jobs at The Gardens that will be directly affected. text:
I oppose the Greyhound Racing Prohibition Bill 2016 and express my absolute disappointment with the Baird-Grant Government's decision to close down greyhound racing in New South Wales without fair consultation or process. Just over six weeks ago, well before this legislation was introduced, the Premier announced by social media that the livelihoods of thousands of people and a favourite pastime of tens of thousands of the citizens of our State would no longer be allowed because the member for Manly thought it had "lost its social licence". Nice guy Mike had woken up to consult with his publicly funded social media guru over a chai latte, perhaps decided that he was receiving a little too much internet backlash over his distaste for late-night socialising in the central business district—unless, of course, that socialising is occurring in the casino—and unilaterally decided that he would stop another part of our society from having fun. 
This is not just policy on the run; it is a violation of the principles of certainty and due process that underpin the rule of law in New South Wales and Australia. There was no forewarning, no consultation and not even a briefing to members of his own Government—just a barefaced attempt to pander for "likes" and the fleeting approval of his Facebook followers. I doubt there could be any clearer display of the Premier's contempt for the junior Coalition partner, The Nationals, than his lack of willingness to inform it in advance of the decisions coming out of his daily e-focus groups. But to add insult to injury the Premier is passing the buck to Deputy Premier Grant to spruik this shutdown to the community, after receiving significant backlash from the media and the broader community for, once again, riding roughshod over the people of New South Wales. 
I believe the Deputy Premier to be a decent person who takes the trust of the people of Dubbo and surrounds—the people who elected him to this place—seriously. I struggle to believe that he honestly believes, in his heart, that it is fair to his constituents—to the many who depend upon the greyhound racing at Dubbo Fields, and to the many more who enjoy greyhound racing—to close down greyhound racing at all, let alone without fair warning. It is simply unfair to Deputy Premier Grant to have a hospital pass thrown to him when nice guy Mike can no longer cope with being held to account for his decisions.    I wrote it, mate. If the member for Manly wants to build apartments on Wentworth Park, he should just tell us. He does not need to make the whole State suffer and close down an industry. While I understand that the Baird-Grant Government might consider it to be a commercially profitable decision to sell off the land under existing greyhound tracks, that still in no way excuses the frankly arrogant advertising campaign that has blanketed our radios, televisions and newspapers over recent weeks. 
Spending public money to generate support for a bill which has not even been passed yet is absolutely astounding and shows scorn for the hardworking people of New South Wales who have to pay out of their pockets for the Michael Baird spin machine. Perhaps most disgusting is the defence of the million-plus dollars being spent on this advertising campaign by a spokesman for the Premier, who told the ABC that "it was less than 1 per cent of the Government's annual advertising budget". No member of the Government should be proud of the reckless spending of this self-obsessed Government on its own vanity. When a decision is made to spend taxpayers' funds, a choice is made. No expenditure is without consequence and this Government is putting on full display that it cares more about its own public image than funding the nurses, the teachers, the roads and the rail that the people of this State expect it to provide. 
If the Government cared about making this argument to the public, it would have been willing to take this debate out to the community before the Premier's dictatorial announcement. There was no need to rush this legislation through Parliament; there was no need to take the action the Government chose to take. It was just a total disregard for democracy and the rights of the people of New South Wales to have their voices heard. Imagine 
how Premier Baird would feel if a government decided to arbitrarily ban something he enjoyed with absolutely no warning or consultation because of problems. One hundred people tragically drowned in New South Wales waterways last year, but we do not see Premier Baird banning his preferred sport of surfing. 
We know that some people misuse social media, that cyberbullying and so on are ongoing problems, but we do not see this Government outlawing Facebook. Increasingly, there is one law in this State for the things that Mike Baird likes and another for everything else. I do not believe it is reasonable for any government to dictate, without a reasoned and open process, what its citizens are allowed to do in their leisure time. When former Justice Michael McHugh referred to the possibility that greyhound racing had lost its social licence, I very much doubt that he was defining "social licence" as whatever the Premier believed was acceptable to his own personal social values. 
I know many members in this House, both from the Liberal Party and The Nationals, hold a genuine belief that governments should not unduly infringe on the freedoms of their citizens that uphold the values of liberty and liberalism. This legislation flies in the face of those values—the fundamental principles of good and decent government and the rule of law. I will be voting against it. I urge all of those Government members who are true to their values to join me and do the same.

I speak in debate on this important legislation, the Greyhound Racing Prohibition Bill 2016. This legislation reflects the complete loss by the greyhound racing industry of its social and moral licence to continue to operate in New South Wales, and it is something that The Greens and, in particular, the late Dr John Kaye, have fought for over many years. The Greens commend the Premier for this decision—and all those who are supporting the legislation—and for having the courage to take action. The reason we have fought for this, and the reason that we have been single-minded about this issue, is the appalling and inhumane facts surrounding the industry that are well known, that were horrendously highlighted by the special commission of inquiry and that have become evident in this debate. 
The Greens get that Labor sees itself as fighting an ideological battle on behalf of working-class people. The Greens accept that it is a difficult legacy to let go of for racing families who have loved their dogs and who have been let down by the industry. But the facts that emerged from the special commission of inquiry shifted this debate and the ultimate decision to ban the industry from 2017 well outside of any ideology. It shifted this debate beyond ideas to a stark unveiling of a reality  a picture of torture, animal cruelty and injury, and dog deaths on a scale that is unprecedented and intolerable in a twenty-first century society such as ours. The facts that have emerged take this debate far from ideology to a line in the sand. Crossing that line—standing by and allowing this barbarism and animal cruelty to continue for the sake of gambling—would say something about the kind of people we are and the kind of community we are. 
The idea that the special commission of inquiry was not a broad enough investigation to trigger such a decision is nonsense. The commission's investigations spread to almost every aspect of the greyhound racing industry in New South Wales and required it to investigate aspects of the greyhound racing industry in other States of Australia and in other countries. The commission examined 43 witnesses over 11 days of private hearings and 26 witnesses in 10 days of public hearings. It also considered 1,143 submissions that were made to the New South Wales parliamentary select committee in 2013 concerning the greyhound racing industry, and it had the benefit of reading the two reports issued by that committee. In the course of its inquiry, the commission received and reviewed over 151,000 pages of documentary material and over 115 hours of videos and other recordings. These came from widespread sources, including greyhound racing industry participants and representative organisations. 
This industry has grown beyond the dog races of my grandfather's ilk and, in its contemporary form, is doomed to kill and injure thousands of dogs each year. It also denies healthy dogs from being rehomed because of the damage to their temperament from the barbaric practice of live baiting. The normal life expectancy of a greyhound is between 12 and 15 years. Over the past 12 years in New South Wales 97,783 dogs were whelped. Currently there are about 6,809 
registered greyhounds—a greyhound is eligible to be registered when it is 12 
months old. Absent death through misadventure or illness, the average life expectancy of a greyhound indicates that another 90,974 greyhounds should still be alive. Some pups whelped in the last 18 months maybe within litters, are being reared and broken in, or are in pre-race training and not registered. However, assuming that none of those juvenile animals—approximately 10,253—have been destroyed, where are the remaining 80,721 
greyhounds? What has happened to them? 
Some of them will have found homes outside the greyhound racing industry or been exported interstate or to other countries, some will have been retained by their owners as pets or breeders, or some will have died of natural or accidental causes. But the evidence before the commission indicated that at least 50,000 of those whelped—perhaps up to 70,000—were deliberately killed simply because they never were or are no longer capable of being competitive racing greyhounds. The evidence suggested that somewhere between 48,891 and 68,448 of the 97,783 greyhounds bred in New South Wales in the past 12 years were killed because they were considered too slow to pay their way or were unsuitable for racing. 
The Greens are compelled by the assertion of the inquiry that Greyhound Racing NSW is concerned about the number of healthy dogs being destroyed each year but that addressing the mass slaughters are beyond the industry's capability. Each year the industry currently needs—and without a dramatic reduction in the number of race meetings it holds will probably continue to need—6,000 or more greyhounds to be whelped in order to maintain its racing schedules. However, the industry cannot and will not be able to find homes for between 50 
per 
cent and 70 
per cent of these dogs. The Australian Working Dog Alliance reported  
If greyhounds are unable to deliver financial rewards, their demise is probable. Indeed, death at an early age is the likely fate of most of the dogs that never make it to the race track. 
I highlight that this comes from the research of the industry's peak body. In recent years Greyhound Racing NSW, like the controlling bodies of greyhound racing in other States and Territories, has attempted to reduce wastage rates principally by the rehoming of greyhounds; those efforts have not been successful. Since 2007 it has rehomed only 593 
greyhounds through its Greyhounds As Pets program at a cost of $200,000 per year. The commission estimates, given the tax facilities of potentially rehoming organisations, that this is extremely fraught and there has been no evidence of a viable plan. 
In evidence before the select committee Dr Karen Cunnington of the Greyhound Rehoming Centre said in 2013 that if only 50 per cent of the dogs being bred in New South Wales each year were trained for rehoming, the cost of that training would be up to $60 million. This indicates that rehoming the number of dogs being bred is not a viable proposition. I commend the RSPCA and Greyhound Rescue for the amazing work they do in rehoming greyhounds. I urge everyone who can to adopt or foster a greyhound through Greyhound Rescue or to donate, sponsor or volunteer. 
We know from the inquiry that until recently the Greyhound Racing NSW policy as to dog deaths on tracks was such that information was not to be included in stewards' reports. This calculated stance by the regulator was intended to prevent the public, including persons who may be critical of the greyhound racing industry such as animal welfare organisations, from obtaining information about the number and frequency of deaths of greyhounds on racetracks in New South Wales. As to misreporting of injuries, in April 2013 the commission found that Greyhound Racing NSW management had adopted a policy of sanitising and misreporting the description of injuries recorded in stewards' reports. The commission had no doubt that the reason management adopted this policy was to avoid criticism of the industry in New South Wales, particularly by animal welfare groups. This was in 2013. 
In February last year we witnessed live baiting. The community saw graphic and disturbing footage of live animals—including rabbits, possums and piglets—being mauled and killed by greyhounds at the command of their trainers. It is estimated that 10 per cent to 20 per cent of greyhound trainers in New South Wales engage in live baiting. The issue is typically viewed as raising animal cruelty and welfare issues in respect of the animal being used as bait, such as the terrified rabbit. However, what is less appreciated is the adverse effect that live baiting can have on the future wellbeing of a greyhound. For a significant number of greyhounds the exposure to live baiting can permanently alter them as a result of introducing increased predatory aggression. This adds significantly to the difficulties in being able to successfully re-home the greyhound after the end of its short 365‑day racing career, and that is only if it has not sustained an injury. 
The existence of the practice of live baiting severely taints the greyhound racing industry in New South Wales because of the barbaric cruelty involved in baiting animals and the future prospects for dogs bred in this way. The history of legislation over the past 200 years shows an increasing recognition by the civilised world that without strong legislative intervention and vigilant supervision by regulatory bodies, greyhound coursing and racing inevitably fosters the cruel and barbaric treatment of animals, including the vast majority of greyhounds. My grandfather loved the dogs, but the industry today is not the industry that he loved. Live baiting is only one of the barbarous practices that has been historically associated with greyhound coursing and racing. The deaths of and injuries to tens of thousands of healthy dogs is the other. I commend the bill to the House.

South Wales is responsible for well-documented and systemic animal cruelty. However, when it comes to gambling industries, Mike Baird is no innocent. Likewise he is no innocent when it comes to profiteering by property developers. Here the duality of stamp duties and gambling taxes meet. Mike Baird has gifted public land in Barangaroo to property developers like Lendlease, Mirvac and Grocon, and he has gifted Jamie Packer a new casino at Barangaroo. Let us join the dots  Mike Baird relies on gambling revenue and stamp duty to fund unpopular projects like WestConnex and the new tolls gantries along the M4. Likewise the Liberal Party relies upon the political donations of developers like Crown Resorts Limited. In the past eight years, $500,000 of donations to the Liberal and National parties have flowed from Crown Limited, Crown Resorts, Crown Ltd, or whatever Jamie Packer calls it these days. This occurred throughout the years that we now know the Federal branch of the Liberal Party was laundering illegal donations from property developers on behalf of the State branch of the Liberals. Under reforms introduced by Labor Premier Nathan Rees in 2009, it became illegal for property developers to make donations to political parties in New South Wales. Labor did this to break the unseemly link between planning policy and political influences in the State. 
Instead, a property developer would give money to the Federal Liberal Party—or sometimes a dodgy front in the form of a foundation whose sole purpose was to raise money for the Liberal Party. This donation would then be transferred back to the State branch in a separate payment that would disguise the true origin of the money. These matters are the subject of lengthy Independent Commission Against Corruption investigations. In any case, this is about stamp duty and gambling taxes. Now we find ourselves looking at the issue of greyhound racing. Prime public assets exist in the form of greyhound racing tracks on Crown land across this State. The most obvious example of this public land that could be turned over by the Baird Government to its corporate backers is Wentworth Park.    Wentworth Park, which is located in the heart of Glebe, smack-bang in the middle of the Balmain electorate which is held by Jamie Parker, will now be vulnerable to overdevelopment because of the decision of his colleagues in the Legislative Council to jump in headfirst with the Baird Government. (a)because of the enactment or operation of this Act, or for any consequence of that enactment or operation 
… 
When the live export issue was reopened there were new protections and the people whose livelihoods depended on trade were supported and assisted in the meantime. The Baird Government specifically ruled out this sort of financial assistance. I am disappointed in The Nationals who speak ad nauseam about the economic impact of live export suspension but who cannot bring themselves to vote for industry assistance for workers and business owners in another industry that is strongly represented in their electorates. The Nationals, bar a few, are silent about the need for industry assistance and financial compensation for law-abiding, caring and ethical participants in this industry. 
I have struggled with my position on this bill, as have many Opposition members. All too often politicians front the media or speak in debate in this Chamber and tell their constituents that they have all the answers. We put our opinions or our policies to the public as a series of self-evident truths and we tell ourselves and those around us that we must deliver those policies with surety and confidence. I have conflicts in relation to this bill and I have been struggling for weeks with how to respond to it. I 
have not participated and I 
will never participate in or enjoy this so-called sport. At this point I 
acknowledge a few hundred constituents who respectfully and passionately informed me of their opposition to greyhound racing, based on the animal welfare issues brought to light by the McHugh inquiry. [Extension of time] 
Many have spoken to me of their anger and despair about these serious and unconscionable animal abuses. I 
say tonight that I 
am with them on that point. But significant human impacts arise from the legislation that is before us tonight. I 
do not accept that the only way to improve animal welfare outcomes is to bankrupt low and middle income earners, many thousands of whom love and care for their animals. Nor do I accept that the main beneficiary of the greyhound racing industry closure should be the white-shoe brigade and the mates of Mike Baird Pty Limited. 
This bill will create as many problems as it aims to solve. I did not come into this Parliament to create financial hardship for workers or to enable the privatisation of public assets. Nor did I come into this place to line the pockets of property developers and major gambling interests. Mike Baird's legislation has failed these tests. Nevertheless, a decision has seemingly been made by the Premier before debate and usurping the proper parliamentary process. This is a complex matter. I note two things in conclusion  an assistance package for those good people who love their dogs must be a priority as the industry is closed down; and the care, protection and welfare of the creatures involved in greyhound racing must be paramount as the Government implements the closure. A Commissioner may, in any such report, make such recommendations relating to the publication of the whole or any part of the report as the Commissioner thinks proper.

The member for Heffron told the House about the Labor Party's discussions, but members opposite claim that they have had no opportunity to voice their opinions. That is not true. 
This is the appropriate place in which to make this decision. This Government's actions and decisions have been clear and transparent since 7 July 2016. This has been a difficult but appropriate decision, and it is one that the Coalition has considered deeply before seeking to have this bill passed tonight. We have heard many different views from the community—many from rank-and-file members of The Nationals—and I acknowledge those views. It is up to each member to do what they think is in the best interests of our society and according to their convictions. I make it clear to members that history will judge us all on what we do tonight. For the benefit of members who cannot recall it, the Leader of the Opposition made a pledge some time ago that if the Labor Party were elected to govern in 2019 he would re-establish the greyhound racing industry. I hope there are more practical members on the benches opposite who will see sense and listen to the arguments from tonight's contributions over many hours. I commend the bill to the House.

It was set up after overwhelming evidence of cruelty and following the original legislation to outlaw these practices, in 1953, and more legislation in 1967. Then there were the upper House inquiry and the Independent Commission Against Corruption [ICAC] inquiry, as detailed by the member for Balmain. On that interjection from the member for Maroubra, if someone from The Nationals crosses the floor, I do not kick them out of the party as the Labor Party does. There is a big difference. I 
wish we could believe that the barbaric practice of live baiting was not going to continue. I wish it were true. I 
wish that the overbreeding was not required to keep the industry sustainable and that the pledges made by the alliance were true.

Given these views, and the highly entrenched nature of live baiting as a traditional training method, there is a very real risk that, once the harsh spotlight of this Commission is removed from the industry, the practice of live baiting will thrive once more.

South Wales. I wish this was achievable. Unfortunately, the industry has a poor record not only in managing the lifecycle of greyhounds but also in keeping records of dogs throughout their life. A Commissioner may, in any such report, make such recommendations relating to the publication of the whole or any part of the report as the Commissioner thinks proper.

I make a contribution to debate on the Greyhound Racing Prohibition Bill 2016, which sees the Baird-Grant Liberal-Nationals Government seeking to rubberstamp its proposed ban on the greyhound racing industry in New South Wales from 1 July 2017—now less than 12 
months away. The way in which the Government has approached this blanket ban on greyhound racing—by effectively shutting down the industry with the stroke of a pen without first debating the matter in Parliament—demonstrates its total contempt for the people of New South Wales. And what a show of arrogance it has been. Media reports reveal that not only were the people of New South Wales caught by surprise but also many Liberals and Nationals on the Government benches were completely oblivious to the impending ban until it was announced at a press conference by the Premier and his deputy. 
I can tell members on the other side that I am pleased to take this opportunity today to put on public record that I 
do not support the complete banning of greyhound racing in New South Wales. I stand with the Leader of the Opposition and say that I do not support the decimation of an entire industry and the loss of thousands of jobs in rural and regional New South Wales on the whim of the Premier and his deputy. For me, the issue that those opposite unfortunately have not been talking about during this debate is the jobs of working people in New South Wales. I joined the Australian Labor Party because I believed that it is the only party that stands up for working-class people in New South Wales. Since being elected to this place, I have stood shoulder to shoulder with hundreds of workers who have been hung out to dry by conservative governments in this country. 
I have stood with the public sector workers who have had their jobs axed as a result of privatisation of a number of State Government authorities and agencies, such as the disability support workers from Ageing, Disability and Home Care. I have stood with workers from the New South Wales energy sector who watched their industry be privatised and their workforce chopped in two by the Liberal Government. I have stood where our trains, ships, buses and ferries are built with manufacturing workers who only last week discovered that $2.3 
billion of their industry will be sent offshore. I have stood with them proudly and I will stand with them always. I have stood with Australian seafarers who have watched their jobs go to workers offshore for as little as $2 
a day. Today I stand with those who rely on greyhound racing for their livelihood. We should not be shutting down an entire industry because of the behaviour of a few. 
No-one in this place condones animal cruelty. Labor could not be stronger in its approach to stamping out animal cruelty in this State. This Government has launched a brutal attack on working people while insincerely masking it as stopping animal cruelty. If it was fair dinkum it would look at animal welfare broadly in this State and not pick out one industry. This is hypocrisy at its best, but the devastation it will cause is immeasurable. Members on this side of the House believe there is no place whatsoever in a civilised society for cruelty to animals. Animal cruelty in all of its forms is absolutely abhorrent and should be punished with the full force of the law. That is why Labor supports mandatory life bans and prison sentences for those who engage in barbaric practices such as live baiting. We say unequivocally to those people who choose to be cruel to animals in New South Wales that they will have the book thrown at them; they will be locked up. 
As we know, on 7 July 2016 the Premier released the report of the Special Commission of Inquiry into the Greyhound Racing Industry in NSW, undertaken by Justice Michael McHugh. The report made 80 
recommendations. The first was for the Parliament to consider whether the industry had lost its social licence and should no longer be permitted to operate in New South Wales. The other 79 recommendations provided a comprehensive and detailed plan for the reform of the industry, including the establishment of a New South Wales greyhound racing integrity commission. In its response, the Government announced that the greyhound industry would be completely shut down in New South Wales from 1 July 2017. On behalf of the New South Wales Labor Party, Luke Foley and Michael Daley declared our opposition to the industry-wide ban. Instead, Labor supports a process of significant reform that would provide a highly regulated and monitored greyhound racing industry with the highest standards for animal welfare. 
We would use those 79 recommendations made by Justice McHugh as a road map to regulate the industry and ensure that animal cruelty and unethical practices were permanently removed from the industry. I know that the industry agrees 110 per cent with that. The decision to ban greyhound racing in New South Wales has obviously hit the entire industry hard. People involved in greyhound racing are completely devastated. The 
thousands of people who have done the right thing are absolutely gutted because of the abhorrent actions of 
a 
few, which have painted them as awful people who are routinely cruel to their dogs and who are undertaking a sport that the Government now deems to be unacceptable and will, in fact, become illegal. The greyhound racing industry contributes more than 2,700 full-time jobs to the New South Wales economy, it delivers more than $335 
million indirectly to the people of New South Wales each year and it pays more than $30 million in State taxes annually. 
This is an industry that is innately important to the New South Wales economy. The Government's report puts the number of people participating in the greyhound racing industry at more than 15,000. Nearly three‑quarters of those participants are in regional areas, like the one I live in and represent, and places such as Wyong, Wallsend, Charlestown, Port Stephens, Maitland, Cessnock, the Hunter, the Central Coast and the Illawarra. Those areas are well represented and the greyhound racing industry is alive and well in them. There is plenty of greyhound racing and training in the Upper Hunter too. It is a shame that the member for Upper Hunter is not in the Chamber because I note that he has broken ranks with The Nationals leader on this issue. The member for Upper Hunter obviously knows how important greyhound racing is in his community. On 12 July 2016 theNewcastle Herald quoted the member for Upper Hunter saying  
I would personally support a reconstituted regulative body with tighter restrictions and more oversight of the greyhound industry. 
I could not agree more. I was very pleased to hear the member for Upper Hunter standing up for his community, as he should. I would be more than happy to discuss this matter with him in more detail. I would be happy to work with any members who have the interests and rights of their community at the front of their minds in relation to greyhound racing. I note that a number of Nationals members have expressed their opposition to this bill and that they have been on the end of an attack by their Nationals leader. The Deputy Premier has been rather arrogant in dismissing his partyroom colleagues. [Extension of time] 
The Deputy Premier has accused those opposing the ban of making ill-informed comments, saying  
I wish the two outspoken National MPs [had] read the [special commission of inquiry] report. One of them rang me, Katrina Hodgkinson, and asked me about it. I encouraged her to read the report before she spoke out. She didn't do that. It's on her head. 
To me, that shows rather peculiar leadership and I am very concerned about that language. In fact, in the last parliamentary sitting week the Deputy Premier referred to the good people involved in the greyhound racing industry as "thugs and bullies, attempting to tar every person in that industry with the same brush". The Deputy Premier is interjecting. I remind him that we can get this material fromHansard, because that is where I got it. We may be able to excuse the Premier a little when he makes these types of allegations, because he does not leave Manly. So we can understand his ignorance, but the Deputy Premier, who comes from a regional area, should not make comments like that. We all find it rather peculiar and very curious. The only bullying that I have seen is by those on the opposite side of the Chamber, so I find the Deputy Premier's comments a bit rich. I grew up in a family that owned greyhounds; we even raced them from time to time. 
I have known many people—in particular my father's friends—who, to this day, race greyhounds. The people I have known throughout my life have helped make me the person I am, and I am proud to say that some of those people owned greyhounds. The Government wants to victimise them and call them bad people who are brutal to animals, but that has never been my experience. I have been fortunate enough to have grown up in the company of respectable people who enjoy the sport of greyhound racing—and horseracing and trotting, for that matter. I have had a lovely life. My life has been not too dissimilar, I think, from the life of the member for Castle Hill, but I do not share his view that greyhound racing is brutal and should therefore be banned. I absolutely understand the distress of many people in the industry. It is distressing for me to have to share with you an email from a constituent in the Swansea electorate. I will not use the person's name because when I spoke with him last night I told him that I would not.    I have not made it up. I am happy to table it, but I would prefer it if members kept it private because I think that we should respect the privacy of our constituents. I know that the member for Kiama would agree.    The person sending the email says, "I am 39 years of age. My wife is 36." They have a son who is three years of age. He continues  
I beg you to help myself and my family. We have just spent $50,000 on new kennels and fencing to comply with the new code of practice that Paul Newson and Greyhound Racing NSW brought in only recently. Since the announcement by Mike Baird and Troy 
Grant to ban greyhound racing I have not slept well, and some nights actually sleep in the kennels with my dogs. 
My constituent went on to tell me that he is now taking drugs for depression. This is personal for me. I can never support the banning of this industry, because it will hurt people and create mental illness in my community.    Wentworth Park is where greyhounds race, Deputy Premier.    He is debating—    It is not on relevance. The Deputy Premier is debating the issue.

In a larger organisation, that probably can be  managed, but in a smaller organisation it can become quite difficult. I will provide members with some examples, a couple of which have already been used today. I have always found extreme value in having someone with a legal background on a committee. It is  almost a constant issue to make sure that women are given an opportunity to serve on our board and the numbers  are well represented, but we do not have targets and we choose on merit. Clause 7: Functions —    My friends have made no accusations that I know of.    I am not sure I have got the exact message, but I have been advised that it makes  a submission, and has made submissions in the past, to the board. The answer is both. Racing is clearly within the legislation and Healthway sponsors it. No, they were not; it was just a housekeeping thing in terms of drafting the legislation. The point has been made to me that it is the foundation that will decide the conditions. This  is not a direction by Treasury or government on how something should or should not be done. No, because I read out to you that it says I am not allowed to. Section 65 has been carried over to clause 8, except section 65(2)(d), as Treasury is of the view that this is better  incorporated in a grant agreement instead of being legislated. Again, that is the requirement of the board.     It is the same answer as before: these are just housekeeping issues that do not change the  functions or the outcomes of the bill, so there was no need to consult on them.    I have not met any of them.    People may or may not trust me or the things that I say, but with me here is a highly  respected person of medical background and a highly respected person of legal background, both of whom have  advised me that these are minor issues that do not affect the bill. I was bringing in the legislation.    Just read it; it makes sense. It is largely the same; there is just some updating of words. The reference to CEO and other  staff members has been updated from the original section, but otherwise it is the same. Clause 30 deals with disclosure of  material personal interest, and clause 31 deals with voting by interested member, and so on. That all relates back  to this clause. The member needs to refer to clauses 16 and 17, which relate to the length of time for which  a member may be absent. At the end of the day, I understand  the point the member is making. People can make judgements on whether I have done that when they see the  composition of the board. I do not regard that as competitive argument. In  fact, some of the feedback we got from some people who were working within the department—I am sure this  was not the case all the time—was that the atmosphere was toxic at times. We see this as a better way of  operating and a better way of moving forward. A significant number of people on that board were still appointed  by government. Some were on the board because of the organisations they represent. Of course there is nothing  preventing government from being involved in trying to influence the appointment of those members but  generally that is not the case. The chair was appointed by the minister on the recommendation of the Premier,  and there were other members, including appointees by chief executives. Remember that we appoint  chief executives. The capacity for influence by government on significant numbers of the previous board was  there, although we never did any of those things. I am comfortable that this is in line with normal boards. It is in  line with the Lotteries Commission Act. It is the standard way of appointing boards in this state, and I am  confident that this board will do the job required of it.    The Lotteries Commission has six members and, although that was based on the  Lotteries Commission Act, I felt that seven was a more appropriate number. It gave me that one extra member to  choose from, and is an uneven number, which is always good for a committee that may have a vote. I believe  that seven is the right number. I have always been of the view that boards should have seven to nine members to  be cohesive and well-functioning. More than that tends to result in too many people trying to have too much  input, which often ends in conflict. I point out once again that—this is not necessarily the specific number— I remember talking to Dr Capolingua about having seven or nine members. Certainly this was something that  was supported, in fact, even promoted by the chair of the board, because of the difficulty that she had  experienced with the structure of the previous board and the problems that that was causing.    As I said, letters were sent. I will correct something I said. I do not know whether they were  specifically told the number of people who would be on the board or that it was changing from that  representative structure to a board that would be appointed. A number of responses came back. Things such as that were incorporated into legislation and we agreed with most of those things. The Chamber of  Arts and Culture talked about a voice with understanding in the arts sector. The WA Sports Federation talked  about the dysfunctionality of the agency and about making sure that there were people on the board who had  contemporary understanding of the importance of sports, arts and government sectors; it referred to an  understanding of the structure of sport, and the management and delivery of all levels of sports.  The Department of Sport and Recreation emphasised the importance of the independence of the foundation,  contrasting the models with other boards such as Vicwest and Lotterywest. It stressed the importance of  employing plenty of people with a thorough understanding of sport and recreation. The Public Sector  Commissioner supported the proposal on changing where the members sat. The Western Australian branch of  the Australian Council for Health, Physical Education and Recreation did not oppose the proposed changes to the  board appointment and made several comments regarding the importance of the foundation’s work and the  expertise it considered appropriate to have represented on the board. That is a summary of the findings.    The foundation will comprise seven members, so there are some limits. The chair will have  a field of expertise; we want two with an arts background and two with a sports background, so that is five. With  seven members, we want to make sure that people have got some expertise in other areas.   I am sure that if someone has expertise in youth and is a lawyer and a lover of the arts, we would have three  things in one. We will be looking for people who have multiple areas of expertise to make sure we get a good  mix of backgrounds on the board. As the member knows, lots of funding is provided to youth organisations,  youth sport, youth art and youth culture, so we will be looking for people who have expertise in those areas, even  if they are not listed. This clause does not stop me from appointing people who have expertise in other areas; it  requires me, largely based on submissions that were put forward, to have at least one person in each of those  areas. I will probably have more than one expert in some of those areas, particularly in health, because the  foundation is about health promotion, research and a whole range of areas related to health, but I will make sure  that those other organisations are well represented as well.    The first three were put forward because of the requirement to provide funding to those  organisations. It was based partially on the Lotteries Commission Act and the Public Sector Commission, and  the requirement for someone with a legal background was put in because it seemed like a good idea, and I think  it is a good idea. I have always found extreme value in having someone with a legal background on a committee.     By the way, members, this is the last clause we will be doing, so once this is finished we will  knock off.    I would like to point out that the last two chairs of the board were female. Although we do  not divulge what goes on in cabinet, I can tell the member that the form we put forward to cabinet about  members of the board contains a section in which the number of men and women is clearly delineated. It is  almost a constant issue to make sure that women are given an opportunity to serve on our board and the numbers  are well represented, but we do not have targets and we choose on merit.    I think it is the latter. Remember, the previous legislation stated that the Premier had to  recommend a person, and had to consult with other parties—I am pretty sure it is “parties” under the definition  of “parliamentary parties”, so that would involve the Liberal Party, the Labor Party, the Greens and the  National Party. Then it would come to me as the minister and I would have to consult with them all over again. I can say that what you need to do is pass this clause and we will let you know tomorrow if  Hon Rick Mazza is listed as one to be consulted.

text: I rise to speak on the Western Australian Health Promotion  Foundation Bill 2015. Healthway is an integral part of our community, and I have huge admiration for the  original legislation, which was first debated, I think, back in 1990. In 2005, Hon Jim McGinty read the second  reading speech for the legislation that would become the Tobacco Products Control Act 2006. This is an amazing  organisation that has had a remarkably productive history, and I think we owe a huge amount to the work of  Healthway and to the individuals involved in its original creation. It has done some amazing work.  My sport has benefited from it. I remember writing applications for many years for the State Equestrian Centre  to sponsor dressage and other competitions. I remembered, with great glee, putting bags of “2 and 5” around the  outside of the equestrian complex when the horses were all on deck to compete. The 2 and 5 is, of course, two  fruits and five vegetables. There were lots of bags of carrots available. A couple of very enthusiastic horses  ended up partaking in the 2 and 5 and cleaning up some of Healthway’s promotional material, much to  everyone’s glee!  I differ substantially from the member for Kingsley’s assessment of what went wrong at Healthway. This comes  from my understanding of what happened. I was not on the inside so I am not completely convinced that I know  the letter of every detail, but I have done a bit of research and I have listened to the debates in this house. I think  the government has taken a sledgehammer to fix something that could have been fixed by making sure that the  management and leadership in the organisation was on track and making sure that some of the government’s  issues within Healthway, as it was structured, were correct. The government has thrown the baby out with the  bathwater. I have gone back to read the debates that occurred in 1990. The Minister for Health probably read  some of them in anticipation as well. The second reading of the Tobacco Bill occurred in 1990. I came across  a number of comments from the then opposition, which would have been the Liberal Party of the day.  Mr Bradshaw contributed to the second reading debate on 4 July 1990. I will quote Mr Bradshaw when  discussing the Liberal Party’s concerns about what might happen with funding that was put into this kind of  foundation —  The next section concerns the Health Promotion Foundation, and though the intent may be quite good  I am concerned that the foundation might be regarded as a slush fund. I would hate to see the situation  come about where, for political purposes, the Government will hand out cheques to sporting bodies  which it may wish to win over for a coming election or for any other reason.  That does resonate a bit, does it not?    That was out of the mouths of the opposition of the day, which was, of course, the  Liberal Party.  Those of us who remember Dr Turnbull, the member for Collie, would remember her fondly. Her contribution to  this debate back in 1990 included the following comments —  We have heard how the Victorian Health Promotion Foundation is building up a large sum of money. It  has been said that this is because it has a good administrator and that it is husbanding its funds well. It  has also been said that the foundation is purposely accumulating money in order to have a large fund to  draw on in a pre-election year. We do not want to presume that pre-election pork-barrelling will be the  action of this Government, but we feel that all moneys should be disbursed within the one year; ….  This amendment, as it was being put on the day, would ensure that happened.  In response, Mr Minson said —  The Opposition is not too concerned about whether it is two, three or six months, but a time frame must  be specified for the distribution of funds, which will prevent the accumulation of large reserves.       I will mention other issues in a minute. I thought that the comments about pork-barrelling, which occurred  several times during the Liberal Party’s debate when this was first put before the house in 1990, were very  interesting because it also reflects the concerns this opposition has about changes that may erode the  independence of this organisation.  Looking at the original debates around membership, it was very clear that membership of this organisation was  meant to be 11 people from organisations representing health, sports, the arts and local government, and  specified worthy organisations such as the Australian Medical Association, the WA Sports Federation, the  WA Sports Council, the WA Association of Professional Performing Arts, the Australian Council on Smoking  and Health, and the WA Municipal Association, and the chief executives of the Department of Health, the  Ministry of Sport and Recreation, the Ministry of the Arts and the Bureau of Youth Affairs. Of the foundation’s  11 members, representatives from outside government would outnumber those from within government. Does  the minister remember that the first appointment was Harry Sorensen? He is a very dear friend of mine.  I understand that he was the head of the very first board of this foundation.  Changing the legislation in order to reduce the independence of Healthway is not a good thing. The concern in  the community is that the Minister for Health has a bit of a track record on this. I refer to the role of the  Commissioner for Children and Young People. I know and understand that no government particularly likes  independent commissioners, and I understand that the opposition would have opinions about independent  commissioners. The position of WA children’s commissioner has been vacant for over two years because the  government simply has not moved to appoint one. It has put an acting commissioner into that role. She is  a public servant. To me, or any person outside these walls, that would be a complete conflict of interest. It is  shameful that the government has allowed that to happen and it is to the detriment of children in this state.  A great concern with this legislative change is that the government is again eroding the independence of an  organisation. My colleague the shadow Minister for Health described the journey with Dixie Marshall and  others. He also described the conflict with Carlton and United Breweries. If it is not something that the  government has used as a background, it is certainly publicly very obvious that the wishes of big alcohol  corporations are very closely aligned to the drafting of this bill. If it is not the government’s intention to do  that—I have heard the minister say it is not his intention to do that—that is a very great misfortune.  Several members interjected.    I understand that Peter Foss was most concerned about the independence of this board.  I will end my speech with a few other things I want to put on the record. Although the focus on smoking has  shifted, Healthway had incredible success in delivering a reduction in the number of smokers in WA that could  have been carried forward into other areas, such as alcohol. There is substantial concern in the community about  the Western Australian and Australian drinking patterns. Eighty per cent of the alcohol consumed by young  people aged 14 to 24 is consumed in ways that puts their health, and the health of others, at risk of acute harm.  By 14 years of age, 80 per cent of WA school students have used alcohol. Of the 16 to 17-year-old WA school  students who reported drinking in the past week of this survey I am referring to, 43 per cent reported that one of  the main reasons they did it was to get drunk. I do not have time to go on this afternoon because the opposition  has committed to keep this short. I could go on and talk in great detail about the current threat that we are  experiencing in our community because of excessive alcohol abuse.  Members know that I have been fighting the big destination liquor outlets that continue to mushroom in the most  remarkable places around this state. I will continue to fight them. I have great respect for Malcolm McCusker  and his wife, Tonya McCusker, who have made a remarkable philanthropic contribution to fund the McCusker  Centre for Action on Alcohol and Youth. The work they are doing was driven home to me in a letter I received  today about the disappointment that the McCusker Centre has in the Western Australian government.  Sitting suspended from 6.00 to 7.00 pm     I would like to conclude my comments by putting on the record a letter that I received on  12 August from the McCusker Centre for Action on Alcohol and Youth about its disappointment with the  Western Australian government’s failure to introduce legislation to ban the secondary supply of alcohol to  minors, which was meant to be introduced this week.    It was?    I blinked! Very good. Was it introduced into the house?  [Quorum formed.]    Thank you very much, Mr Acting Speaker (Mr I.C. Blayney). I am much reassured by the  presence of my parliamentary colleagues.    Those on the other side of the house are disappearing. During that brief interruption I was  informed that the Minister for Racing and Gaming actually presented the bill on secondary supply in the upper  house today. I am absolutely sure that the McCuskers will be delighted with that, as will Samantha McKenzie,  who has been a strong advocate for that legislation. I congratulate her and the McCusker centre on the work they  have done.  Just before I sit down, I advise the minister that there are three issues that I particularly want him to address in  the consideration in detail stage. My concern is that the movement of this foundation into the public sector  regime has the capacity to let it be treated like any other public sector agency, so I need some reassurance on  a number of things. My first concern is with the efficiency dividends that apply across the sector. I would be  very sad if Healthway, or this new iteration of Healthway, were suddenly subjected to the sort of funding cuts  that public sector agencies have been subjected to by not just this government but also many governments in the  past. If that were to occur, it would be absolutely retrograde for this organisation. I know the minister would not  want that. I hope that some assurance will be easily given that Healthway will be quarantined from the impact of  those kinds of budget cuts and measures; they do not impact now and they should not impact in the future.   Secondly, I talked earlier in my speech about the granting of funds. Concern was expressed by many members on  the Liberal Party side when the debate around the tobacco bill was originally held back in 1990 about what happens  if this body collects funds and does not distribute them and whether there would be some compulsion for the  organisation to give out a certain percentage of its funding over time. I have already read into Hansard that that was  an issue that the minister’s side, when in opposition, debated heavily when this legislation was first considered.  I would like some assurance on that. The final thing that concerns me is that when a government agency is in  receipt of consolidated revenue funds, at the completion of a budget year funding that has not been spent is quite  often subject to return to the consolidated account or goes back into the central revenue fund of government. That  cannot happen with this foundation; it would be completely counterintuitive. As far as I can see from my  experience in the charitable and non-government sector, the independence of Healthway is, in many respects, being  cut on a number of levels. Hopefully some of the changes might be improvements, but the thing that worries me  most is the effect of Healthway being treated as a government agency and coming under the various legislative  regimes that exist for agencies that are part of government. Will it be exempt from cuts to its budget? How will the  money that is in Healthway be disposed of within the appropriate period, be it six months or 12 months, and not  held over as a slush fund for a pre-election campaign? Finally, will the agency be forced to return money to the  consolidated account if it has underspent funds? With those comments on the record, I look forward to the  consideration in detail stage. I understand that the opposition will not be supporting the bill as it stands.    I snuck up on the member for Kwinana. We believe that this  bill is essentially an attack upon their approach to public health. Initially these sorts of measures were  opposed by the Liberal Party in Western Australia, but it too came to the party. I want to acknowledge the role of  Hon Peter Foss in terms of the Tobacco Products Control Act 2006, and the contribution that he made on that  particular debate.  This is about the real public health debate. It is not just about tobacco anymore. This is about the incidence of  and the patterns of behaviour around alcohol consumption. It is around obesity and the impact that obesity has  upon the health of people in our community. We are of the view that not only should someone be able to access  healthcare as they need according to their health needs, but also that people should enjoy quality health  throughout their lives so that they do not spend it living sicker lives, whilst other members of the community  enjoy much more fruitful and better health and well-being simply because they are not from a disadvantaged  background. We understand that if we are to make an improvement with alcohol, tobacco and obesity, it will  take a lot of work.
