Braidwood, which is a satellite service area for the Queanbeyan hospital, has an excellent multipurpose centre that was funded largely through the work and efforts of the local community. 
 
Concerns have been raised that funding has not been provided to repair the hospital's security doors. That may seem a minor matter when one considers the multibillion dollar funding that is spent on health services, but the community—which takes enormous pride in the multipurpose centre, having raised money for its construction—considers that the hospital is not being given any priority by the Government. The lack of action on the part of the Government to ensure the safety of staff, who work in the hospital 24 hours a day, is a sign to the people of Braidwood that the Carr Government does not care about the delivery of services to them. They are a small dot on the Government's map. 
 
 
 
The fact that money was spent on a paediatrics ward that has never been opened highlights a significant lack of appropriate planning by the Government. We recently became aware that the Southern Area Health Service was in debt and had not paid some of its creditors' bills. That matter was addressed in very recent times, but the Government had to be shamed into addressing it. Patients from one area told me that last Friday night they were asked to take bandages home and wash them. That is further proof of a breakdown in the delivery of services in the Southern Area Health Service. One only has to look at the expenditure by the Carr Government in the Southern Area Health Service to understand the nature of the problems. 
 
 
Though staffing figures increased by 3.1 per cent between 1996-97 and 2001-02, 25.5 per cent of that increase has been in the clerical-administrative area. At the same time, the number of specialist professionals has increased by 5.6 per cent, yet bed numbers have decreased by 19.5 per cent. There has been an increase in the number of professionals, but there are fewer beds. We are talking about a significant growth area, one of the fastest-growing areas in the State. One would assume that there would be an increase in the provision of services in such an area, but, to the contrary, bed numbers have decreased in that time. 
 
 
The problems all relate to the Government's administration of health services generally. It was well pointed out by the shadow Minister for Health after the budget was delivered last year that during the period of the Carr Government the proportion of the health budget spent on capital works has halved. When Labor was first elected, capital works expenditure represented 10.4 per cent of total health spending. It is now down to just 4.9 per cent. The Government has not had a clear policy on infrastructure expenditure. The Treasurer is besotted with reducing debt, but the consequence is that money has not been spent on infrastructure in important areas. Communities such as the rapidly growing Queanbeyan community have received funding commitments, but the money will be spent over many years. The community expects to have a redeveloped hospital soon, but it will not occur until at least 2007-08. And I suppose the Government will loudly tout the redevelopment before the next election. Therefore, I move  
 
That the motion be amended by omitting "18 months" in sub-paragraph (a) and inserting instead "more than 2 years ago". 
 
Once again, I emphasise the failure by the Carr Government to underpin health services for the people of Queanbeyan and the electorate of Monaro.

text:
The Greens support the intent of this motion. It is significant that over the past eight years or so the Government has trumpeted its budget surpluses and always suggested that they are the hallmark of its good management. However, we now see the results of that management, including consistent underfunding of transport and health in particular. During this period the Government has consistently refused to maintain, replace or enhance essential infrastructure. Nowhere is this more apparent than in the provision of health services. The people who have to bear the brunt of this underfunding are the underpaid and overworked staff who attempt to maintain systems that are, in fact, falling to pieces. In that regard, I refer to an article that appeared in the Canberra Times on 2 April which stated A local hospital is placing patients at risk in advising them to reuse disposable medical equipment, including bandages, by washing the equipment in boiling water at home, an infectious diseases specialist warns.Some patients treated at the Queanbeyan Hospital had been sent home with sterile probes designed for single use, advised to boil the equipment and reuse it.Other patients with lymphodema—a build up of lymphatic fluid that causes swelling—were told that they could reuse bandages by washing them at home.Obviously, this advice is of major concern in relation to the potential to spread infection. As the article notes, it is difficult to treat equipment at home properly. Equipment can be disinfected by being boiled for 10 to 15 minutes, but that does not sterilise it. In addition, people may experience burns and accidents when they are trying to sterilise or disinfect equipment. The article further stated  Professor Collignon—who is also ACT Salaried Medical Officers' Federation—said the problem reinforced the inadequate funding for the Southern Area Health Service.The service, which runs hospitals and health clinics throughout the Monaro, South Coast and Southern Tablelands, is more than $6 million in debt.I am sure the debt has increased since that time. The provision of acute and critical care and hospital care is a real problem, but other issues also deserve to be canvassed in this debate. Looking only at hospital care is taking a very narrow view of the services that should be provided by a State Government that is interested in the health and welfare of the community. I draw attention to home care support services, particularly in relation to the Queanbeyan area. One should bear in mind that more than 50,000 people rely upon such support services across New South Wales. I am afraid that it is only too true that what happens to the people of the Monaro and Queanbeyan areas is merely a reflection of what happens to people elsewhere in the State. 
 
Home care services are vital because they help to keep people out of hospital and living functional lives in their communities. Not only do those services improve the quality of life for those with disabilities or in poor health, they enable people to live self-sufficient lives and help take the pressure off an already overstretched hospital system. The area surrounding the Australian Capital Territory severely lacks adequate home care support services for people with disabilities, mental illness and chronic conditions, and the elderly. If Queanbeyan residents lived in the Australian Capital Territory rather than in New South Wales they would have access to far superior facilities and services, including access to four centre-based respite houses, to six autism units, to Family Based Respite Care Inc.—an in-home recreational and respite service—to child health and development services, to a child health and development service, to community options services and to a plethora of dedicated in-home physiotherapy, speech therapy, occupational therapy, autism and counselling programs, and to dedicated home support aged care services. 
 
 
Such services are either not provided by the New South Wales Government to people in New South Wales or they are provided at a greatly reduced level in the Australian Capital Territory. The Queanbeyan District Unmet Needs Campaign is a community-based group that formed approximately a year ago to lobby for better services for New South Wales carers and the people for whom they care. They found that in many cases Queanbeyan residents travel across the border into the Australian Capital Territory to access services that are simply not available in New South Wales. In most cases people are in a crisis situation and have no choice but to pay for those services from their own pockets. 
 
 
I am talking about preventive care  providing support services that help to keep people out of the hospital system and living healthier, better quality lives. However, the Government refuses to provide adequate funding for such services. We are seeing the benefits—or rather the disbenefits—of an economic rationalist approach to the provision of health care. In the 1980s a Labor Government embarked on a program of hospital closures and cutbacks. Between 1988 and 1995 the Coalition Government pursued the privatisation of public hospitals, closing 11 public hospitals, partially closing two more, downgrading five, cutting one in half and converting another into a nursing home. This policy has continued under the current Carr Government, with the further loss of small rural and suburban hospitals and the abolition or amalgamation of health services and facilities. 
 
 
Cost cutting measures including early patient discharge, operating theatre closures and the deinstitutionalisation of mental health patients, combined with the reduction of home support services, have resulted in a system in crisis. Whether it is the police shooting mental health patients, increased suicide rates, single mothers living in cars or the aged malnutrition rates, cost cutting and inadequate support services are contributing factors. The Greens reject the ideology of economic rationalism. We believe that communities and social impacts should underpin all health decision making, not financial priorities and the short-term private profit. Government should regard health care as an investment, rather than a cost. Health funding should be allocated where it is needed most, not according to those who can afford to pay. The most cost effective of all health funding should be investment in preventive health and services that keep people out of hospitals and, wherever possible, in their own homes and communities. 
 
 
The Government knows that Queanbeyan residents have inadequate home support services. It knows that Queanbeyan residents travel across the border to access services available in the Australian Capital Territory that are not funded in New South Wales. On 18 January 2003 Canberra hospital had its busiest day on record, with more than 300 people registering at the casualty ward. On the same day Queanbeyan District Hospital had only 34 people registering at its casualty ward. Between 1996 and 2000 the population of Queanbeyan increased at twice the rate of that of the Australian Capital Territory. However, health funding increased only marginally. 
 
 
A damning report by the Australian Capital Territory Labor Government earlier this year was highly critical of the discrepancy in health funding between New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory. The 2004 Australian Capital Territory Treasury document notes that the Australian Capital Territory health system is struggling to cope under the strain caused by the reduction of services in New South Wales. The report states  
 
NSW continues to reduce services and/or has not established new services to provide for increasing need …The Southern Area Health Service … NSW has the second lowest self-sufficiency ratio of all NSW area health services, measured as a ratio of public supply to public demand of acute hospital services for residents …Later it continues A more disturbing development, again outlined in discussions to date, is the observation from service providers of a marked reduction in service levels provided by New South Wales regions. This has created a ratcheting effect, entrenching greater usage and reliance on ACT services.That is what one Labor government has to say about another. It says that New South Wales is seriously disadvantaging not only the people of New South Wales but also the people of the Australian Capital Territory by failing to provide sufficient services to meet demand. In New South Wales hospital bed availability in the Southern Area Health Service has fallen significantly every year from 1996. In 1996 there were 949 available beds, but by 2001 there were only 812. 
 
Finally, I turn to the Health budget. A disturbing trend has emerged over the term of this Treasurer's reign towards providing less and less detail in the budget. Each year it gets harder to determine what funding has been allocated to specific programs and services. Increasingly, the budget is an opaque document, with funding often diverted from one program to another, or with program funding aggregated to make it impossible to ascertain the funding for discrete programs. Thousands of people working in the community health care sector, not to mention the thousands more who are clients of the services, are left in the dark as to the full funding available to specific programs. 
 
 
The Council of Social Service of New South Wales, the peak community sector organisation in the State, has been particularly critical of the increased use of smoke and mirrors tactics by this Government to hide the true picture of health funding deficiencies in New South Wales. No doubt deficiencies and smoke and mirrors will be a hallmark of the coming budget in June. The Greens deplore the level of funding for community support services. We deplore the lack of funding for services in Queanbeyan and surrounding areas. And we condemn this Government's reliance on services and funding in the Australian Capital Territory.

I am afraid that it is only too true that what happens to the people of the Monaro and Queanbeyan areas is merely a reflection of what happens to people elsewhere in the State. 
 
Home care services are vital because they help to keep people out of hospital and living functional lives in their communities. Not only do those services improve the quality of life for those with disabilities or in poor health, they enable people to live self-sufficient lives and help take the pressure off an already overstretched hospital system. The area surrounding the Australian Capital Territory severely lacks adequate home care support services for people with disabilities, mental illness and chronic conditions, and the elderly. If Queanbeyan residents lived in the Australian Capital Territory rather than in New South Wales they would have access to far superior facilities and services, including access to four centre-based respite houses, to six autism units, to Family Based Respite Care Inc.—an in-home recreational and respite service—to child health and development services, to a child health and development service, to community options services and to a plethora of dedicated in-home physiotherapy, speech therapy, occupational therapy, autism and counselling programs, and to dedicated home support aged care services. 
 
 
Such services are either not provided by the New South Wales Government to people in New South Wales or they are provided at a greatly reduced level in the Australian Capital Territory. The Queanbeyan District Unmet Needs Campaign is a community-based group that formed approximately a year ago to lobby for better services for New South Wales carers and the people for whom they care. They found that in many cases Queanbeyan residents travel across the border into the Australian Capital Territory to access services that are simply not available in New South Wales. In most cases people are in a crisis situation and have no choice but to pay for those services from their own pockets. 
 
 
I am talking about preventive care  providing support services that help to keep people out of the hospital system and living healthier, better quality lives. However, the Government refuses to provide adequate funding for such services. We are seeing the benefits—or rather the disbenefits—of an economic rationalist approach to the provision of health care. In the 1980s a Labor Government embarked on a program of hospital closures and cutbacks. Between 1988 and 1995 the Coalition Government pursued the privatisation of public hospitals, closing 11 public hospitals, partially closing two more, downgrading five, cutting one in half and converting another into a nursing home. This policy has continued under the current Carr Government, with the further loss of small rural and suburban hospitals and the abolition or amalgamation of health services and facilities. 
 
 
Cost cutting measures including early patient discharge, operating theatre closures and the deinstitutionalisation of mental health patients, combined with the reduction of home support services, have resulted in a system in crisis. Whether it is the police shooting mental health patients, increased suicide rates, single mothers living in cars or the aged malnutrition rates, cost cutting and inadequate support services are contributing factors. The Greens reject the ideology of economic rationalism. We believe that communities and social impacts should underpin all health decision making, not financial priorities and the short-term private profit. Government should regard health care as an investment, rather than a cost. Health funding should be allocated where it is needed most, not according to those who can afford to pay. The most cost effective of all health funding should be investment in preventive health and services that keep people out of hospitals and, wherever possible, in their own homes and communities. 
 
 
The Government knows that Queanbeyan residents have inadequate home support services. It knows that Queanbeyan residents travel across the border to access services available in the Australian Capital Territory that are not funded in New South Wales. On 18 January 2003 Canberra hospital had its busiest day on record, with more than 300 people registering at the casualty ward. On the same day Queanbeyan District Hospital had only 34 people registering at its casualty ward. Between 1996 and 2000 the population of Queanbeyan increased at twice the rate of that of the Australian Capital Territory. However, health funding increased only marginally. 
 
 
A damning report by the Australian Capital Territory Labor Government earlier this year was highly critical of the discrepancy in health funding between New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory. The 2004 Australian Capital Territory Treasury document notes that the Australian Capital Territory health system is struggling to cope under the strain caused by the reduction of services in New South Wales. The report states  
 
NSW continues to reduce services and/or has not established new services to provide for increasing need …The Southern Area Health Service … NSW has the second lowest self-sufficiency ratio of all NSW area health services, measured as a ratio of public supply to public demand of acute hospital services for residents …Later it continues A more disturbing development, again outlined in discussions to date, is the observation from service providers of a marked reduction in service levels provided by New South Wales regions. This has created a ratcheting effect, entrenching greater usage and reliance on ACT services.That is what one Labor government has to say about another. It says that New South Wales is seriously disadvantaging not only the people of New South Wales but also the people of the Australian Capital Territory by failing to provide sufficient services to meet demand. In New South Wales hospital bed availability in the Southern Area Health Service has fallen significantly every year from 1996. In 1996 there were 949 available beds, but by 2001 there were only 812. 
 
Finally, I turn to the Health budget. A disturbing trend has emerged over the term of this Treasurer's reign towards providing less and less detail in the budget. Each year it gets harder to determine what funding has been allocated to specific programs and services. Increasingly, the budget is an opaque document, with funding often diverted from one program to another, or with program funding aggregated to make it impossible to ascertain the funding for discrete programs. Thousands of people working in the community health care sector, not to mention the thousands more who are clients of the services, are left in the dark as to the full funding available to specific programs. 
 
 
The Council of Social Service of New South Wales, the peak community sector organisation in the State, has been particularly critical of the increased use of smoke and mirrors tactics by this Government to hide the true picture of health funding deficiencies in New South Wales. No doubt deficiencies and smoke and mirrors will be a hallmark of the coming budget in June. The Greens deplore the level of funding for community support services. We deplore the lack of funding for services in Queanbeyan and surrounding areas. And we condemn this Government's reliance on services and funding in the Australian Capital Territory.

It is not a black hole and we should not be experiencing continued delays in relation to the Royal Hobart Hospital. This has been the case for at least five years now. That expenditure I am referring to in relation to moving the hospital site was prior to the last state election, In September 2006, if the Labor government at the time had been serious about the Royal Hobart Hospital and selected an appropriate site, a new hospital could have been built by 2011. Going through the history, it is important to note that in April 2007 the government of the time under the leadership of Paul Lennon announced that the waterfront had been selected by cabinet as the preferred site. However, not five months later the government embarked on a two - month, $500 million spending spree before the state election was announced and then, of course, clocked up promises worth a similar amount during the campaign. It is an important hospital to the state, being our main teaching hospital.  It is now important to the whole of the health and health sciences precinct because of the Menzies Centre's buildings number 1 and 2 being heavily invested in by the federal government to the University of Tasmania. I am conscious of time and that there are other people wishing to make a contribution but I thought it important to highlight the history since around 2006 in relation to expenditure, promises, broken promises, and delays.

text: I do, and thank you for acknowledging my great interest in this.  The redevelopment of the Royal Hobart Hospital is one of the largest health infrastructure spends in the country and is vital for the future of the Tasmanian health network. The redevelopment will cost around $586 million, of which $225 million is state funds and around $340 million is commonwealth funds.   The Royal Hobart Hospital redevelopment is progressing and new medical services have already been open to the public.   The first $100 million spend by the state government has been delivered within budget, which is very positive to see, and a credit to the Minister for Health, who has been on her feet earlier discussing the redevelopment. We have seen so far a new assessment and planning unit which is already in operation, providing a more streamlined assessment service for acute medical patients, which has a theatre in it too. A new production kitchen is fully operational at Cambridge, providing healthy meals and increased capacity, which in turn can generate income for the hospital. The department of medical imaging has been expanded to include six new ultrasound suites, a new PET CT scanner and a fluoroscopy machine. New day - chemotherapy and acute rehabilitation units are also now operational and an extensive modern fire alarm system and other infrastructure upgrades have also been installed. Other works are due to be finished during 2013. We have seen an improved intensive care unit featuring increased natural light for patients and a new cancer centre on the corner of Liverpool and Campbell Streets with a new linear accelerator which will soon be in use. We have seen outpatient clinics which are already being provided from the new Wellington clinics, with an air bridge across Argyle Street providing clinicians with efficient access to the main hospital campus. In peak construction periods up to 175 construction workers have been employed and this is expected to double when we undertake the next phase of building the multi - storey inpatient precinct buildings. We have seen the Wellington Centre, where patients are already benefiting from the newly established clinics. The leasing of the Wellington Centre has been put in place to enable decanting to take place in the hospital site and create space for the further redevelopment of the hospital.   Some $11 million has been spent upgrading the Wellington Centre. Seven floors of the centre have been leased for 10 years with a four - year option and negotiations are underway to lease a further floor to accommodate women's clinics in the Wellington Centre. This will provide significantly improved space and a layout which is compliant with contemporary standards and expectations and can be achieved at an affordable cost. We have seen the opposition discuss the $10 million that was spent in terms of developing what was then proposed for a new Royal Hobart Hospital on the waterfront. It is important to note  -  and the Opposition has been told time and time again  -  that this has not been a wasted investment.   The early work that has been spent around that $10 million has been utilised by the Sullivan's Cove Waterfront Authority and has greatly assisted in the remediation of the site around contamination. Also, the early planning work and clinical engagement has been used to inform and support the vision for the redevelopment of the Royal Hobart Hospital on the existing site.   In terms of the design, extensive work has been ongoing to ensure that the best, most efficient use of available space is realised. Clinical input has been very strong and a recent value management study has identified increased efficiencies which the project team is working hard to implement. The redevelopment will be two 10 - storey buildings and the volume of floor space has been agreed upon.   The floor plate has been locked down and the overall schematic layout of the rooms on each floor is on the final stages of being agreed with the clinicians. The Hobart City Council has approved the projects and this remains the case today.  With the changes in outputs to the floor space of the project an amended application will need to be lodged with the Hobart City Council.  We are assured that the project team has been working closely with the Hobart City Council and it is expected that an amended application will be lodged in the very near future. The project has a fixed budget envelope and it is essential that we build the best hospital we can within the funds available.  Surely even Mr Rockliff can agree on that.   We have seen a comprehensive government structure that has been created, comprising an executive steering committee, a project control group and the utilisation of the THO south executive as the executive user group. To ensure the best governance for this project into the future, we will continue to update this government structure so that we can put in place the most effective one. The executive steering committee is chaired by the secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services and he is being joined by the Crown Solicitor, as well as the Deputy Secretary of the Department of Premier and Cabinet, and the Deputy Secretary of the Department of Treasury and Finance.   The project control group has membership from the Chief Financial Officer of DHHS, the Strategic Director and Project Director, the Assistant Crown Solicitor and a representative from an external consultant group, Capital Insight, as well as two infrastructure experts: Philip Marcus Clark AM, who has had extensive experience across the areas of infrastructure in relation to large projects and currently holds the chair of the Australian Government's Education Investment Fund Advisory Board; and David Beveridge who has had extensive experience in large projects of this nature. It is expected that this project will have a significant impact on local business. We have seen the $586 million redevelopment of the Royal Hobart Hospital already improving services and creating jobs in Tasmania. The project is creating hundreds of jobs for Tasmanians right now.  You only have to drive past the Royal to see the bustling construction site as the government continues to deliver the biggest infrastructure project in Tasmania for a generation. During 2012 more than 175 tradespeople have been employed on the project, and the vast majority of these are Tasmanians.  We expect that number to double on the site during 2013. Works are already underway or being completed using Tasmanian construction firms such as Hazell Bros and Fairbrother, who are also employing local apprentices, which is fantastic to see.  An example of this is the new Wellington Clinic, which used local architect firm, Tim Penny; building surveyor, Lee Tyers; as well as service engineers, Engineering Services Tasmania. The cancer centre is being constructed by Fairbrother and all the medical imaging works and the ICU is being delivered through Hazell Bros. Local job opportunities have been rigorously promoted on the industry capability network gateway, and tenders have been publicly advertised. Presentations have been delivered at various industry forums to urge local businesses to get involved in the project. Local contractors who want to work at the Royal Hobart Hospital redevelopment are helped to get the information they need to become involved through this industry capability network. This has significantly strengthened the project and will drive it into its next critical phase, which is the signing of the managing contractor and the negotiation of the guaranteed construction sum. The project director has been managing the commercial negotiations with the managing contractor and has also undertaken work to provide confidence that the design can be delivered within the strict budgetary envelope available. This is the largest infrastructure project in Tasmania in a generation and it is vital for the health network we have in Tasmania for the future. It is a very important project and I commend the minister for her work on making sure this project is the appropriate hospital for our needs in Tasmania.

text: It's time for you to be honest.  I don't make determinations about right to information; they are not approved or disapproved by ministers.  That would be entirely inappropriate.  I do not think I was even looking at you.  He told you, didn't he? That is why you are not making eye contact now, because he told you.  You did not see him yesterday?  I am pleased to speak to the motion on what is an incredibly significant project, the largest health infrastructure project undertaken in Tasmania.  It is incredibly important which is why I am a little disappointed that what we see from the opposition is political point - scoring and game - playing. I have lost count of the amount of times we have offered to provide Mr Rockliff and the opposition with a briefing on the project. After I address the substantive motion, I will use the time available to go through some of the very significant work that has taken place and the importance of this project. The motion seeks to refer the matter to the Standing Committee on Community Development to inquire and report into governance administration expenditure associated with the Royal Hobart Hospital, any other matters thereto and that they report by 18 November. I have absolutely no confidence that the Liberal Party opposite understand how to complete a project of this size and how to follow the appropriate processes around that. They have a very unsophisticated set of simple political ploys they roll out, as they are today, but they are reckless and irresponsible. One strategy we have seen is to make outrageous claims about the project without ever checking their facts first. They not only get it wrong time and time again and have no shame about that, but they are too lazy to do the proper research, make the calls and have the conversations to see if what they claim is right. We have seen that before from the opposition. They go out and say something quite extreme, then they check their facts later or have those facts pointed out to them. Mr Rockliff, as we know, has form on getting it wrong and coming to this House and being incorrect. The second strategy is what they call the unnecessary red tape. The trouble now is that is exactly what they are attempting to implement here because they want to duplicate a highly rigorous independent audit that is taking place around the governance administration expenditure associated with the Royal Hobart Hospital that has been completed by the Auditor - General. I would hope this is not an indication the opposition has no confidence in the Auditor - General.  This is an important independent statutory role and we take it extremely seriously. The third strategy is a special one  -  to pretend there are secret deals going on. If they do not know something, it must be secret. The sad thing is, though, that the reason they do not know about them is that they do not even bother to look at what might be on the public record. It is very easy to come out and say, 'It's a secret deal, leaked document', but if you look on the public record you can see that what they pretend is secret is actually there for the whole world to view  -  except for the Liberal opposition, which fails to look. Because they do not do the hard work, they then want to get others to spend time on an inquiry because that is a bit easier for them. If they get other people to do the work they can continue their political agenda, their political attack, and not be responsible for these conversations, not step up and say, 'I'll come to that briefing. I've got questions to ask and input I'd like to make.' We hear it time and time again when they say, 'We've got a plan to fix that', but then when you say, 'Tell us the plan', they say, 'No, you might copy it'.   There is a fundamental thing about leadership in a community and about wanting to be in a leadership role. If you have a good idea it is not good enough to say, 'I'm not going to tell you in case you do it', because if it is that good then go out with it. Get people to adopt it, because the most important thing is that good things happen. If they have good ideas I encourage them to come forward and share them. If they have the solution to unemployment, tell us now and let us get on with it. If they have the solution to somehow getting around appropriate governance and providing a really good structure for a hospital, tell me what it is. If they could fund the health promises they have because they somehow know where there is additional money in the budget, show us where it is because if there is a way to do that we will do that. This goes on because they do not want to do the work. At the same time there is the inquiry. The Tasmanian Audit Office is undertaking exactly the matters that the opposition now wants undertaken by a parliamentary committee, and it will report before the parliamentary committee. This is nothing but a political ploy that they are implementing pretty much through their laziness. They have had a claim for some time that there has been an 18 - month delay in construction. I have been open that the project will take longer than initially forecast. Politically, would I have liked it to come in exactly on the date? Absolutely. Responsibly, am I going to force them to an arbitrary date for my political wellbeing? Absolutely not. It was originally forecast for a completion date of June 2016. Very careful consideration of every aspect of the project tells us that it will take up to 12 months longer than planned, not the 18 months that Mr Rockliff advised the House in May 2013. I know Mr Rockliff does not like hearing this because I have drawn this analogy before and he says that it does not matter. Well, it does matter. I am determined not to follow the path we have seen with the Fiona Stanley in Perth. That project started out with a budget of $420 million and as of 30 June it is now estimated to cost $1.7 billion. So, there has been a $1.3 billion cost blowout. The project was reviewed by the Western Australian Auditor - General, who found extreme blowouts in cost and scope. I tabled that Auditor - General's report at Estimates when this matter was very briefly discussed. The report said the reason the Fiona Stanley hospital has gone off the rails is that they did not do the appropriate planning and scoping work in the beginning. It is 44 months late and now costing $1.7 billion.   I have looked at hospital projects all over Australia. I have not physically gone and looked because I do not have the money to go and do that; I would rather spend my money in health. I have done the desktop work and I have spoken to people involved in those builds. All of them say that, when they have had cost blowouts, it is because they did not get their planning right. I am not prepared for that to be the case here. We have a defined budget; we only have the money that we have so we have to make sure that we can build within scope and within budget. There has been the suggestion that there is not clinical sign - off on the project. I have signatures of a lot of the heads of the clinical departments right here so I know that that is not true. A massive amount of work has been undertaken to ensure the clinicians have been fully consulted.   This redevelopment has offered a huge opportunity for us to rethink models of care for patients within the hospital and make sure that the care and treatment practices are efficient; that they are effective, contemporary, and able to grow to reflect clinical changes in the future.  Clinical sign - off means that the models of care have been supported as well as more technical aspects related to where the place and the specialities might be within the new towers and the decanting strategy, which is crucial.  I am happy to take people through how that will work. Mr Rockliff has claimed that there has been no sign - off to changes in theatre numbers.  However, after consultation and value management which is very important in a project of this size, a new, much larger, operating theatre suite is being developed within the new Royal Hobart Hospital inpatient precinct. The surgeons who head all the surgical specialities have been involved from early in the design process. Clinical director of surgical services of THO South, Dr Tony Xabregas, has publicly said that the three new theatres are bigger and far more suitable for the new technology. Steve Wilkinson, head of the Department of General Surgery, commented on the consultation process, and I quote: A regular program of consultation of the surgeons has characterised the process of designing this new theatre complex. It means that when they are built, they will reflect the needs of the people who are going to be carrying out the surgery in them. This is so much better than having an external team try to fit some generic theatre design into a building designed around unique local needs. It would have been too late to discover deficiencies after they are built. We were invited at key points in the design process to examine and modify the design until it reflected optimal patient flow and operating environment.   I note that Mr Rockliff does not lift his head at this because he would not want to listen to the fact that the head of general surgery says that the consultation has delivered what they want.  Cheryl Carr, assistant director of nursing of perioperative services, has stated that there have been regular opportunities to inform the design which have been critical to the surgical, and anaesthetic and nursing teams. This has ensured specific local requirements have been incorporated into the design. The new operating theatre complex is in addition to the existing theatre complex and will be operational in 2017. The THO, which is the client for this project, has confirmed that these new theatres would allow an additional 50 sessions per week, allowing them to improve from 80 sessions per week to 130 sessions per week. I am advised by THO South, 'that the new theatres are larger, have greater capacity and flexibility which will help reduce waiting lists'. I had just been meeting with the AMA and I encourage him to have a conversation with them about their position. They said that they are very comfortable with the consultation that has taken place and is ongoing. They have acknowledged that it has taken place, that it is ongoing and that they are comfortable with it. The doctor Mr Rockliff refers to under parliamentary privilege is comfortable to have that conversation with anyone around the questions he was asked. You cannot do that by driving through, because you want to meet an arbitrary time frame. Consultation is a key part of making a project like this happen, as is making sure that there is value for money for every single dollar that is spent. We have to get the best value for every dollar. Everyone involved has been incredibly aware of their responsibility that they have to build the best hospital possible. The clinicians at the Royal have been willingly participating in this process with, I think, an absolutely genuine desire to achieve a great result.  I have been stunned by the energy and effort that many of them have put into this. I know that everyone has in mind specific outcomes for their areas. That is completely natural in any building process; you scope out the best that you could absolutely get the best that you could have. Then you work out what is possible within the scope of the project. Those are the vital steps that have to be proceeded through to negotiate against the budget. Our responsibility is to deliver a whole project in line with the available funds. Mr Rockliff can choose to snipe from the sidelines, and he can choose to undermine public confidence. It is very easy but it does not get the job done. We will continue to do the work that we need to do on this project to get it right. In the future I would suggest that Mr Rockliff spend a little bit of time in checking the sorts of claims he makes before he makes them. For instance, last week he claimed there were parts of a hospital that were moving, but that were not. He decided to weigh in with his so - called expert advice on where the neonatal intensive care should be. ICU, which is now actually called the Department of Critical Care Medicine, is not moving. Mr Rockliff got that wrong. There is no plan to move the currently newly -  redeveloped Department of Critical Care Medicine. ICU and the new Critical Care Medicine Unit has had a wonderful redevelopment using $100 million of Tasmanian government funding allocated in 2009. The paediatric and neonatal intensive care unit has traditionally been delivered close to maternity, obstetrics and paediatrics and this is reflected in the new redevelopment. The current space in which paediatric - neonatal intensive care is located was redeveloped and opened in 2007.  Mr Rockliff did get it right that there was a redevelopment there. However, he seemed to be presenting the argument that therefore you did not need to do anything else with them and you did not need to move them again. Early consultation for the current redesign identified some difficulty in relation to that redeveloped space. On advice from clinicians a decision was made to incorporate MPICU into the new tower. Whilst MPICU schematic designs I think have just received their final tick - off today, the new design will address deficiencies which are identified in the current situation, particularly with regard to the size of the ICU base. There was a redevelopment done but the reality is that the Australian Health Facility Guidelines have to be reflected in the new design. They will be and the bays will significantly exceed AHFG compliance. MPICU will be part of the women's and children's precinct on level 8 of the second tower when it is completed. I was a little worried when Mr Rockliff raised a concern that they were going to be so far away and that this was somehow terrible. I had always understood that you should put a neonatal ICU close to the birthing unit  -  that is actually the safest place for it to be, and it is. There is a belief that the neonatal ICU needs to be near the ICU.  However, there is a lot of very developed thinking that it is quite dangerous because the models of care are absolutely different. What you do not want is your neonatal ICU being run in the same way as your adult ICUs, because they are quite different issues. The MPICU will be part of the women's and children's precinct on level 8 of the second tower when it is completed. Mr Rockliff also claimed that changes in the cashflow were to prop up the state budget; that was a line he used. He said the adjusted cashflows showed the project was, and I quote, a 'stuff - up.' Is it a 'stuff - up' to recklessly spend money and not think carefully about where it is? It would be reckless and ill - conceived if I did that and I know Tasmanians would agree with me. We are not putting up a shed on a farm. This is a modern working hospital, Tasmania's tertiary hospital. His approach would lead to a stuff - up, the sort of mismanagement that Tasmanians were used to from Liberals in past years. The budget papers reflect the allocation of funds and show we are budgeting for more than $40 million to be spent in the financial year, cashflow projections for the redevelopment needed to change to reflect the intensive planning, design and review processes. Like all major projects, cashflows are routinely adapted to accommodate detailed processes prior to the engagement of a managing contractor and the commencement of construction. That is not unusual. For a major project such as the Royal Hobart redevelopment, preliminary cashflows are prepared to assist budget development and are regularly reviewed. The Royal Hobart Hospital cashflows will continue to be reviewed and adjusted if required in relation to the project program, particularly with the commencement of the managing contractor. Once again Mr Rockliff has it wrong. I am really puzzled by the public stance Mr Rockliff has taken on red tape, which is to get on with doing it; do not think about it too hard, just do it. We all remember that very famous football motto, 'just do it.'  That is the attitude Mr Rockliff has.  That was it. Mr Rockliff seems to think that is what we should be doing at the Royal Hobart Hospital and that is concerning. Now they are calling for an inquiry. Like any half - billion dollar project, the Royal Hobart Hospital redevelopment project has needed to undergo rigorous independent assessment. Since we received funding for this project a number of key activities were undertaken to appraise the planned approach and this has resulted in an improved project design. As part of the project's quality assurance program, during the second half of 2012 external reviews of the project were undertaken. They provided the project team with a number of recommendations to improve the build design. There has been workshopping with the crucial involvement of clinicians related to value management and, as a result, further options providing value were identified to be explored. One would hope that every project would follow this pathway. External verification of the planning process has been commissioned to provide confidence in the status of planning and design prior to the finalising of the managing contract. These processes include finalising robust documentation, validation of costs and a build proposal that is best suited to the operational needs of the Royal Hobart Hospital. The work includes a changed design that incorporates additional benefits to patients. The project's executive steering group will be endorsing by signing the managing contract and the managing contract will move to a phase of early works and negotiation on details prior to the construction of the towers. These processes have taken additional time but this sort of work is absolutely crucial if you want to have rigorous project management. It is strange that the Liberals, who talk so much about red tape, claiming it holds up projects, now want to duplicate an independent inquiry by the Auditor - General. I also rebut the opposition spokesperson's claims of secret deals. When you are in government  -  and I know not many of you have been  -  as and when necessary, we negotiate with the commonwealth regarding any changes in time frames, as is acknowledged in the project implementation plan signed by both state and commonwealth governments. The Australian Government has been advised of changes in the proposed completion date, as is standard with these sorts of agreements. I will quote an extract from the project implementation plan, page 3: The project implementation plan is expected to be a flexible document that will vary over time to accommodate changed circumstances. However, variations to the project plan that directly affect milestones and their achievement, as outlined in table 2, are subject to agreement between the minister and their delegates. They will continue to be apprised of any potential future changes to the project implementation plan if required. The state government has consistently reported progress to the commonwealth and we will continue to do so. The department has worked collaboratively with the Australian Government in relation to the intergovernmental agreement and this has recently resulted in a variation being made to the agreement. The variation does not alter the intent of the original Health and Hospitals Fund bid but provides for three slightly altered outputs. One, as I have previously advised, is that the redevelopment now has a later completion date, reflected in the amended agreement with the new completion date being 30 June 2017, 12 months later than originally anticipated. Two is that, because of updated planning and generous size of the proposed theatres, it has been identified that seven additional operating procedure rooms will be sufficient. They will deliver improved flow, as they will be collocated in the same corridor and will also connect to the existing theatres in the hospital. Three is that the original intention to deliver approximately 50 000 square metres of floor space has now been agreed to as a minimum of 50 000 square metres, so we have gone from approximately 50 000 square metres to a minimum of 50 000 square metres, which is not, as Mr Rockliff said, a significant reduction in floor space. Whilst the original bid to the HHF projected over twice as much refurbished space than new space, the design will now deliver much more new space with the two - tower design. This supports the development of complete medical and surgical zones or precincts.   All these changes have resulted from the vast amount of consultation within the hospital that has gone on to deliver the best possible value for money from the available funding. This variation was not, as the opposition tried to portray, a last - minute variation. The Department of Health and Human Services has been in discussion with the federal government for many months in relation to the three altered outputs and we have formally reported to the commonwealth about the impact of the detailed planning and design process we have been undertaking in two progress reports on the project. Mr Rockliff made another outrageous claim about fewer beds being delivered. The redevelopment will meet our obligations under the intergovernmental agreement in terms of bed numbers. There will be capacity for an additional 195 on - site overnight beds, increasing capacity from 371 to a total of 566. Further, I am advised by the project team that it is quite possible this number could be exceeded in the final configurations of the project. I take my public obligations very seriously, I take reporting to this House very seriously, and I take having things I am involved open to public scrutiny very seriously, so I welcome the Auditor - General's decision regarding the Royal Hobart Hospital. From time to time the Auditor - General inquires into major projects and, given that this redevelopment represents a significant investment in Tasmania's health infrastructure, it is entirely appropriate that the Auditor - General has chosen to take such a step. I am sure the House would acknowledge that the highest order of scrutiny on public administration and the use of public resources is via the Office of the Tasmanian Auditor - General. The Tasmanian Auditor - General has commissioned an audit on the performance of the Royal Hobart Hospital redevelopment and advised the Department of Health and Human Services of such on 14 December 2012. The objective of the audit is to form an opinion as to the effectiveness of the governance, project management and initial implementation of the project. The scope of the audit is the women's and children's precinct for $100 million, and the Royal Hobart Hospital redevelopment, including erection of new buildings, of $365 million. The audit criteria are comprehensive and include how adequately the redevelopment's requirements have been defined, including the appropriateness of stakeholder consultation; the adequacy of the functional requirements and scope definition; that proper consideration of alternative solutions has occurred, such as the completion of options analysis, functionality comparison, cost comparison and the production of the rationale for the solution; that governance arrangements are appropriate, including compliance with government project governance requirements, the adequacy of budgetary oversight, the adequacy of the establishment and monitoring of delegations, the appropriateness of the risk management framework and the appropriateness of approvals to proceed; that the planning processes are appropriate, such as the adequacy of the output definitions, the definitions of the roles and engagement of contractors and consultants, the adequacy of documentation, the adequacy of resourcing of probity, audit and legal advice functions, and the relationship of the budget to the availability of funds along with the adequacy of monitoring and reporting, including scope, responsibility and progress reports to the parliament. There are three fundamental stages of the audit. The first is planning, which develops a scope in terms of the audit. This stage is now complete. Second is implementation, where fieldwork is conducted. This audit is currently in its second stage. The third is reporting, where the findings will form a formal report which will ultimately be tabled in parliament. The Department of Health and Human Services is fully cooperating with the Tasmanian Audit Office, and supportive of the audit, by working collaboratively with the audit office to provide timely and accurate information and provide an overview document, containing context and progress information to the audit office. They are meeting regularly with officers of the audit office to provide ongoing information and to identify and respond to potential issues where they arise. They are continuing this collaborative relationship with the audit office as the audit office moves into its reporting phase. We need to acknowledge that significant public resources are already engaged in insuring the issues of governance, administration and expenditure, that they are fully transparent and publicly accounted for. We need to do this because we know that all Tasmanians want to see the Royal Hobart Hospital redevelopment delivered successfully and appropriately. The loading bays become absolutely crucial in terms of being able to continue the services that are necessary for the provision of health services in Tasmania from our tertiary hospital. The B - fan and the links are the first bit of work that has to happen. When the B - fan is demolished there will be a space where the corner of B block sits. The very difficult work that has to happen there  -  and that is why some of the decanting is absolutely crucial  -  because it is a blackfield site at that point we need to lift very large pieces of infrastructure over the top of B block from Campbell Street. The cranes will be all through Campbell Street, lifting into that space. That is an incredibly complex and difficult piece of work. Getting the planning right for that is absolutely crucial, not only from a safety perspective, but because it is a working and operating hospital that needs to keep doing its job every single day. Managing that decanting is absolutely crucial. Then we start building K1, the tower that sits within that space that is provided as a result of the demolition of the fan and also sits over the bottom part of the B block site. When K1 is done, we have to demolish building B, which is on the Campbell Street site. That is demolished whilst we have decanted people into the K1 site. We then have to build K2 and the new Campbell Street drop - off has to be constructed as well. K block is a new 10 - storey building that is going to be built in two halves in a 'H' configuration. The 'H' configuration has been done quite deliberately. I know there have been discussions around where the space is and how big the space is, but it is about maximising light. There is a lot of research around the wellbeing of patients in a hospital facility with natural light, so they can see morning and night. That is crucial. When we were designing what might fit on each floor it has been very important to make sure all the patients areas are able to access as much natural light as possible while the storage areas and stairwells et cetera are in the central area so you are not using up that space. One of the reasons we have been able to shave off some of the sides of the buildings is quite important. We have made the space work harder for us by locating the stairwells where we have rather than on the fringe, which was one of the original designs. We have staff able to access all parts of the hospital much faster, so you lose that time and delay in travelling.   In our original plan, a wish list of what you would put on every floor, were training rooms, staffing rooms and places for education. One of the things that is very clear from many of the larger hospitals around Australia, and internationally, is that if you set up each floor and each area completely self - contained you end up with each of them operating effectively as a separate hospital. Mr Rockliff would be familiar with something we talked about at the Tasmanian Health Conference recently  -  how hospitals connect and how you make your patient flows work. The Princess Margaret in WA is an example, as is the new Gold Coast Hospital. You end up running every single floor as a separate hospital, so they run completely self - contained. Therefore what might be happening in ED, in discharge and in ICU, happens somewhere else. A lot of really good work has happened in the UK and Canada  -  and WA has done quite a bit as well, and it is the work our lead clinicians are doing  -  on patient flow. Patient flow works best when the whole hospital works as one entity, as opposed to separating. One of the reasons for putting all those training rooms on one floor together is that when you have staff intermingling and having conversations you create a culture of the whole hospital being one entity. That has been one of the reasons behind that.   We have the H configuration. The first H in K1 is the first build; K2 is the second H. There is a decanting process. What will happen by 2017 in K1 is that we will be seeing that loading dock area in the lower ground, admissions and the reception area on the ground floor. Level 2 is going to house those staff amenities I just talked about; PICU is on level 3; theatres will have an extended access across from DL4; on level 5 we have CSD; on level 6 we have adolescents and some therapy areas; level 7 is maternity, which is coming from DL3 and transition to home; neurosurgery is on level 8; general surgical on level 9; and general medicine and respiratory on level 10.   They will connect with that central stairwell and reception area with what is happening in K2, which will see general medical respiratory linked up on the same access to stroke, neurology, renal dialysis and medical subspecialties. General surgical will then be able to connect with orthopaedics and surgical specialties and there will be therapy there as well, and neurosurgery on the next floor down on level 8 is part of that section. On the two towers are the women's and paediatrics and birthing areas. On level 8 we have the neonatal ICU, birthing is on level 7 and paediatrics on level 6 and that connects with adolescents and maternity in transition on K1. Level 5 will have some more staff amenities and plant. Level 4 creates that whole extension of the theatres, which extend from DL4. As to levels 2 and 3, this has been really important. One of the reasons for the delay, and I take responsibility for it, is that I did send them back because I was uncomfortable with the feedback I was getting on the location of mental health. Whilst there was an option for an eleventh floor, there was a decision that part of mental health could be up on that floor. That made me particularly uncomfortable after speaking to two people in the mental health community.  Levels 2 and 3 will house mental health on the two floors, with that link to PICU as well. There will be outdoor areas where that is appropriate. It is a much safer and more appropriate model of care that will be provided. For those people who are familiar with the existing facilities in the Royal Hobart Hospital in mental health, they are certainly dated and not at the cutting edge of levels and models of care. That will shift substantially so I am really looking forward to those new areas as well, and we have that discharge lounge linking up with admissions and reception. There was a reduction from four stairs located in each corner to those two centrally located stairs, which will make the building work so much harder for us; it makes the space work better.  That has been the work that has come out of the value management Mr Rockliff is quite dismissive of. It said that if you change the way you design it and your location, you can make your space work harder. You can cut the distances that staff are travelling and make sure that people are getting to where they need to be much faster. Far from being a purely budget - related thing, they are about making the space work really hard. There has been a huge amount of work that people have gone through to ensure we will be building a hospital for the future that meets the needs of not just the Hobart community but the Tasmanian community in the future. I do not agree with Mr Rockcliff's proposition that you can just get on with building something and everything will be okay, because we have seen that has failed in other projects, particularly the Fiona Stanley project. We will not be supporting the motion before the House. Time expired.  You have taken up the offer of a formal briefing and I am sure others will also decide to do that.  Once again I offer it to anyone who wants it.  The work we did then has actually informed a lot of the models of care work as well, so it is not wasted work.  If the Auditor - General says that, then okay.  There is a lot of evidence that removing the capacity to distinguish between night and day impacts on recovery times, so the daylight has been crucial in the changed planning.  Even knowing it's daytime makes a difference.  They reduce bed stays as well, so they are critical to free up space. You reduce the bed night stays if you incorporate all that, so it is about a more efficient hospital.  Sometimes risking personal safety.  Mr Deputy Speaker, I rise to oppose the motion. In doing so I would like to commence on a similar vein to the member that just resumed his seat and the previous member that just resumed her seat. Time and time again, there are examples of excellence, compassion, and exemplary care provided to the Tasmanian community by the wonderful staff of the Royal Hobart Hospital. As we see in other public health institutions across Tasmania, we have time and again seen friends, neighbours, or friends of friends who have confronted some pretty distressing and difficult circumstances. Overwhelmingly, the feedback I receive from the service and support that people get from the Royal Hobart Hospital is exemplary. I would also like to place on record my thanks to the staff at the Royal Hobart Hospital for the work they do, not only in times of emergency. Every day they turn up for a shift to provide support to the Tasmanian community. It is at times taken for granted, and the human stories get lost in some of these debates. Our health professionals, our surgeons, nursing staff, also cleaners and people from the top all the way to the bottom, all work in a collaborative way to provide that support. My mother was a cleaner in a hospital, so I have first hand experience. Particularly in the maternity hospital in Launceston, mum virtually knew everyone on every ward and would chat to see how they were. It was all a part of the continuum of care and the environment that they would work to provide. In terms of this issue around the Royal Hobart Hospital, the issue of privatisation of the Queen Alex, as was touched on in the contribution by the member for Denison, Ms O'Connor, is important. It shows that the Liberal Party, not only in Tasmania but across the country, have a certain view about health. It is in their DNA. That is, 'It is not our problem; we are going to privatise it'. You privatised it; you sold off the Queen Alex, and you were contracting out responsibility. We have seen that most recently in Queensland with Campbell Newman.  Campbell Newman has privatised a children's hospital. He is talking about making profits off sick children. Look at the values of people that come into politics and want to be leaders in the community and members of government. If there is one thing that you would want to take responsibility for, I reckon it would be for children's health. I would not be privatising it. I can guarantee that in Tasmania the Labor government will not be walking away from public health.  We will not privatise.  It is ironic that Mr Rockliff is clearly sensitive of that because we have just uncovered his plans. If the Tasmanian community are ever unfortunate enough to have the Tasmanian Liberals in government, we have just tumbled their game in terms of their plans  -  they will privatise. In the first 100 days, you can see it, they will be sacking 500 public servants; they have already said they are going to do that. They are already sacking 500 public servants and then they will be making decisions on health. They will be starting to privatise it. They will be sitting down with all the private operators and saying, 'This is all a bit difficult for us; we really do not want to take responsibility for health.  Can we just contract out and privatise?'.  It is in your DNA. Whenever a Liberal Party has got into government at a state level across the country, you have taken decisions to give it away and to get someone else to take responsibility  -  to privatise and contract out. In WA, Victoria, NSW, and Queensland it is a litany of failure. It is a conga line of failure in terms of taking responsibility for public health. It is a challenging piece of public policy because of the increasing costs, the increasing demands, the ageing population, and the increasing costs in terms of the provision of quality health. It is a challenging area of public policy and the Labor Government will not walk away from taking the challenge.  It is ironic that Mr Rockliff would get up and say, 'He is misleading the House'. It is outrageous. He is claiming we have missed reporting time frames and they have been met; he has claimed that the ICU is moving and it is not. He claims doctors have not been consulted but the minister has debunked that comprehensively today. There was a reference by Ms O'Connor that Mr Rockliff is hardworking. Well, he is definitely hard work  -  not necessarily hardworking. He gives someone a call and gets a little bit of information, then seeks to run an argument in this House or in the community on public health. We know there is a plan. At no stage in taunts across the chamber, or in debates in this place, have the Tasmanian Liberals ruled out a level of privatisation.  At no stage have you ruled that out. You judge people and parties by what they do. Last time you were in majority government you sold off the Queen Alex and look what happened with the Federal Liberals with the Mersey Hospital. Everyone knew it was the worst public policy decision to make. Tony Abbott flew in, in the shadow of an election, and made this disastrous decision around the Mersey, which caused a whole range of difficulties and complexities. Again, it takes Labor to fix public health because that's what we stand for. We know the Royal Hobart Hospital is a very complex project. The role of the hospital in the modern health system has changed dramatically over the past decade. The role has been defined through service and policy reforms at both the state and national level as well as through massive change in medical technology and knowledge. The Royal Hobart Hospital has operated on its current site since 1820. It has been added on and added on and changed and retrofitted.   It is a very difficult site. It is a complex project. Do we have on the other side of this House people who managed major projects before? No, not one of them has, and this is a very complex project. We do not want decisions made with political expediency to get a headline to try to satisfy  -  Time expired.

Sentence:  It's time for you to be honest.  I don't make determinations about right to information; they are not approved or disapproved by ministers.  That would be entirely inappropriate.
