I am pleased to speak to the motion on what is an incredibly significant project, the largest health infrastructure project undertaken in Tasmania.  It is incredibly important which is why I am a little disappointed that what we see from the opposition is political point - scoring and game - playing. I have lost count of the amount of times we have offered to provide Mr Rockliff and the opposition with a briefing on the project. After I address the substantive motion, I will use the time available to go through some of the very significant work that has taken place and the importance of this project. The motion seeks to refer the matter to the Standing Committee on Community Development to inquire and report into governance administration expenditure associated with the Royal Hobart Hospital, any other matters thereto and that they report by 18 November. I have absolutely no confidence that the Liberal Party opposite understand how to complete a project of this size and how to follow the appropriate processes around that. They have a very unsophisticated set of simple political ploys they roll out, as they are today, but they are reckless and irresponsible. One strategy we have seen is to make outrageous claims about the project without ever checking their facts first. They not only get it wrong time and time again and have no shame about that, but they are too lazy to do the proper research, make the calls and have the conversations to see if what they claim is right. We have seen that before from the opposition. They go out and say something quite extreme, then they check their facts later or have those facts pointed out to them. Mr Rockliff, as we know, has form on getting it wrong and coming to this House and being incorrect. The second strategy is what they call the unnecessary red tape. The trouble now is that is exactly what they are attempting to implement here because they want to duplicate a highly rigorous independent audit that is taking place around the governance administration expenditure associated with the Royal Hobart Hospital that has been completed by the Auditor - General. I would hope this is not an indication the opposition has no confidence in the Auditor - General.  This is an important independent statutory role and we take it extremely seriously. The third strategy is a special one  -  to pretend there are secret deals going on. If they do not know something, it must be secret. The sad thing is, though, that the reason they do not know about them is that they do not even bother to look at what might be on the public record. It is very easy to come out and say, 'It's a secret deal, leaked document', but if you look on the public record you can see that what they pretend is secret is actually there for the whole world to view  -  except for the Liberal opposition, which fails to look. Because they do not do the hard work, they then want to get others to spend time on an inquiry because that is a bit easier for them. If they get other people to do the work they can continue their political agenda, their political attack, and not be responsible for these conversations, not step up and say, 'I'll come to that briefing. I've got questions to ask and input I'd like to make.' We hear it time and time again when they say, 'We've got a plan to fix that', but then when you say, 'Tell us the plan', they say, 'No, you might copy it'.   There is a fundamental thing about leadership in a community and about wanting to be in a leadership role. If you have a good idea it is not good enough to say, 'I'm not going to tell you in case you do it', because if it is that good then go out with it. Get people to adopt it, because the most important thing is that good things happen. If they have good ideas I encourage them to come forward and share them. If they have the solution to unemployment, tell us now and let us get on with it. If they have the solution to somehow getting around appropriate governance and providing a really good structure for a hospital, tell me what it is. If they could fund the health promises they have because they somehow know where there is additional money in the budget, show us where it is because if there is a way to do that we will do that. This goes on because they do not want to do the work. At the same time there is the inquiry. The Tasmanian Audit Office is undertaking exactly the matters that the opposition now wants undertaken by a parliamentary committee, and it will report before the parliamentary committee. This is nothing but a political ploy that they are implementing pretty much through their laziness. They have had a claim for some time that there has been an 18 - month delay in construction. I have been open that the project will take longer than initially forecast. Politically, would I have liked it to come in exactly on the date? Absolutely. Responsibly, am I going to force them to an arbitrary date for my political wellbeing? Absolutely not. It was originally forecast for a completion date of June 2016. Very careful consideration of every aspect of the project tells us that it will take up to 12 months longer than planned, not the 18 months that Mr Rockliff advised the House in May 2013. I know Mr Rockliff does not like hearing this because I have drawn this analogy before and he says that it does not matter. Well, it does matter. I am determined not to follow the path we have seen with the Fiona Stanley in Perth. That project started out with a budget of $420 million and as of 30 June it is now estimated to cost $1.7 billion. So, there has been a $1.3 billion cost blowout. The project was reviewed by the Western Australian Auditor - General, who found extreme blowouts in cost and scope. I tabled that Auditor - General's report at Estimates when this matter was very briefly discussed. The report said the reason the Fiona Stanley hospital has gone off the rails is that they did not do the appropriate planning and scoping work in the beginning. It is 44 months late and now costing $1.7 billion.   I have looked at hospital projects all over Australia. I have not physically gone and looked because I do not have the money to go and do that; I would rather spend my money in health. I have done the desktop work and I have spoken to people involved in those builds. All of them say that, when they have had cost blowouts, it is because they did not get their planning right. I am not prepared for that to be the case here. We have a defined budget; we only have the money that we have so we have to make sure that we can build within scope and within budget. There has been the suggestion that there is not clinical sign - off on the project. I have signatures of a lot of the heads of the clinical departments right here so I know that that is not true. A massive amount of work has been undertaken to ensure the clinicians have been fully consulted.   This redevelopment has offered a huge opportunity for us to rethink models of care for patients within the hospital and make sure that the care and treatment practices are efficient; that they are effective, contemporary, and able to grow to reflect clinical changes in the future.  Clinical sign - off means that the models of care have been supported as well as more technical aspects related to where the place and the specialities might be within the new towers and the decanting strategy, which is crucial.  I am happy to take people through how that will work. Mr Rockliff has claimed that there has been no sign - off to changes in theatre numbers.  However, after consultation and value management which is very important in a project of this size, a new, much larger, operating theatre suite is being developed within the new Royal Hobart Hospital inpatient precinct. The surgeons who head all the surgical specialities have been involved from early in the design process. Clinical director of surgical services of THO South, Dr Tony Xabregas, has publicly said that the three new theatres are bigger and far more suitable for the new technology. Steve Wilkinson, head of the Department of General Surgery, commented on the consultation process, and I quote: A regular program of consultation of the surgeons has characterised the process of designing this new theatre complex. It means that when they are built, they will reflect the needs of the people who are going to be carrying out the surgery in them. This is so much better than having an external team try to fit some generic theatre design into a building designed around unique local needs. It would have been too late to discover deficiencies after they are built. We were invited at key points in the design process to examine and modify the design until it reflected optimal patient flow and operating environment.   I note that Mr Rockliff does not lift his head at this because he would not want to listen to the fact that the head of general surgery says that the consultation has delivered what they want.  Cheryl Carr, assistant director of nursing of perioperative services, has stated that there have been regular opportunities to inform the design which have been critical to the surgical, and anaesthetic and nursing teams. This has ensured specific local requirements have been incorporated into the design. The new operating theatre complex is in addition to the existing theatre complex and will be operational in 2017. The THO, which is the client for this project, has confirmed that these new theatres would allow an additional 50 sessions per week, allowing them to improve from 80 sessions per week to 130 sessions per week. I am advised by THO South, 'that the new theatres are larger, have greater capacity and flexibility which will help reduce waiting lists'.   That is what the clinicians in surgery are saying about the changes, regardless of the claims that Mr Rockliff has made under the privilege of the House. Maybe he did not speak to the AMA. I did tell him that they were here yesterday when we crossed paths at the end of parliamentary sitting last night. I had just been meeting with the AMA and I encourage him to have a conversation with them about their position. They said that they are very comfortable with the consultation that has taken place and is ongoing. They have acknowledged that it has taken place, that it is ongoing and that they are comfortable with it. The doctor Mr Rockliff refers to under parliamentary privilege is comfortable to have that conversation with anyone around the questions he was asked. Mr Rockliff was talking about the impact on the building construction industry, which we all take very seriously. We should be driving this in order to meet that need but this is not a case of making a sketch on the back of an envelope, knocking down a couple of walls and calling it a brand new hospital. There are very complex levels of technology that this project will be required to deliver as well as quality and safety issues of the most critical kind. There are matters of the ongoing operations, the decanting strategies and the future needs that have to be taken into appropriate consideration. You cannot do that by driving through, because you want to meet an arbitrary time frame. Consultation is a key part of making a project like this happen, as is making sure that there is value for money for every single dollar that is spent. We have to get the best value for every dollar. Everyone involved has been incredibly aware of their responsibility that they have to build the best hospital possible. The clinicians at the Royal have been willingly participating in this process with, I think, an absolutely genuine desire to achieve a great result.  I have been stunned by the energy and effort that many of them have put into this. I know that everyone has in mind specific outcomes for their areas. That is completely natural in any building process; you scope out the best that you could absolutely get the best that you could have. Then you work out what is possible within the scope of the project. Those are the vital steps that have to be proceeded through to negotiate against the budget. Our responsibility is to deliver a whole project in line with the available funds. Mr Rockliff can choose to snipe from the sidelines, and he can choose to undermine public confidence. It is very easy but it does not get the job done. We will continue to do the work that we need to do on this project to get it right. In the future I would suggest that Mr Rockliff spend a little bit of time in checking the sorts of claims he makes before he makes them. For instance, last week he claimed there were parts of a hospital that were moving, but that were not. He decided to weigh in with his so - called expert advice on where the neonatal intensive care should be. ICU, which is now actually called the Department of Critical Care Medicine, is not moving. Mr Rockliff got that wrong. There is no plan to move the currently newly -  redeveloped Department of Critical Care Medicine. ICU and the new Critical Care Medicine Unit has had a wonderful redevelopment using $100 million of Tasmanian government funding allocated in 2009. The paediatric and neonatal intensive care unit has traditionally been delivered close to maternity, obstetrics and paediatrics and this is reflected in the new redevelopment. The current space in which paediatric - neonatal intensive care is located was redeveloped and opened in 2007.  Mr Rockliff did get it right that there was a redevelopment there. However, he seemed to be presenting the argument that therefore you did not need to do anything else with them and you did not need to move them again. Early consultation for the current redesign identified some difficulty in relation to that redeveloped space. On advice from clinicians a decision was made to incorporate MPICU into the new tower. Whilst MPICU schematic designs I think have just received their final tick - off today, the new design will address deficiencies which are identified in the current situation, particularly with regard to the size of the ICU base. There was a redevelopment done but the reality is that the Australian Health Facility Guidelines have to be reflected in the new design. They will be and the bays will significantly exceed AHFG compliance. MPICU will be part of the women's and children's precinct on level 8 of the second tower when it is completed. I was a little worried when Mr Rockliff raised a concern that they were going to be so far away and that this was somehow terrible. I had always understood that you should put a neonatal ICU close to the birthing unit  -  that is actually the safest place for it to be, and it is. There is a belief that the neonatal ICU needs to be near the ICU.  However, there is a lot of very developed thinking that it is quite dangerous because the models of care are absolutely different. What you do not want is your neonatal ICU being run in the same way as your adult ICUs, because they are quite different issues. The MPICU will be part of the women's and children's precinct on level 8 of the second tower when it is completed. Mr Rockliff also claimed that changes in the cashflow were to prop up the state budget; that was a line he used. He said the adjusted cashflows showed the project was, and I quote, a 'stuff - up.' Is it a 'stuff - up' to recklessly spend money and not think carefully about where it is? It would be reckless and ill - conceived if I did that and I know Tasmanians would agree with me. We are not putting up a shed on a farm. This is a modern working hospital, Tasmania's tertiary hospital. His approach would lead to a stuff - up, the sort of mismanagement that Tasmanians were used to from Liberals in past years. The budget papers reflect the allocation of funds and show we are budgeting for more than $40 million to be spent in the financial year, cashflow projections for the redevelopment needed to change to reflect the intensive planning, design and review processes. Like all major projects, cashflows are routinely adapted to accommodate detailed processes prior to the engagement of a managing contractor and the commencement of construction. That is not unusual. For a major project such as the Royal Hobart redevelopment, preliminary cashflows are prepared to assist budget development and are regularly reviewed. The Royal Hobart Hospital cashflows will continue to be reviewed and adjusted if required in relation to the project program, particularly with the commencement of the managing contractor. Once again Mr Rockliff has it wrong. I am really puzzled by the public stance Mr Rockliff has taken on red tape, which is to get on with doing it; do not think about it too hard, just do it. We all remember that very famous football motto, 'just do it.'  That is the attitude Mr Rockliff has.  That was it. Mr Rockliff seems to think that is what we should be doing at the Royal Hobart Hospital and that is concerning. Now they are calling for an inquiry. Like any half - billion dollar project, the Royal Hobart Hospital redevelopment project has needed to undergo rigorous independent assessment. Since we received funding for this project a number of key activities were undertaken to appraise the planned approach and this has resulted in an improved project design. As part of the project's quality assurance program, during the second half of 2012 external reviews of the project were undertaken. They provided the project team with a number of recommendations to improve the build design. There has been workshopping with the crucial involvement of clinicians related to value management and, as a result, further options providing value were identified to be explored. One would hope that every project would follow this pathway. External verification of the planning process has been commissioned to provide confidence in the status of planning and design prior to the finalising of the managing contract. These processes include finalising robust documentation, validation of costs and a build proposal that is best suited to the operational needs of the Royal Hobart Hospital. The work includes a changed design that incorporates additional benefits to patients. The project's executive steering group will be endorsing by signing the managing contract and the managing contract will move to a phase of early works and negotiation on details prior to the construction of the towers. These processes have taken additional time but this sort of work is absolutely crucial if you want to have rigorous project management. It is strange that the Liberals, who talk so much about red tape, claiming it holds up projects, now want to duplicate an independent inquiry by the Auditor - General. I also rebut the opposition spokesperson's claims of secret deals. When you are in government  -  and I know not many of you have been  -  as and when necessary, we negotiate with the commonwealth regarding any changes in time frames, as is acknowledged in the project implementation plan signed by both state and commonwealth governments. The Australian Government has been advised of changes in the proposed completion date, as is standard with these sorts of agreements. I will quote an extract from the project implementation plan, page 3: The project implementation plan is expected to be a flexible document that will vary over time to accommodate changed circumstances. However, variations to the project plan that directly affect milestones and their achievement, as outlined in table 2, are subject to agreement between the minister and their delegates. They will continue to be apprised of any potential future changes to the project implementation plan if required. The state government has consistently reported progress to the commonwealth and we will continue to do so. The department has worked collaboratively with the Australian Government in relation to the intergovernmental agreement and this has recently resulted in a variation being made to the agreement. The variation does not alter the intent of the original Health and Hospitals Fund bid but provides for three slightly altered outputs. One, as I have previously advised, is that the redevelopment now has a later completion date, reflected in the amended agreement with the new completion date being 30 June 2017, 12 months later than originally anticipated. Two is that, because of updated planning and generous size of the proposed theatres, it has been identified that seven additional operating procedure rooms will be sufficient. They will deliver improved flow, as they will be collocated in the same corridor and will also connect to the existing theatres in the hospital. Three is that the original intention to deliver approximately 50 000 square metres of floor space has now been agreed to as a minimum of 50 000 square metres, so we have gone from approximately 50 000 square metres to a minimum of 50 000 square metres, which is not, as Mr Rockliff said, a significant reduction in floor space. Whilst the original bid to the HHF projected over twice as much refurbished space than new space, the design will now deliver much more new space with the two - tower design. This supports the development of complete medical and surgical zones or precincts.   All these changes have resulted from the vast amount of consultation within the hospital that has gone on to deliver the best possible value for money from the available funding. This variation was not, as the opposition tried to portray, a last - minute variation. The Department of Health and Human Services has been in discussion with the federal government for many months in relation to the three altered outputs and we have formally reported to the commonwealth about the impact of the detailed planning and design process we have been undertaking in two progress reports on the project. Mr Rockliff made another outrageous claim about fewer beds being delivered. The redevelopment will meet our obligations under the intergovernmental agreement in terms of bed numbers. There will be capacity for an additional 195 on - site overnight beds, increasing capacity from 371 to a total of 566. Further, I am advised by the project team that it is quite possible this number could be exceeded in the final configurations of the project. I take my public obligations very seriously, I take reporting to this House very seriously, and I take having things I am involved open to public scrutiny very seriously, so I welcome the Auditor - General's decision regarding the Royal Hobart Hospital. text: We're all for a good retrofit now, though.  This has been a very interesting and informative debate. There has been possibly a little too much politics within the debate, but we are in the chamber. I believe it is very important that we restate in this place collectively that the Royal Hobart Hospital is one of the best public hospitals in the country. What it lacks in modern infrastructure it more than makes up for in the quality of its staff, the quality of its clinical staff and its very strong commitment to patient care. What happened to the Queen Alex was the Liberals.  Unfortunately, because the Liberals made the decision last time they were in government to sell off the Queen Alex and privatise that part of the hospital, the public hospital's footprint was considerably smaller. What is now Hobart Private, which I acknowledge is a good private health facility, could have been retained within the footprint of our major public hospital. It could have been available as part of the redevelopment and refurbishment of our public hospital here in Hobart, but it was because of a Liberal decision to privatise that public hospital that we have many of the dilemmas that we do today in terms of upgrading that site to a contemporary standard. I want to commend the Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services, Matthew Daly, for being a part of that work as $100 million of state government funds has been invested improving the facilities, the amenity and the medical quality of the services that are delivered through the Royal Hobart Hospital. We have a new Assessment and Planning Unit with a theatre attached and a new production kitchen out at Cambridge. We have a new day chemotherapy centre. The Department of Medical Imaging has been significantly upgraded. I visited a very dear friend of mine in the Intensive Care Unit a couple of months ago and I was quite struck by the improvements. The place does have more light in it.  Sunshine and vitamin D are very good for human health and wellbeing.  Yes, I hear you, minister. I have seen the designs of what will be the final redeveloped new Royal in 2017 and  -  that is the first big part of it  -  I have real faith that a lot of intelligent thinking has gone into the design around creating the most healing possible environment for Tasmanians who spend time in the Royal Hobart Hospital. There is a whole body of scientific and medical work that shows if you bring light into the healing environment you will have better patient outcomes. If people can see out their window and have a beautiful view, or distance in their view, that improves their healing outcomes. With lovely wall spaces and art, while they might not seem to be the core business of medical practice today, design is integral to contemporary healing.  It is a more healing environment, a more efficient hospital. People are spending less time in hospital and are able to go back into their homes with that follow - up care that often comes with the early departure from hospital. I have come full circle on that position. First of all, I do not think the state had the right space and the railyards was not the right site or the resources needed to build a new greenfield hospital. The cost would have been somewhere in the vicinity of $2 billion. Many old buildings, whether they be public facilities or private properties, can be extremely well retro - fitted to make them very sustainable buildings. It is a very efficient use of resources. I think a retro - fit, contemporary upgrade and a rebuild on the current Royal Hobart Hospital site is sound. I am disappointed there have been delays but I understand that they happen and I know the Minister for Health, by interjection, has agreed that she has also been frustrated by the delays. How do we, as a state, make sure that we are investing in health and wellbeing? I want to acknowledge that the Minister for Health has discussed this question a number of times, and that there are resources going into preventive health and enhanced wellbeing. There is not enough resourcing in preventive health because we need to be actively working with Tasmanians around their diet, fitness and lifestyle. We still have some of the highest smoking rates in the country, although they are declining, but they are way too high. We still have some individuals and families who are beset by drug and alcohol problems.   Preventive health has to be core to any approach to clinical public health and acute care in the future. Whatever political party or parties are in government after the next election, we cannot continue to shy away from this as a really important health matter that needs to be addressed. We cannot keep building bigger hospitals and hiring more doctors and nurses and other clinical staff to meet that acute end of the health spectrum if we are not investing more in the front end, which is encouraging healthy lifestyles and encouraging people fundamentally to look after themselves.  I do not support the Liberals' motion. I think it is a political gesture. I understand that it is politics, but at the moment the Auditor - General is examining these very questions, so why would we, as a House, move to support what is so clearly a political play on the part of Mr Rockliff?  Mr Rockliff, the first thing I want to do is acknowledge that you work hard in your capacity as shadow health spokesperson. You are a very keen bean in question time  -  you hop up  -   That is right  -  there is a preventive health issue there. Mr Rockliff, just watch yourself when you hop to your feet. I acknowledge you work hard in your portfolio but I think you could be more constructive on this one. First, take up the Minister for Health's offer of a comprehensive briefing on the redevelopment and the process of redevelopment. I think that would be helpful to you. Certainly when I was health spokesperson any opportunity I had to take a briefing from a minister from government on an issue within my portfolio I would take up. I never felt it would compromise my capacity to operate politically. I always thought the more information you had at your disposal the better your capacity to represent that portfolio, so I think you should take up the offer of the briefing. I also think you should acknowledge that your motion is going to fall over today because we have confidence in the Auditor - General and his capacity to examine these very issues you have raised today and it will be a forensic examination of the issues. With those few words, I want to end by thanking every one of the clinical staff, the marvellous nurses, the people who work in the emergency department, our ambulance drivers and all the people who make the Royal Hobart Hospital the functional environment it is, where patient care is front and centre. They do a great job in a daggy old building. Come 2017, when we have seen some very significant construction upgrades to that facility, we will have happier staff and patients will also benefit. I wish the managing committee in this process all the speed they can deliver here in making sure that the project is delivered within the new timeframe. I know there is a huge amount of commitment from within the department and consultants who have been engaged, and certainly on the part of the Minister for Health on behalf of the Tasmanian government.

That is why the Tasmanian Greens and I are advocating to consolidate funding so that we retain control of our health system but consolidate funding to shake off some of these problems we have in our current health system. This is an issue that is faced right across Australia. There have been growing expectations for greater value from increasingly costly health systems. There is mounting quality and patient safety scrutiny and ever more complex regulation and legal frameworks. People expect health care at their door stop and are less satisfied with having to travel long distances for treatment even though the treatment may be more professional and deliver better health outcomes. This in turn gives rise to short - term political vision and decision - making where eleventh hour cash flashes to marginal electorates often are driven more by the promise of votes than the real need or delivering on a more positive health outcome.   Health has become big business. There is increasing consumer responsibility to make better health and wellness choices. Pharmaceutical  marketing is more prominent than ever before and our relationship with pharmaceuticals has also changed substantially. While most changes are for the better we live significantly longer than our parents and they live significantly longer than their grandparents. Unfortunately we are facing a situation where our children, the next generation, could be the very first generation that has a shorter lifespan than our own generation.  Unfortunately the drivers of this in the main are lifestyle - related illness. It is around lack of fitness,  obesity levels, increasing stress and a whole range of things. We have talked about it before and I think we are in agreement on that, which is terrific. I note that we have a preventive health committee and we will be meeting again very soon to have a look at some of these indicators of ill health, and prevention, and try to drive a system that is based on keeping people out of hospitals and keeping well. The Greens believe that the health system needs to be insulated as far as possible from these economic peaks and troughs that we face all the time. It is dependant very much on GST revenues and that people living in regions more vulnerable to economic downturns, such as Tasmania, will not be disadvantaged in terms of accessing health services. The final constraints being faced by the current government are real and extreme and cannot be ignored. I have already talked about a single funded model. How are these changes being proposed right now by the minister and the state government going to impact on patient outcomes? The vice - president of the AMA, Tim Greenaway, is reported as saying that the revised plan was proposed by government for cost - cutting concerns.  The Australian Nursing and Midwifery Federation says that the changes will impact on patient care. Emily Shepherd, who is president, has accused the state government of showing a lack of leadership during the Royal Hobart Hospital redevelopment. Ms Shepherd has said there has been no strategic direction throughout the process and a lack of leadership around the process. We need to keep in mind that I have already talked about the difficulties of strategic planning over a long period of time, on a redeveloped site. Many groups, clinicians, nurses and others consider that these changes and the time blowout are going to impact on how professionals can deliver care to patients. I would like to talk specifically now about the motion. The motion moves to set up an inquiry into the rebuild program and process at the Royal Hobart Hospital. A committee would be set up and report in a couple of months. We already have a fairly stressed committee system I have to say and I do not know if the time frame is realistic. There is ample evidence that our current committee system is not working effectively and not meeting time frames. I have alluded to the preventive health committee established almost a year ago; it has only met for half an hour in that intervening period. We are almost crippled with the committee system. I know Mr Booth and others are committed to the committee system and we are really stretched. Committee members are spread too thinly. Mr Hidding admitted as much this week. We currently have the Auditor - General reporting into matters pertaining to the Royal Hobart Hospital. I am informed that the Auditor - General may report back by the end of October which is before the time that this proposed committee would report back which is around mid - November. I cannot understand why we would duplicate this process and listen to many of the same groups and individuals that the Auditor - General will be talking to and consult with.   We have an Auditor - General report about to be presented. It will be very instructive, based on evidence and inform us about where we go after that Auditor - General report is handed down.  Why not wait a couple of months and use the information and the data contained in this report?  There are plenty of precedents for this approach and for making a properly informed decision.  For example, the federal Auditor - General was asked to prepare a report into the federal government forestry buy - back scheme. The federal parliament waited for the information and evidence contained in the Auditor - General report and then the Senate moved for a parliamentary inquiry, which we saw emulated at the state level by Mr Booth and Mr Gutwein. We waited for the Auditor - General, who is a professional in this area, to gather the evidence, write a report, make recommendations which would then inform us about a way forward. I cannot see, for the life of me, how this is any different in this situation. We have an Auditor - General report that will handed down by the end of October, in a couple of months. If we were genuine about getting to the bottom of the time and cost blowouts and reductions in scale related to the Royal Hobart Hospital, then surely we would use best available evidence to inform our decision - making. Why would we duplicate the Auditor - General's report? Is it not a bit like creating more red tape? It does not make any sense. We would be talking to the same people, using the same processes and same groups.  It is duplication, pure and simple.   Our view is we are better to make an informed rather than a politically opportunistic decision on this. We will not be supporting this motion. We will wait for the Auditor - General to hand down his report and then make a decision, on best available evidence, as to whether there should be a parliamentary inquiry.  That is right. We will be informed by the Auditor - General's report. If the Auditor - General's report finds that we should be having a parliamentary inquiry, the Tasmanian Greens will be the first to support it. I also find it interesting that Mr Rockliff has not bothered to talk to me. If you wanted our support in this motion, at least you would have picked up the phone.   I would have expected this.  If I was wanting your support in a motion, I would have had a chat with you but I note that you chose not to do that. We will not be supporting the motion. text: Mr Speaker, I move  That the House refers to the Standing Committee on Community Development to inquire into and report upon: the governance, administration and expenditure associated with the Royal Hobart Hospital redevelopment project; and any other matters incidental thereto, and that the committee report by 18 November 2013. I welcome the opportunity to speak on this motion the Liberal Party put forward yesterday.  We believe the Standing Committee on Community Development is the appropriate body to look into this matter. It is a serious matter. I do this with a heavy heart because I am absolutely appalled at the procrastination of this government in relation to this redevelopment. I say 'with a heavy heart' because this redevelopment has had a long history. In 2005 it was first announced that something would be happening in this area by former premier Paul Lennon to get him out of a political tight spot, but it is now some eight years later and nothing has happened. Not a single brick has been laid when it comes to this major redevelopment.   This government is all about procrastination when it comes to this development. They are very good at the press release but appalling at the policy implementation. That has been a hallmark of this government over the last 15 years. They are great with the announcements and making heroes of themselves, but rarely do we see something come to fruition and if we do it is way beyond the time frame as originally outlined and public expenditure blows out.   The Royal Hobart Hospital redevelopment is important, not just to the southern region of Tasmania. Of course it is the major hospital for the southern region, servicing southern Lyons, Denison and Franklin, but it is also the major hospital for Tasmania. a number of constituents of the north - west coast and the north  -  including King Island  -  utilise services of this hospital. All Tasmanians are united in wanting a new Royal Hobart Hospital but they have been let down by this government that is appalling when it comes to process and project management skills. Ever since the government appointed consultants to assess the short, medium and long - term needs of the hospital in 2005, the redevelopment has been bogged down with delays, incompetence, lack of leadership and poor governance. There have been decisions made and decisions changed. There have been consultants, expert consultants, plans, reviews of plans and more consultants. All the while there has been a shocking waste of taxpayers' money. Over a period of eight years I would conservatively estimate that over $50 million has been spent and got us absolutely nowhere. Since 2005  -  and the minister can challenge these figures but I am being very conservative in my estimation  -  we have wasted $50 million when it comes to this Royal Hobart Hospital redevelopment, with nothing to show for it. We are still no closer to having a hospital that is benefiting the capital city and the entirety of this state. Most children are taught in school how many vegetables they should eat, how much fruit they should eat, what exercise they should do. The difference is taking that knowledge and applying it to the way you make your daily decisions. That is why this Government has released a new strategic direction for preventive health in Tasmania, identifying the actions that need to be taken. We know what we need to do and we are already applying our efforts to work towards those goals and outcomes. In August I launched A Healthy Tasmania, the policy that will set out these directions. A Healthy Tasmania is the Government's vision for a fair and healthy Tasmania. It is a first step but a particularly important one. It sets us on a path to deliver much better health outcomes for Tasmanians and also ensures that they can take up the opportunity of more fulfilling lives. These changes will help us to turn the powerful tide of chronic disease that is swamping our health system, a tide of preventable conditions created by our more affluent lifestyles. A Healthy Tasmania sets out the work that needs to take place to improve health outcomes and reduce avoidable health inequities in Tasmania. The type of action required is primarily about working across sectors on the conditions that determine health and wellbeing in the first place, and working with communities to develop their resilience and release their capacity to address needs and concerns at a local level. In Tasmania, as in other regional and rural parts of Australia, many of our health and wellbeing outcomes lag behind national averages. We can recognise these impacts on our health system with chronic and preventable disease, along with an ageing population, placing increasing demands for health services. I do not accept that this is inevitable. I do believe we can turn these outcomes around and improve Tasmania's health and wellbeing. With all the community and natural resources that Tasmania has to offer, we can  -  in fact we should  -  do better. We all know Tasmania is a strong and resilient community and we know it is a community that gets things done. Improving health and wellbeing is a complex dilemma of the modern era. In the early days of public health, improving health outcomes was in fact a much simpler affair. In the past, health inequality meant that some communities had poor sanitation. In our advanced society, health and socioeconomic outcomes are absolutely intertwined. For example, the introduction of sewerage systems had a profound impact on population health, and today significant lifestyle factors have dramatically increased chronic disease in our communities. We are grappling with the impact of those lifestyle factors and the choices we make about the food we eat, the opportunities we have to be active and the impact of social inequity in a changing society, so it does call for action in all areas of our lives, not just in the health services we use. It is a complex task, of course, and there is no single, simple solution. Our health and wellbeing strategy, A Healthy Tasmania, provides the framework we need to make this happen. A Healthy Tasmania is about giving Tasmanians and their communities more control of their own health and wellbeing. It is a framework that comes out of the findings of the Fair and Healthy Tasmania strategic review, which was one of my first initiatives when becoming Minister for Health. Fair and Healthy Tasmania recognised that health and wellbeing was not only a case of improving exercise levels or watching diets; it showed us that health and wellbeing is a complex matter and that community is at the very heart of wellbeing. Importantly, the review told us that if we want to make a real difference to health and wellbeing in Tasmania then we have to work across and beyond the health sector and target that inequity. By pulling together, deciding on an effective plan and tapping into the resources we have, I believe we can achieve great things in relation to health and wellbeing.   A Healthy Tasmania lists six key directions to drive our long - term agenda. These directions are to keep health and wellbeing at the forefront of all we do and make sure the decisions we make help Tasmanians live longer, healthier and more fulfilling lives. Expressions of interest have recently closed for a health and wellbeing advisory council to support the implementation of this strategy. This council will tell us how to move these directions forward so that we can give the appropriate amount of attention to areas of health and wellbeing. The council will be made up of experts and leaders from across government, community and community organisations and will report progress to Cabinet. We already spend $15 million on prevention and health - and - wellbeing promotion through population health and across the whole of government and on many other initiatives and programs that support Tasmania's wellbeing. The council's role will be to lead a broader community and sectorial discussion on how we invest our future dollars for health and wellbeing or how we interconnect those dollars that we currently spend.  The department is also establishing an interagency working group to drive the recommendations of that advisory council across all departments so that together the two groups will provide the essential leadership that is required to put the vision of a healthy Tasmania into practice across sectors. It is about recognising that at every level of government and across the non - government sector there is massive investment and engagement of time spent on areas that contribute to health and wellbeing. We really need to look at how we spend those dollars and maximise opportunities for integration and getting the outcomes that we necessarily would like to see from that.  Over coming years we need to find more effective ways to stem the tide of demand that is flooding costly acute and tertiary services such as hospitals and reactive services, and direct more funding upfront towards early intervention and education. We need a strategy that gives us a stronger framework about how we make our future government investment decisions. I look forward to announcing the membership of the council in the very near future.   We are doing some valuable things to improve the lives of Tasmanians. I think we can learn a lot from the work that is being done but importantly we can build on that work. We can do a great deal to help Tasmanians become more health - literate and empower them to be healthier. We need to bring people together to do these sorts of things. We need to concentrate our efforts and we need to make sure that what we do is as effective as it can be. We will continue to work collaboratively with the Australian Government who are implementing measures such as increased tobacco taxes, a national tobacco media campaign, subsidised nicotine patches and the proposed plain packaging legislation. In contrast, as we know, the Liberal Party remains committed to continuing to take donations from tobacco companies. With a strong health and wellbeing framework and targeted initiatives we will do all we can to ensure Tasmanians are able to live longer, healthier and more fulfilling lives. E - health is also a critical enabler of a safer, more effective and efficient health system. Providing clinicians with appropriate information at the point of care allows better - informed decisions to be made about patient care. Health services are delivered by both the State and Australian governments and the delivery of e - health involves the State Government working with the Australian Government. I am happy to inform the House that we are already working with the Australian Government to introduce electronic health records and legislation was recently passed in the Australian Parliament to this end. At the State level there has been a concentration on delivering foundational, administrative and clinical systems.  Systems implemented recently include a patient administration system, a medical imagining system, an obstetric system and an endoscopy system. At the national level, over the past five years the National E - Health Transition Authority has been building foundation infrastructure to enable a national e - health record system to be built.  The authority has been funded by the Australian and State governments and their work to date has produced an individual health identifier for all Australians; health provider numbers for individuals and health organisations; tokens for health providers to allow them to send information securely between providers and to the e - health record; development of standardised terminologies across medicines  -  and that will be extended to other sectors; development of standards for discharge summaries; and other information sets to allow them to be transmitted securely over the network. This will require the Department of Health and Human Services to implement systems to meet the electronic information capture and reporting to support the national initiative and will necessitate major investment in e - health over the next few years. Tasmania has the opportunity through e - health to shape a health care system that is both patient - centric and focused on a networked model of care through which healthcare services will be delivered. Significant improvements to the health and care of consumers can be achieved through investment in a fully - integrated clinical healthcare model underpinned by supporting technology. This is particularly relevant for Tasmanians, as we have noted. We score poorly in many health indicators and changes need to be made to improve our health outcomes. I hope to hear about the success of this application from the Australian Government. There is a whole host of other activities underway as part of the national health reform agenda that is also addressing some of the issues the member raises. For example, we are working with the Australian Government through Foods Standards Australia and New Zealand on food labelling and advertising regulations, a strategy that is most effective when pursued at a national level.  There is quite a bit of debate in the community now about the value of such things as 'traffic light' systems. I mentioned by interjection that I have downloaded the application that allows you to do the traffic light identification. It gives you the red light if your salt level is too high and tells you when sugar might be low or whether it is at a medium level. There is a challenge in that because it does not necessarily give you an overall outcome  -  if some of the lights are green and some are red or orange, what does that mean in terms of your overall decision - making about the food? That is one of the concerns that has been raised.   The other side of the argument is that if you put all the data onto a package that is required for people to make those decisions there would be so much data it would be very small to read and people would probably then not read it, so it is how you find that happy medium. We have had some progress with kilojoule counts and the publication of those and we are working with fast food companies and some smaller companies in Tasmania about what that might mean. One of the challenges of having a kilojoule count is that something might have a lower kilojoule count, or even their entire kilojoule count in one dish, but it does not give you a nutritional value associated with that. So you might be within your kilojoule count for the day, which can be around 7 000 kilojoules which is the average for adults  -  although I hasten to add there are many different opinions on where that level might sit. You could use your entire 7 000 on one item, which I probably will not name in Parliament, and still be within your kilojoule intake for the day without necessarily getting any nutrition from that 7 000 kilojoules. I think that is the other challenge here and that is where health education information has to be so that people understand that kilojoules are not about nutrition but about the energy that you take in. We are working currently on developing a new health service commissioning framework.  That will include a preventive health focus and we are working with the Australian Government to introduce the activity - based funding in order to drive the efficiency of public hospital services in Tasmania. It is not that there will not be challenges within that as our current cost of service delivery is high but it does allow us to focus on those areas to ensure that we can reduce costs where possible. We have made it very clear to the Australian Government that there are some areas, due to the size of our jurisdiction, where we will not be able to be as efficient as other areas. Neurosurgery is probably one of those areas and we would all have to agree that you are never going to get to an efficient cost within Tasmania given the numbers that we deal with so we would certainly be seeking the negotiations that we have asked for with the IPA to ensure that we can look at the opportunities for block funding in those areas and that of course applies to some of our regional community facilities as well. A lot of our community hospitals of course have significant aged - care beds and aged care is a responsibility of the Australian Government but does not necessarily fit within activity - based funding. So we would not want to in any way disadvantage our community facilities that often provide those services because they are the provider of last resort because there is not a private provider who will work in that area. It is important and something that I think has been highlighted through the Productivity Commission Report. We always keep an eye on that because we are the provider of last resort but we do not want to be the provider that keeps the sector out of being sustainable in its own environment as well, so that is something that we need to watch. Across government we have been undertaking a range of other initiatives and partnerships that support better health for Tasmanians such as through Population Health, the Premier's Physical Activity Council and of course other parts of government where we are attacking the prevention and management of chronic disease through programs such as Move Well Eat Well Tasmania and the Get Healthy Information Coaching Services to name a couple. Through the whole - of - government Children and Youth Agenda we are bringing key players together and investing significantly to give our children the best start towards a healthy life.  Through the Social Inclusion Unit we are developing some practical actions that government, business communities and individuals can take to ease the cost of living in Tasmania and which will have flow - ons obviously to individuals' health. Through the Housing Innovations Unit and Housing Tasmania we are investing significantly to increase the supply and condition of social and affordable housing and to reduce homelessness in Tasmania which again will have a positive impact on health and wellbeing. The best way to address ill health is to prevent it from happening in the first place. The best way to do this is to work on the conditions that underpin an individual's chance of achieving good health and wellbeing and this means working within and outside the health sector. Outside the health sector means schools, clubs, workplaces, communities and families. It is about addressing food security, transport, employment and social inclusion for those other things that determine wellbeing and there is no doubt that we all agree on the direction that we need to head in. I will end, Mr Deputy Speaker, with just a couple of examples about the challenge between knowing the right thing to do and being able to make the ease of the decision being okay. The other one is that a particular fast food chain was selling one of its products for 50 cents each and staff were regularly dispensing 50 and 100 of this particular product that people were taking home and putting in their freezers. What I am indicating in this is that they become the easiest choice.   The challenge for all of us is to make the healthiest choice the easiest choice and I really do commend projects such as the one in Launceston where the nature strip trees will all be fruit trees so that people can get local produce. I commend the project in the north - west where people's excess food, the lemon tree, with all the lemons on, is collected and shared around the community. I think there are lots of things that we can do towards making the right decision, the easiest decision, and that is very much the focus. But it does also mean looking particularly at a community and what will work for that community because what is clear is that one size will not fit all and we need to respond to individual community's interests and needs in a flexible way and recognise that may change as the community's demographics may change or as it embraces certain wellbeings and knowledges. I believe there is no impediment to Mr Rockliff's seeking to move an amendment to this because the other motion stands on its own. Mr Rockliff can choose to bring it on at a time of his choosing, including this afternoon in private members' time for the Liberals.  It is not too hard to manage that, Mr Rockliff, if you really want to.  Point of order, Mr Deputy Speaker. Mr Rockliff is misrepresenting the House. Get back to your farm.  Do you think the Australian Government should take money away from us?  With your extensive knowledge of the elective surgery agreement, do you think we are in breach?

Need for economic structural reform within the health sector: -  preventative health models and capacity to deliver appropriate economic savings and structural reform; and a preferred Federal and or State funding model that allows sufficient integration of a preventative health focus. Any other issue incidental thereto. Mr Deputy Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to be talking about a more sustainable approach to health funding in this State, particularly in these times where we have taken a bandaid approach to health spending. We know that the costs are escalating at a rate that is not sustainable and we need to take a more integrated, collaborative, sustainable approach to everything to do with health, not only in this State but also in this nation. There needs to be a focus on delivering the win - win possibility of preventive health to drive the necessary economic structural reforms that would put the Health budget onto a sustainable footing.   Healthcare costs are increasing at three times the rate of inflation and it has been predicted that without action to bring down costs, healthcare spending will consume the entire State Budget within the next 25 to 30 years. It is worth noting that nationwide spending on health is about $110 billion a year, and 50 per cent of that is used in treating chronic lifestyle - related diseases and yet we put only 1.8 per cent of this $100 billion - plus Health budget into preventive health care.  Governments have been ignoring warning signs for decades that the burden of chronic and preventable disease is a ticking time bomb for the health system and the current health funding crisis is partially a result of that failure.   Evidence from 600 national and international studies demonstrates unequivocally that a focus on prevention and wellness delivers outcomes in terms of risk reduction, behaviour change, health costs and productivity. I note that the Australian Medical Association's budget submission to the State Government for 2011 also backed the need for a more coordinated approach to healthcare delivery to reduce the number of hospital admissions, and I quote from that submission: 'If access to coordinated multidisciplinary care is improved, then patients will benefit, the number of avoidable hospital admissions can be reduced and long - term savings to the health system will be generated'. Mr Deputy Speaker, an emphasis on preventive health and early intervention makes good health sense, good economic sense and will help move the State's health system onto a sustainable footing to end the boom - bust cycle of crisis - driven management where you pop bandaids on to try and fix up a crisis every five or six years. I would like to first of all put things into a national perspective. Evidence from 600 national and international studies demonstrates unequivocally that a focus on prevention and wellness delivers outcomes in terms of risk reduction, behaviour change, health costs and productivity. They are: introducing a levy on junk food and alcohol advertising; extending the time designated as children's television viewing to limit junk  food  advertising to children; introducing a simple health information labelling system for food and beverages. I am sure we all go into supermarkets and shops and have a look at what we are buying and we have a look at the information around the nutritional value on the side of these products and you basically need a PhD in science to unravel what it all means and that is why we Greens have been advocating a much simpler food labelling system  -  for example, like a traffic light system  -   No.  That is fantastic. Thank you, Minister, for telling me that. I will certainly pick that one up. Not everybody will have access either to an iPhone or an app like that and there needs to be much clearer labelling in terms of the nutritional value of foods that are sold, and that is for sure. The issue of food labelling is further masked by misleading statements on the side of food products like low in salt but they can be very high in saturated fats, for example. We need to create a safe drinking culture.   Mental health intervention  -  and I will talk about mental health in a little while  -  at the primary care level needs to target those in need, the vulnerable and long - term clientele working within the community and the NGO sector and of course the Greens have long advocated for a national denticare model which provides universal, comprehensive, basic primary non - cosmetic dental care for all Australians. Preventive health strategies should be a fundamental component of our health system.  Keeping people well is fundamental to improving the health of our society. Our health policies seek to help keep people healthy and reduce the incidence of chronic disease in our community. Reducing the incidence of unnecessary hospital admissions through a greater focus on prevention and primary health care will reduce State health costs and keep a check on future budget blowouts. If we put this into a State context, we all agree I think that our budgetary dollars are best spent in preventing people from falling off the cliff, that is, with preventable illness such as heart attacks, strokes, some forms of cancer and many others I could cite right now. Primary health care, which has a focus on prevention and community empowerment in health, is critically important to this. There are, however, some very disturbing trends noted in the DHHS Annual Report 2009 - 10. One of the good bits of news is that life expectancy for both males and females is increasing but unfortunately in Tasmania life expectancy is below the national average and has not improved, strangely enough, for the last few years. The proportion of the adult population that eats at least two serves of fruit per day has decreased. Physical inactivity amongst Tasmanian adults has increased and is above the national rate. Overweight and obesity rates among Tasmanian adults have increased. We know that substance use during pregnancy can result in poor foetal outcomes. There is sufficient scientific evidence available to support this and yet Tasmania has the highest number of people who smoke during pregnancy at 26 per cent, compared with the national average of 16 per cent. The really alarming part of this is that for those who are under 20 and pregnant the rate is more than 50 per cent. Braddon does not stack up very well in some of these statistics either. I am now quoting from a document, 'Key Braddon Facts and Challenges by Our Island, Our Voices' authorised by TasCOSS. It was commissioned by EMRS to do a survey in November 2000. Braddon's obesity rate is higher than the State rate, which is higher than the national rate, at 58.4 per cent, compared with the State rate of 55.8 per cent and the Australian rate of 54.9 per cent. It is all very high.  Braddon's smoking rate of 29.8 per cent is 9.7 per cent above the national average. Many of these things can be prevented.   In this motion there is a reference to donations from tobacco companies to political parties. I would like to read a document from the Heart Foundation and the Public Health Association and ASH. It is called 'Ending Tobacco - linked Political Donations Long Overdue, Health Groups Tell Inquiry'. So often we hear that donations to political parties do not influence policy. I will read this and those who read  Hansard can make up their own minds: 'Public health groups will urge public hearings today, August 8'  -  This is a release of 8 August 2011  -  'to close loopholes in political funding laws to prevent the tobacco industry from channelling secret donations through third parties. The tobacco industry hopes to gain backdoor influence over health policies so it can continue to promote and sell addictive products that each year kill over 15 000 people and drain our national economy of over $31 billion." ' That reference is that the Federal Government gets in the order of $6 billion from taxes on tobacco but the cost to the health system is $31 billion, five times as much as is gained. The Gillard Government and the Greens have agreed that there will be a report to Parliament by October in relation to political donations from big tobacco, with recommendations for reform. That is quite interesting, 'some State Liberal parties'  -  not this one unfortunately.   'Voluntary actions are no substitute for comprehensive legislation to prevent third parties, including fundraising fronts and events, beings used as channels to push tobacco agendas.' Just to finish  -  'This inquiry represents a real opportunity for reform after decades of delay. It is a chance for all parties to protect our democratic processes from the world's most lethal industry.'    I would like to talk a little about mental health, especially with last week being Mental Health Week. Prevention needs play a key role in determining mental health policy. Having worked in many counselling roles myself, certainly as an educator and more recently as chair of the House of Assembly Select Committee on Child Protection, the depth and number of mental health issues in the Tasmanian community have become clear, and no doubt this is replicated right across Australia. The Australian figures are that 20 per cent of Australians will experience some form of mental illness in any given year, with 500 000 Australians having to take time off work as a consequence. Young people living in the most disadvantaged areas are particularly affected. Up to half the inmates in our prisons have some form of mental illness. Some of the statistics I have seen from Western Australia place that figure closer to 70 per cent. It is an unbelievable figure. If we focus on prevention and wellness, keeping people mentally robust and well, a lot of these issues can be dealt with and the cost will not be shifted onto taxpayers. Mental health issues have wideranging implications across all areas of government, including lost productivity, increased reliance on financial support, increased dependence on families and carers, increased pressure on the education system and prisons and many other areas. If there are inadequate mental health support services then people are likely to end up turning to already overloaded emergency departments and GP practices for services. More needs to be done to assess the benefits to people, communities and the overall economy of upstream spending in mental health, especially in early identification and intervention which can potentially stop people progressing to more severe illness and all it entails. We need to move away from a hospital - oriented model to a more collaborative, community - based, integrated system of care in mental health, as we do in other areas. It is good for individuals, great for communities, and a focus on wellness and prevention is great for future budgets.  Oh!  For your information, Mr Rockliff, it is exactly at times like this when we need to take a broader view of health and particularly focus on preventive health so that the bandaid approach that you have supported for so long is not continued and we can put health on a sustainable footing. In response to some of your comments, I point out that you tabled your motion on 9 March this year.
